"Where warranted, we will take action under Singapore's Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and also explore joint action with other countries," said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong.

Authorities said Singapore had put on notice seven Indonesian firms whose "activities caused or contributed to unhealthy haze levels".

Legal experts have cautioned that pursuing companies linked to the smoke is challenging, with investigations reliant on cooperation from foreign authorities.

Singapore has no plantations or forests of its own, but several companies with concessions in Indonesia are reportedly based in the city state.

Indonesia's forestry department said there was a significant jump in hotspots in several areas in six "priority provinces" where 615 hotspots were detected.

A hotspot is a location where a satellite detects an unusually high temperature, indicating a potential fire or other strong heat source.

Singapore's investigations into four Indonesian companies over their alleged role in the 2015 haze crisis remain open, a case that strained relations with Jakarta at the time.

An official at Indonesia's national police investigations agency on Wednesday said it was probing companies responsible for the fires, but did not give specific names.

Indonesia experiences wildfires regularly during its dry season, but this year the blazes have been especially severe because a strong El Nino has brought drought.

While drought contributes to the fires, experts say deforestation and drying of peatlands has damaged previously fire-resistant landscapes.

"We cannot control the weather or the winds, nor can we directly control what happens beyond our borders," said Singapore leader Wong.

"But we will do everything we can to protect Singaporeans, while working with our neighbours to address the underlying causes of the haze."
ir_summary: Four people died fighting forest fires in Indonesia, causing toxic haze across Southeast Asia and prompting Singapore to threaten legal action.

title: Strengthening LGs
text:
THE ECP has done well to refuse to allow the Punjab administration to push the local government elections to April. It should now hold its ground. Four years after the last elected councils left office, the province is still looking for reasons not to hold the polls. The reasons, though, keep changing. In August, the provincial authorities agreed to a window between Dec 15 and Jan 15. Two months later, they discovered that the months of December and January are foggy and cold, and that Ramazan would begin in February. None of this is news. Winter arrives every year, and the Ramazan calendar was not a surprise to anyone who signed off on the August consultations. LGs are the tier of the state closest to the people. They handle sanitation, water supply, street lighting, primary health and schooling, and local roads, and generally keep the town running. In functioning democracies, this is where citizens learn to hold someone accountable, and where future political leaders learn to govern. Provincial and federal parties know this, and many are uncomfortable with the fact. An elected mayor with a budget and a mandate is a rival centre of power. A commissioner or deputy commissioner who answers to the chief minister is not. So elections are delayed, laws rewritten whenever the government changes, and administrators fill the space that elected representatives should occupy.

The Constitution requires each province to set up an LG system and devolve political, administrative and financial responsibility, and authority to its elected representatives. Holding elections is only the first step. Every provincial government, especially Punjab, has treated even that step as optional, and the ones that have held elections have often hollowed out the institutions afterwards. Councils without control over their own funds, staff or functions are decorative. This matters more now than it did before. The debate on improving governance by creating new provinces has gathered pace, and it rests on a sound observation. Provinces are too centralised to serve their citizens from afar. A new provincial map, however, will not help. The new provinces will continue to behave like the old ones, hoarding power and funds at the top. If the aim is better governance, the more direct route is to strengthen the tier that already exists in the Constitution but has never been allowed to work.
ir_summary: ECP resists Punjab's attempt to delay local government elections, highlighting constitutional requirements for devolved governance.

title: No talks
text:
THE opposition Tehreek-i-Tahafuz Ayin-i-Pakistan hasannouncedthat there will be no more talks with the government till the latter yields on the one thing it has resolutely sought to prevent: a meeting with jailed former prime minister Imran Khan. Having handed authority for further negotiation to Leader of the Opposition in the National Assembly Mahmood Khan Achakzai, the TTAP has made that meeting a precondition for a return to the table.

If there is any desire among the decision-makers to keep political temperatures in check, the government will take up Mr Achakzai's offer to reason with Imran. The opposition leader is, after all, a veteran politician viewed with respect across party lines. Unfortunately, it is unlikely that the government is in a reflective mood. It not only managed to dismiss the elected PTI government in KP, but has also had its decision approved by a joint sitting of parliament.

That move has poisoned the well. The trouble is that few, other than those who imposed emergency andgovernor's rule on KP, are convinced of the government's 'security' rationale, which they see as a fig leaf for an overreaction by the government and its allies, that is unlikely to hold for long: the set-up imposed on the province faces daunting odds.

In the four-and-a-half years since the PTI's government in the centre was ousted, its successors have failed to deliver better living conditions to the people. The people have only heard the words 'austerity' and 'stabilisation' during this period, and it has often seemed that the former, in particular, has applied only to the public at large, while those responsible for steering the country out of a protracted polycrisis have merely assigned blame and levelled accusations. Every day that passes adds to the public's disaffection with the mode of governance.

The government should understand that the PTI's protest march and its reaction to it will look like nothing more than a storm in a teacup on the timescale against which governance is measured. It may not realise it, but it has fallen into the same trap the PTI fell into during its truncated time in power.

The PTI remained obsessed with hounding its opponents over corruption; the governments that have followed it have similarly consumed themselves with hounding the PTI out of the political sphere. All seem to be missing the big picture — an economy stretched to its limits and a populace experiencing increasing levels of hunger and poverty while outsized egos clash against each other.

It is regrettable that the politics of one of the largest, most populous nations of the world has been reduced to single-item vendettas. This must stop. Mr Achakzai has offered a way back to the table, and the government should seize the opportunity.
ir_summary: Pakistani opposition party TTAP refuses talks with government until allowed to meet jailed ex-PM Imran Khan, escalating political tensions.

title: CAD swells to $874m in July-Sept
text:
KARACHI: The current account posted a deficit of more than $874 million in the first quarter of the current fiscal year, mainly due to a widening trade gap.

State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) data on Friday showed the current account deficit (CAD) swelled to $874m in July-September, up from $755m in the same period last year.

The deterioration was particularly pronounced in September, when the current account recorded a deficit of $356m compared to a surplus of $133m in the same month last year.

The first-quarter deficit has already exceeded the $391m CAD recorded for the entire FY26.

During July-September FY27, the country's trade deficit increased by more than 15 per cent to $10.79bn from $9.37bn in the corresponding period last year.

The widening trade gap reflects not only higher international oil and gas prices but also a rising food import bill. After cotton, Pakistan has also been importing wheat, while edible oil imports remained a major burden as they reached $3.357bn in FY26.

The total food import bill stood at $8.3bn in FY26, while petroleum imports amounted to $15.5bn.

The rising import bill has increased pressure on the current account despite remittance inflows of more than $41bn in FY26.

Goods exports during July-September FY27 rose by $604m to $8.454bn from $7.853bn a year earlier. However, imports increased by more than $2.2bn to $17.784bn from $15.558bn during the same period last year.

Both exports and imports of services also increased by almost half a billion dollars during the first quarter.

The faster rise in imports relative to exports suggests that the current account deficit could widen further during FY27 unless the trade imbalance eases.

Financial experts believe the CAD could increase further if the conflict in the Gulf persists and international oil prices remain elevated.

Meanwhile, foreign direct investment (FDI) increased by 20pc during the first quarter of FY27 despite regional and domestic uncertainty.

SBP data showed FDI reached $719.7m during July-September FY27 compared to $600.4m in the corresponding period of last fiscal year, showing an increase of $119.3m.

While the inflow remains modest relative to the size of Pakistan's economy, the year-on-year increase could support stronger investment flows during the remaining nine months of the fiscal year.

FDI in September alone rose to $219.5m from $185.3m in the same month last year, an increase of about $34m.

China has traditionally been Pakistan's largest source of foreign investment, but Canada emerged as the biggest investor during the first quarter, with inflows of $229m compared to $225m a year earlier.

FDI from China increased to $197.5m from $121m during the same period last year.

Other major inflows included $83.4m from the United Kingdom, $54.8m from the United Arab Emirates and $25.6m from Hong Kong.
ir_summary: Pakistan's current account deficit widened to $874 million in Q1 FY27 due to a growing trade gap and high import costs.

title: Joint sitting gives blessing to emergency, governor’s rule
text:
ISLAMABAD: A joint sitting of parliament on Thu­rsday approved the federal government's imposition of emergency and governor's rule in Khyber Pakh­tunkhwa amid a strong protest from the opposition.

The session had been summoned to consider separate resolutions on the two measures imposed in the PTI-ruled province on Oct 11, as the government cited the provincial administration's alleged "deliberate disengagement" from the fight against terrorism.

The move followed weeks of tensions between the Centre and PTI, as well as negotiations aimed at bridging differences, after the opposition party announced a protest march seeking the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan.

Opposition members attended the joint sitting carrying placards bearing slogans such as "emergency na manzoor" (emergency is unacceptable). Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif attended part of the proceedings and shook hands with opposition leaders in both houses.

Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry tabled the proclamations and resolutions relating to the emergency and governor's rule.

Earlier, he moved a motion under Rule 232 of the Parliament (Joint Sitting) Rules, 1973, to suspend certain sub-rules to allow the resolutions to be moved. Amid loud opposition protests, the motion was adopted by 214 votes to 56.

Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar, opening the debate, said treasury members were ready to respond to any questions raised by the opposition and explained the constitutional procedure for approval of the proclamations.

After hours of debate, National Assembly Spea­ker Ayaz Sadiq put the two resolutions to a vote as opposition members continued chanting against the emergency. Both resolutions were passed.

The joint sitting came a day after both houses of parliament separately endorsed the proclamation of emergency.

Under Article 232 of the Constitution, if the president issues a proclamation of emergency on his own, it must be placed before both houses for approval within 10 days.

A proclamation of governor's rule under Article 234 must be placed before a joint sitting and ceases to operate after two months unless extended by parliament. It cannot remain in force for more than six months.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said the federal government had been left with "no option" but to impose emergency and governor's rule and insisted that it had tried until the last moment to avoid such a step.

"By God, our hearts did not want to do this," he said, urging the opposition not to accuse the government of exploiting terrorism for political purposes.

Mr Naqvi rejected PTI's claim that the government delegation had walked out of negotiations, stressing that the Centre remained engaged until the end.

He said the government had proposed declaring an emergency in 12 districts of KP and claimed PTI leader Asad Qaiser had initially been willing to sign an agreement, but was advised to consult the provincial government.

The interior minister acknowledged that PTI representatives involved in the talks had taken a clear position against terrorism, but said the Centre and province could not pursue "two different policies" on the issue.

He criticised Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, whose role became non-functional after the imposition of governor's rule, for insufficient engagement with counterterrorism efforts.

He claimed that Mr Afridi had not gone to the site of "even a single operation with the army and only used to say, 'I cannot afford this politically'".

Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar later defended the measures as a "difficult decision" taken in accordance with the Constitution.

He recalled previous counterterrorism operations and the National Action Plan adopted after the 2014 Army Public School attack, arguing that terrorism had to be addressed before political differences.

Mr Dar alleged that certain individuals within PTI had contributed to policies that allowed terrorists to regain space, while stressing that he did not regard the party as a whole as supportive of terrorism.

He also criticised Mr Afridi for political mobilisation while KP faced a worsening security situation, insisting that governance in the province had "collapsed".

PTI interim chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan strongly rejected allegations that the provincial government had supported terrorists and sought an apology from the prime minister.

"The prime minister has alleged that we are supporting terrorists. We are disappointed to hear that. You have to apologise to the entire population of KP and us," he said.

He warned that portraying a federating unit as supporting terrorism could have serious implications for Pakistan internationally.

Barrister Gohar reje­cted both the emergency and governor's rule as unconstitutional and said PTI would challenge the measures at every available forum.

He also disputed government claims that PTI had caused the breakdown of talks and urged the Centre not to politicise terrorism.

National Assembly Opposition Leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai also opposed the measures and blamed "faulty decisions" by successive rulers for the current security situation.

He said the opposition was ready for dialogue on strengthening parliament and eliminating terrorism, and sought meetings between Imran Khan and his family, friends and party workers.

Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas also accused the government delegation of derailing negotiations and said more time should have been allowed for dialogue.

PPP Vice President Sherry Rehman disputed PTI's account of the Oct 3 talks, insisting that the government delegation had remained at the negotiating table and was prepared to continue discussions late into the night.

She said President Asif Ali Zardari and PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari had consistently favoured dialogue, while stressing that terrorism remained a "red line" for the party.

However, she said the PPP would not support any emergency that violated the Constitution.

"If you think PPP is going to support any sort of emergency which is against the Constitution, you are wrong," she said.

JUI-F Senator Kamran Murtaza, who had earlier submitted a resolution opposing governor's rule, argued that parliament had not been provided documentary evidence justifying the decision.

He said a proclamation under Article 234 required a report from the KP governor and contended that no such report explaining the necessity for governor's rule had been presented before parliament.
ir_summary: Pakistani parliament approves emergency rule and governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province amid opposition protests.

title: Riyadh points the finger at Iran amid fresh Houthi salvos
text:
RIYADH: The Saudi-led military coalition fighting in Yemen accused regional actors on Thursday of helping the Houthis acquire advanced military technologies, while Riyadh pointed the finger at Tehran for encouraging an escalation in the long-running conflict.

The accusations came as the Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace complex in Yemen's southern city of Aden on Thursday, killing at least four people, while the coalition detailed dozens of cross-border strikes on Saudi infrastructure.

During a briefing in Riyadh, coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said the Houthis had worked with unidentified regional actors to obtain advanced weaponry, including ballistic missiles, attack and suicide drones, and fast explosive-laden boats.

While al-Malki did not name the countries involved, Saudi Arabia's deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry pointed the finger directly at Tehran during a separate virtual briefing with reporters.

"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthis in violation of UN Security Council resolutions," Dr Rayed Krimly said. "We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran."

"Overall, it doesn't seem yet that the Iranians are able to provide the necessary concessions for a solution," Krimly said.

He also accused the Houthis of refusing to attend peace talks in Oman as fighting ramped up.

"At the beginning of this escalation, we asked them to meet in Mus­cat, Oman, and they refused," he added. "This was the last communication which happened a few weeks ago."

On the ground in Yemen, Houthi forces struck the Al-Maashiq presidential palace in Aden, the seat of Yemen's Saudi-backed and internationally recognised government.

It was the first attack on the complex since Yemen's civil war flared back to life in July following the collapse of a 2022 UN-brokered truce.

Yemeni government sources said at least four people were killed and 10 wounded in the strikes, while officials told Reuters that two guards were among the dead. Witnesses reported hearing loud booms and seeing smoke rise from the site.

Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the prime minister and cabinet members were safe following the attack, which involved five missiles and drones.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had bom­bed what he described as a Saudi military operations headquarters and weapons depots run by Saudi officers inside the palace complex, calling it part of a policy of targeting "Saudi reinforcements wherever they were located".

Yemeni government forces added that the Houthis also fired several ballistic missiles at the central oil-rich city of Marib on Thursday, while residents in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, reported intensifying bombardment and dwindling supplies.

Al-Malki told reporters the Houthis had launched 20 attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh in October alone, killing 17 people and wounding 333 others.

"The Houthis must immediately cease all terrorist operations targeting civilians and civilian facilities, including airports, ports, oil facilities, and infrastructure," al-Malki said.

Earlier on Thursday, the coalition said it intercepted and destroyed Houthi drones launched toward Saudi Arabia's southern region and the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, after civil defence authorities issued a brief early-warning alert in the southern province of Najran.

Al-Malki also announced on the social platform X that coalition forces had achieved the "interception and destruction of a cruise missile in the Madina region".

The Houthis quickly denied targeting the region, but Saree warned airlines that Saudi airspace and airports were unsafe.

"The Yemeni armed forces confirm that they have not carried out any operation today targeting Saudi territory, and that the Saudi enemy's claims of an attack on Madina are a shameless and brazen lie," he wrote on X.

At the United Nations on Thursday, Pakistan strongly condemned the Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia's civilian and economic infrastructure.

Speaking at a UN Security Council debate on the Middle East, Ambassador Usman Jadoon demanded an immediate end to the strikes and backed the UN special envoy's efforts to resume dialogue in Yemen.

"We reiterate our unwavering support for the security, sovereignty and territorial integrity of the brotherly Kingdom, and reaffirm its right to self-defence under international law against any external attacks," Jadoon said.

France's ambassador, Jérôme Bonnafont, also cited Tehran's support for the Houthis as a destabilising regional activity during the debate and reaffirmed solidarity with Saudi and Yemeni authorities as the council considered a presidential statement on the escalation.
ir_summary: Saudi-led coalition accuses Iran of arming Houthis and escalating Yemen conflict amid missile attacks and cross-border strikes.

title: ATC directs jail trial in security breach case against Imaan, Hadi
text:
ISLAMABAD: An anti-terrorism court on Thursday directed lawyers and witnesses in a case against incarcerated rights activist and lawyer Imaan Zainab Mazari-Hazir and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, to appear at Adiala jail today (Friday) for the next hearing after police cited difficulties in transporting the accused to court.

The court also directed the Adiala jail superintendent to arrange a meeting between Ms Imaan and her counsel, after the defence submitted an affidavit detailing alleged difficulties during a previous meeting.

ATC Judge Tahir Abbas Sipra was hearing a case concerning the alleged disruption of a security route for an international cricket team and incitement to public unrest. The couple have been accused of removing barriers from the route and were indicted on Oct 7.

Defence lawyer Aimal Khan Mandokhail submitted an affidavit stating that he had presented the court's order to the jail deputy superintendent and sought a private meeting with his client.

According to the affidavit, the accused said they were not boycotting the trial and wanted to appear in person, citing audio and internet problems during video-link proceedings that hindered their ability to follow hearings and consult their lawyers.

The court was informed that jail authorities had requested a vehicle to transport the couple, but Islamabad police had said they lacked the required vehicle and three constables to accompany them.

Superintendent of Police (Headquarters) Pari Gul told the court that a large police contingent was deployed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and suggested holding the trial on jail premises.

Expressing dismay, Judge Sipra said he had repeatedly directed that the accused be produced in court and questioned why police had not made the request earlier. He said their "actions have completely altered the course of the matter".

Ms Imaan's mother, former human rights minister Shireen Mazari, asked how her daughter and son-in-law had previously been brought to court at 10pm, accompanied by 12 vehicles.

Ms Imaan and Mr Chattha subsequently appeared via video link, and the judge briefed them on the proceedings. Ms Gul said a formal notification regarding the jail trial would be issued the same day.

Mr Chattha said he had no objection to appearing in person or undergoing a jail trial, but stressed that lawyers and journalists should also be allowed to attend proceedings at the jail.
ir_summary: Anti-terrorism court orders jail trial for activists accused of disrupting security route for international cricket team.

title: No compromise on law and order: Ziaullah Langove
text:
QUETTA: Balochistan Home Minister Ziaullah Langove said on Thursday that there would be no compromise on maintaining peace and order and ensuring security in the province.

Presiding over a meeting to review the law and order situation in Qila Abdullah district, Mr Langove said the provincial government was taking all possible steps to fulfil its basic responsibilities, including maintaining law and order, combating drug abuse and trafficking, and protecting citizens' lives and property.

A day earlier, opposition and treasury members had expressed concern over the deteriorating law and order situation in Qila Abdullah, a district bordering Afghanistan, during a session of the Balochistan Assembly.

The meeting was attended by MPA Engineer Zamarak Khan Achakzai, Additional Home Secretary Hamza Shafqaat, the inspector general of prisons, the Qila Abdullah deputy commissioner, Pishin District Police Officer Khalil Bugti and other relevant officials.

Participants reviewed the overall law and order situation in Qila Abdullah. Relevant officials briefed the meeting on security measures being implemented in the area and the challenges they faced.

"Protecting citizens' lives and property is the government's top priority," Mr Langove said, adding that further measures were being taken against those involved in kidnapping, drug trafficking and other illegal activities threatening law and order in the area.

He said security forces were also conducting intelligence-based operations (IBOs) against terrorists in Qila Abdullah and other parts of the province to provide a peaceful environment for residents.

He directed the relevant authorities to take effective measures to improve law and order, prevent crime and eliminate drugs, emphasising that these efforts were essential to ensuring a safe and secure environment for citizens.
ir_summary: Balochistan Home Minister reviews law and order situation in border district, vows no compromise on security and anti-terror operations.

title: IHC seeks PTI response in case about Imran’s X account
text:
ISLAMABAD: The Isla­mabad High Court (IHC) on Thursday granted PTI interim chairman Barris­ter Gohar Ali Khan additional time to submit a written response to a petition seeking a ban on party founder Imran Khan's official X account, adjourning the hearing until Nov 23.

Justice Arbab Muham­mad Tahir heard the petition, filed by Ghulam Mur­taza, while Barrister Gohar appeared in person.

The court observed that Barrister Gohar could have submitted his response in writing.

The PTI leader told the court his party did not cla­im ownership of the X ac­­c­ount in question. However, citing a change in circumstances, he sought additional time to submit a detailed response.

Meanwhile, Judicial Magistrate Shaista Kundi issued arrest warrants for the accused who failed to appear in cases registered against the PTI founder and others in connection with the 2014 sit-in.

Mr Khan could not be produced in court as he is currently incarcerated in Adiala jail. The magistrate then adjourned proceedings till Nov 25 and directed that evidence be presented at the next hearing.
ir_summary: Islamabad High Court hears petition to ban Imran Khan's X account and grants PTI more time to respond.

title: HRCP report paints grim picture of minority rights
text:
LAHORE: The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) warned that religious minorities continue to face violations of fundamental rights, including the misuse of blasphemy laws, forced marriages and conversions, and discriminatory practices, despite recent legislative measures aimed at protecting them.

In its seventh annual report on freedom of religion or belief, released on Thursday, the commission welcomed the passage of the National Commission for Minorities Act 2025 and laws in Punjab and Balochistan raising the minimum marriageable age to 18. However, it noted that the National Commission for Minorities had yet to be constituted, raising questions about the government's commitment to implementing the legislation.

The report said hundreds of people accused of blasphemy remained in legal limbo, while alleged perpetrators of an organised entrapment network had yet to be investigated. It also documented attacks on the Ahmadi community, including two extremist attacks in Chenab Nagar, and increasingly overt attempts to exclude Ahmadis from public and commercial life.

Similarly, girls belonging to Christian and Hindu communities continued to face abductions and forced marriages, compounded by poverty and inadequate police responses, the report said. Discriminatory employment practices, the 'distortion' of school curricula, and the marginalisation of minority concerns in mainstream media further undermine the principle of equal citizenship, it added.

At the report's launch, HRCP Director Farah Zia warned that the state's approach to religious minorities was becoming increasingly exclusionary. Minority rights defender Nabila Feroz Bhatti highlighted the case of Kamran Gill, a Christian medical practitioner from Sheikhupura, whose dispensary was set ablaze by a mob on Oct 9 following allegations that he had shared blasphemous content on social media. HRCP Punjab vice-chair Raja Ashraf said blasphemy accusations had become a means of exploiting and endangering vulnerable people.

Community representative Amir Mahmood drew attention to restrictions on Ahmadis' freedom of expression and assembly, recalling that the community's last public gathering had taken place more than 40 years ago.

Former HRCP chairperson Hina Jilani highlighted the institutional nature of discrimination against minorities, saying: "Democracy should have no concept of 'minority' and 'majority'."

The report called on the federal government to implement the National Commission for Minorities Act without further delay by constituting the commission, framing its rules and appointing its chairperson and members in accordance with the law.

It urged federal and provincial governments to publish annual, disaggregated data on blasphemy cases, mob violence, forced conversion complaints and prison conditions to improve transparency and enable independent scrutiny of official claims.

The HRCP also called on Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to enact legislation setting the minimum marriageable age at 18 for both men and women, bringing the province in line with the laws recently adopted in Punjab and Balochistan.

It recommended prompt legal action against individuals and groups inciting violence, mandatory training for police and investigative agencies, including the Federal Investigation Agency, on freedom of religion or belief, and stronger safeguards for human rights defenders, lawyers and journalists working on minority rights.

The report further called for an end to discriminatory recruitment practices that confine many religious minorities to sanitation work and urged an overhaul of the Evacuee Trust Property Board to make it more transparent, accountable, and representative of minority communities.

It recommended that the federal government constitute an inquiry commission under the Pakistan Commission of Inquiry Act 2017 to examine findings of the Punjab Police Special Branch and the National Commission for Human Rights in October 2024.

The report also called for regular monitoring of seminaries linked to allegations of forced conversions and underage marriages, and recommended that religious conversions take place in court or in the presence of a government official.

Emphasising the need to curb hate speech, the HRCP urged authorities to take legal action against incitement to violence, particularly on social media, while respecting the freedom of speech guaranteed under Article 19 of the Constitution.

It called for improvements in pol­ice intelligence gathering, crowd con­­trol and community policing to prevent mob violence, as well as effective departmental accountability mechanisms to address corruption within law enforcement agencies.

The report recommended reviewing school curricula to counter religious bigotry and promote inclusivity and pluralism, operationalising provincial research centres envisaged under countering violent extremism laws, and keeping interfaith committees active throughout the year.

It also urged authorities to prevent pressure from bar associations and religious groups from influencing police and district administrations to act against particular sects or minority communities.

The HRCP called for full implementation of the Supreme Court's 2014 judgement on religious freedoms, protection of minority places of worship and the reopening of Ahmadi places of worship closed on grounds of alleged threats to public order.

Given the severity of blasphemy charges, it recommended that investigations under Section 295C of the Pakistan Penal Code be conducted by senior-ranking officials. It also called for public awareness campaigns explaining sensitive laws carrying capital punishment, the methods used in alleged entrapment schemes in the digital age and developments in cyber laws.

The report stressed that mainstr­eam media should represent all segments of society, particularly marginalised groups, and stated that no place of worship should be demolished without a clear court order issued after hearing both sides.
ir_summary: HRCP report documents ongoing rights violations against religious minorities in Pakistan including blasphemy law misuse and forced conversions.

title: Trump shuts down Hegseth plan to livestream execution
text:
WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump scrapped plans to livestream the execution of the former Army major who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, overruling Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth on Thursday after the proposal drew opposition from Republicans, religious leaders and the public.

The reversal ended a plan to broadcast Nidal Hasans Dec 3 firing-squad execution. It also marked a rare public disagreement between Trump and one of the presidents closest allies, although the Pentagon said the two were completely aligned.

Hegseth had announced plans to livestream the execution at the Fort Hood military base in Texas, the site of Hasan's 2009 attack. No other country is known to televise or livestream judicial executions.

Trump and his advisers had been unaware of the livestream plan, said a White House official. "I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Trump wrote in a social media post.  "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed."  The families of Hasan's victims will be able to view the execution in person if they so choose, as is standard at US executions.

Some of Trump's fellow Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, as well as religious leaders had expressed everything from doubts to outright condemnation of the Pentagon's livestream plan. Opinion polls showed a majority of Americans opposed livestreaming it. Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of Catholic members of the US armed forces, also raised objections, while Pope Leo condemned capital punishment in all its forms.

An attorney representing Hasan could not immediately be reached for comment, and it was unclear if the scheduled Dec 3 execution date would be delayed by legal challenges. It was Trump's first major public split with Hegseth, a Trump ally. But it was unclear whether the split would politically imperil Hegseth given their strong ties. In a statement, the Pentagon said Trump spoke with Hegseth about the decision before announcing it on Truth Social.

"The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement. Capital punishment in the US already was facing renewed scrutiny after Christa Pike, convicted of murder in the 1990s, survived two lethal injections in a failed execution attempt by Tennessee last month that left her badly injured and requiring hospitalisation.

A military jury convicted Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist, of premeditated murder for fatally shooting 13 unarmed soldiers and wounding 32 others in a medical facility at the vast base. Law enforcement shot Hasan during his rampage, paralysing him from the waist down, and he now uses a wheelchair.

Hegseth had said the broadcasting of the execution was needed to ensure that people understand that  "there's serious consequences for these types of things."
ir_summary: President Trump cancels Pentagon plan to livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter after public and political opposition.

title: What options does Indian law provide for CEC’s removal?
text:
AMID growing calls for the resignation of India's top election official Gyanesh Kumar for alleged voter roll manipulation, a key issue has come to the fore: the process of the chief election commissioner's appointment, resignation and termination. The campaign to remove Gyanesh Kumar from office began after a newspaper report alleged that he was responsible for removing the names of 130 million voters from India's electoral rolls — a figure slightly higher than Bangladesh's entire voting population.

While the Congress Party, India's "cockroach" youth movement and others demand Kumar's resignation, which is simple enough, Kumar's removal from office is a lengthy and complicated affair, similar to the removal of a Supreme Court judge.

Article 324 of the Indian constitution, whi­ch deals with the Election Commission, outlines the procedures for removal of the election chief. Article 324 (5) stipulates that the top election official shall not be removed fr­­om office "except in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court".

In India, the CEC is appointed under the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023. The CEC is appointed by the president.

The law stipulates that people who are serving or have served in positions equivalent to a secretary to the Indian government will be eligible. They also have to be "persons of integrity, who have knowledge of and experience in management and conduct of elections". A search committee, led by the law minister, compiles a panel of five persons for consideration of the selection committee.

The election chief and commissioners are subsequently appointed by the president upon the recommendation of this selection committee, which currently consists of the prime minister, who serves as the chair, along with the leader of opposition in Lok Sabha and a minister as nominated by the prime minister.

The law governing their appointment, however, witnessed a significant change in 2023 where the constitution of the selection committee was changed. Earlier, the selection panel consisted of the prime minister, opposition leader and chief justice of India. The top judge was replaced by a union cabinet minister, for which Narendra Modi chose his home minister, Amit Shah.

Critics argue that this change increases executive influence over the appointment process, as two of the three members of the selection committee would be from the ruling party. As for resigning from office, it is a simple procedure where the election chief or any of the commissioners "may, at any time, by writing under his hand addressed to the president, resign his office".

The election chief's removal follows a quasi-judicial procedure in line with the procedure stipulated by the Judges Inquiry Act, 1968. Supreme Court and High Court judges can be removed on two grounds — proven misbehaviour and incapacity. A written notice must be signed by at least 100 members of the Lok Sabha or 50 members of the Rajya Sabha. The Lok Sabha Speaker or Rajya Sabha Chair examines the notice and available information, and decides to admit or refuse the motion.

If admitted, a committee is convened with one Supreme Court judge, one High Court judge and one distinguished legal expert. The election chief will have the right to defend against the allegation as the committee investigates. If the committee concludes that the charges are not proved, the motion is dropped, and the process ends.

If the committee finds that allegations are true, the report is submitted to the parliament. The motion to remove the election chief will have to carry a special majority (two-thirds of voters present and voting) in both houses, in order to pass. If the motion passes both houses, a formal address is presented to the president, who issues the official order of removal.

The election chief, Gyanesh Kumar has denied accusations of manipulating the voter list during an exercise to verify India's one billion voters.
ir_summary: Article explains the legal process for removing India's Chief Election Commissioner amid calls for resignation over voter roll manipulation.

title: UN chief urges nations to end ‘war on nature’
text:
PARIS: UN chief Antonio Guterres said on Thursday that the  "war on nature has not yet ended" as he launched a report showing the world was falling short of its biodiversity commitments. Nations will assess progress and pitfalls toward a 2030 goal to stop the destruction of nature when they meet in Armenia next week for the UN biodiversity negotiations.

Nearly 200 countries joined the landmark  "Paris Agreement for Nature" four years ago but have been slow to act on its objectives. The pact laid out 23 targets for halting and reversing nature loss by 2030, including reducing pollution, protecting threatened species and conserving 30pc of the world's land and oceans.

But many of these targets are off track, said Guterres as he launched a global report spotlighting the gaps between ambition and action. "It's not all bad news... There is progress, but not enough. We are far from what is necessary," he told reporters in the Armenian capital Yerevan where the COP17 talks start on Monday.

"The report shows that many of the critical elements of progress... are still missing in action".
ir_summary: UN chief warns nations are falling short of biodiversity targets and urges action ahead of COP17 talks in Armenia.

title: 7 sailors missing after drones hit two ships near Romania
text:
BUCHAREST: Rescuers searched on Thursday for seven missing sailors after drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania's Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze and raising fresh security concerns along a vital shipping route used by Ukraine.

Romanian President Nicusor Dan said the two ships had been struck by drones but declined to say whether Russia was responsible, while a Nato military source said the drones came from Russia. "The drones that caused the fires on board two tankers inside Romanian territorial waters were of Russian origin," the Nato source said.

The two vessels were anchored near the mouth of the Sulina canal leading into the Danube River, a major export route used by Ukraine as Russia has repeatedly attacked Ukraine's Black Sea ports. One was inside Romanian territorial waters and the other just outside. The missing crew were among 12 sailors aboard the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader, which was hit 13 nautical miles southeast of the Sulina canal, one mile outside Romanian waters. Five crew members were rescued, Romanian officials said.

The second vessel, the Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J, caught fire after being struck 8-10 miles southeast of Sulina inside Romanian waters late on Wednesday. All crew were safe.

The attacks are the latest in a series of strikes on commercial shipping in the western Black Sea. At least five other cargo vessels have been hit near the coasts of Romania and neighbouring Nato member Bulgaria over the past 10 days, with at least 23 sailors reported missing or dead. Those attacks occurred outside Nato territorial waters.

"The situation in the Black Sea is serious," Romania's Dan said. "Commercial ships are being attacked and sunk. Seafarers killed, injured, and missing, very close to the shores of Romania and Bulgaria. Lives, global trade, and critical infrastructure are at stake."

The interior ministry said it had sent two Black Hawk helicopters to the search and rescue mission, as we­­ll as two ships with medical staff on board. "At the moment, the rescue cannot be done safely because of very big waves," it said in a statement.

Nato said in a statement it was in contact with Romanian officials. It added two other vessels had been targeted in the Black Sea overnight, Marshall Islands-flagged bulk carrier Sea Destiny inside Romanian waters and Tanzanian-flagged tanker Dania J, moored in the Ukrainian Danube port of Izmail. It did not mention casualties.

"Nato will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed," Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte said after meeting Dan and Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev on Thursday.

Romania shares a 614-km border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube, and has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions into its airspace since the start of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The escalating attacks on Black Sea shipping have heightened concerns over grain exports from the region.
ir_summary: Drones of Russian origin attacked two chemical tankers near Romania's Black Sea coast, leaving seven sailors missing and raising security concerns.

title: Zelensky must go, says Musk after SpaceX satellite dispute
text:
WASHINGTON: Tech billionaire Elon Musk called on Wednesday for Volodymyr Zelensky to  "go" as Ukraine's leader, after insisting any disruption to the war-torn country's use of his satellite communications system was the fault of the US government, not his company.

The comments came as Kyiv raised doubts over US support for Ukraine in its war with Russia, accusing Washington this week of helping Moscow by failing to warn it of incoming missile strikes and hobbling Kyiv's military response through changes to the SpaceX-designed system it uses for communications.

"And so the slaughter continues," Musk wrote on X.  "Time for Zelensky to go." Musk earlier said that  "any limits on speed or usage" of his SpaceX company's Starshield systems were  "decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," referring to US President Donald Trump.

He drew a distinction between Starshield, which Ukraine relies on for battlefield communications, and the parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, which Kyiv also deploys but is not allowed to use for offensive operations.

Musk was responding to a post on X by Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said that  "Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h is being restored," but that  "removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense."

Ukrainian defense officials have suggested Washington is behind slower speeds reported on some internet terminals that help the country's military hit Russian-occupied territory and operate interceptor drones.
ir_summary: Elon Musk calls for Zelensky's removal amid US-Ukraine dispute over SpaceX satellite communications in the war with Russia.

title: Deadly classrooms
text:
AT LEAST 30 children, most of them younger than 13, and a teacher have died in Peshawar after the roof of their private schoolcollapsedduring morning classes. Dozens more were injured, some critically.

The victims had arrived at the Al Khair school expecting an ordinary day. Instead, rescue workers spent hours searching through rubble as parents gathered outside. Police say the building was structurally weak and its roof overloaded with additional construction. The owner has been arrested, while an inquiry is under way. These preliminary findings demand scrutiny. So do reports that concerns about the building's condition had previously been raised. In June, 14 children died when the roof of a tuition centrecollapsedin Lahore's Kahna area. Two days later, another schoolroof collapsein Baghbanpura killed an eight-year-old. Three incidents in a few months should be enough to force an examination of the places where Pakistan's children are taught.

Across the country, schools and tuition centres operate in buildings ill-suited to accommodating large numbers of pupils. In crowded urban neighbourhoods, houses are converted into classrooms, sometimes with additional floors, makeshift rooms, and roofs carrying more weight than they were designed to support.

Yet questions about construction quality, structural approvals, and inspections are too often left unanswered until a disaster occurs. The Lahore inquiry found that the Kahna tuition centre operated from an unregistered residential house. Peshawar presents a troubling contrast: according to the KP private schools regulator, Al Khair was registered in March, but technical personnel were absent from its inspection.

If a school can receive registration without a structural assessment, what assurance does that certificate provide? Investigators must establish whether alterations were authorised, who inspected the premises, and whether warnings were received and ignored. They must also examine the regulators' role, not merely the decisions of school management.

The KP authorities' decision to establish district-level committees to inspect private school buildings is welcome, but its value will depend on what follows. The committees have been instructed to examine buildings, identify hazards, and submit reports within three days. Authorities must make the findings public, close premises posing danger, and require independent engineering clearance before they reopen. Similar checks are needed across every province, including at tuition centres and schools operating inside residential properties. Building permission, school registration, and periodic safety certification should be linked, with clear responsibility assigned to qualified inspectors. Owners who make dangerous alterations must face consequences, as must officials found to have neglected their duties. Parents should not have to become structural engineers to judge whether their children are safe at school. After so many deaths, another round of condolences and inquiries without enforcement would be an intolerable response.
ir_summary: A school roof collapse in Peshawar killed 30 children, raising questions about building safety and government oversight of private schools.

title: Diplomatic options
text:
AS Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi movement continue totrade fire, and theUS-Iran waris locked in a stalemate, regional states continue to stress the need for a diplomatic solution to the conflicts in both theatres. Numerous attempts have been made in the past to find a negotiatedoff-rampin both conflicts, but they have met with little success.

Regional states know that the alternative to talks — a fully fledged war on both fronts — will bring immeasurable destruction to the Gulf, the Red Sea and the surrounding areas. The need for diplomacy was stressed during Omani Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi'svisitto Pakistan on Wednesday. Though the visit was of a bilateral nature, the regional situation was high on the agenda, with Oman's top diplomat reiterating that "diplomacy is the only way forward".

Both Pakistan and Oman have played integral roles in trying to find anegotiatedsettlement to the US-Iran dispute, while the sultanate is also a key link between the Saudis and the Houthis. Both Pakistan and Oman know that any further escalation either in the Gulf or in Yemen will destabilise the whole region.

With regard to the Yemeni conflict, while Pakistan has pledged to stand "shoulder to shoulder" with Saudi Arabia, the prospect of a long war of attrition involving the kingdom and its allies, and the pro-Iran Houthis, is in no one's interest. The goal, therefore, should be a renewed ceasefire, which promises Saudi security and an end to the Yemeni civil war. Pakistan, Oman and other regional states should concentrate on achieving this goal.

Where Iran is concerned, it is likely that the US will make its next move after themidterm electionsin early November. However, media reports that America plans on dropping the 'mother of all bombs' on Iranian energy and nuclear sites should be a matter of concern for all. America's aggression has failed to make Iran capitulate, and it is hard to see what more violence will achieve, other than perpetuating chaos in the region.

What is needed is a holistic ceasefire that addresses all fronts — Iran, Yemen, Lebanon — along with a long-term peace between the US and Iran. The US must also refrain from initiating more wars in the Middle East, along with reining in its bloodthirsty ally Israel.
ir_summary: Pakistan and Oman discuss diplomatic solutions to the Yemen conflict and US-Iran tensions during a bilateral visit.

title: Hunger in Pakistan
text:
PAKISTAN'S position as the country most affected by hunger in South Asia is not surprising. An economy battered by weather-related disasters, persistent food inflation, weak growth, terrorism, poverty, and joblessness cannot ensure that its people eat enough and well. The findings of the 2026 Global Hunger Index reveal the inadequacy of our economic, agricultural and social policies. Food insecurity is not simply a problem of inadequate agricultural production, but also of access and affordability. The availability of food in the market matters little to families whose incomes cannot keep pace with the prices. Weak farm productivity, inadequate water management, poor storage, post-harvest losses, and flawed market arrangements have long undermined the food system. High input costs, disrupted livelihoods, and falling purchasing power have made nutritious food difficult for poorer households to afford.

Climate change compounds these pressures. Repeated floods destroy crops, livestock, homes, and rural livelihoods. Droughts, erratic rainfall, and rising temperatures threaten harvests. Farmers face risks alongside costly agricultural inputs and uncertain returns. The resulting losses push up food prices, reduce rural incomes, and increase dependence on relief. Policies that fail to encourage investment in modern farming, improve yields or protect farmers' incentives leave production vulnerable. The human cost is particularly severe for children. The GHI notes that undernourishment has worsened since 2018, and child wasting has moved towards the high threshold. Persistent malnutrition damages physical growth, cognitive development, and future earning capacity. Hunger, therefore, perpetuates poverty and poor productivity across generations. The government must move beyond temporary subsidies. Social protection must reach households that cannot afford basic nutrition, particularly during disasters and price shocks. Besides productive agriculture, climate-resilient infrastructure, better water management, reduced food wastage, and stronger rural employment, lasting progress demands sustained investment in maternal and child nutrition, clean water and primary healthcare.
ir_summary: Pakistan faces severe hunger due to economic crises, climate disasters, and policy failures, requiring urgent government action on agriculture and social protection.

title: Textile exports rise
text:
ISLAMABAD: Pakis­tan's textile and clothing exports rose 5.26 per cent to $5.026 billion in the first quarter of 2026-27 from $4.775bn in the same period last year.

The marginal rise in export proceeds was attributed to elevated input costs, which eroded exporters' competitiveness, and external shocks that disrupted shipments, according to data from the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics released on Thursday.

Textile exporters have already warned the government that exports could slow further in the second quarter if no corrective measures are taken.

Two major setbacks mainly contributed to slowing exports — suspension of trade with Afghanistan since October 2025 and falling exports to the Middle East due to the prevailing war in the region, especially the United Arab Emirates.

PBS data showed readymade garment exports surged 15.69pc in value and 17.38pc in quantity during July-September FY27, while knitwear rose 4.14pc in value but fell 0.46pc in quantity. By contrast, bedwear dipped 0.07pc in value and 0.71pc in quantity.

Pakistan's oil import bill rose 6.50pc in 1QFY27 to $4.02bn from $3.77bn a year ago. Data showed import of crude oil jumped 23.10pc in value, with a decline of 6.87pc in quantity, indicating that the higher value of crude oil is due to rising international oil prices.
ir_summary: Pakistan's textile exports rose 5.26% in Q1 2026-27, affected by trade suspension with Afghanistan and Middle East war impacts.

title: UNDP warns of poverty surge after Iran war
text:
BANGKOK: Millions could be thrown into poverty by surging energy costs, the impact of an intense El Nino phenomenon and higher interest rates, with vulnerable countries being pushed to the brink by repeated crises, the UN's development chief told AFP.

Global fuel prices have soared since the United States launched its war on Iran in late February, with Tehran's retaliations against Washington's Gulf allies curtailing major oil and natural gas supplies.

Fiscal deficits and debt-to-GDP ratios around the world have ballooned since the 2008 global financial crisis, with governments firefighting against a series of shocks including the pandemic and wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.

Speaking on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, UN Development Programme (UNDP) head Alexander de Croo said many developing countries had responded to the current spike in energy prices with blanket subsidies, but a succession of crises had left them with limited resources to keep that up.

"You have to repair your roof while at the same time your home is on fire," he told AFP, adding governments in the developing world did not have time to rebuild buffers or resolve previous shocks before being hit by new crises.

The IMF warned this week that while global growth had held up in the face of the energy crisis, that resilience was highly dependent on the boom in AI technology investments, and poorer countries not exposed to that were still struggling.

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva had warned that "winter is coming" — an allusion to popular fantasy book series Game of Thrones —implying that a cataclysm was around the corner if the world did not prepare for it.

And De Croo added: "Some countries have a well-insulated house with money in the bank. Other countries have a house without a roof and no money in the bank.

"We're stumbling from one crisis into the other, and what countries need is some space, and some time, and access to financing." Not getting the response right could be devastating. The UNDP warned in a new report that about 130 million people were at risk of being pushed into poverty this year if energy and food price increases were fully passed on without subsidies.

People in South and East Asia and sub-Saharan Africa are at particular risk, the agency said.'Difficult to manage'

With advanced economies seeing bond yields surge — owing to elevated inflation expectations, surging debt ratios and AI capital-raising activities — global borrowing costs have been rising.

That in turn, de Croo warned, had tightened space for developing countries to access the capital they needed to combat the shocks, with rising interest rates feeding into increasing debt payments.

According to UNDP, the median developing country now spends about 9.5 percent of government revenue on interest payments — the highest in a quarter of a century, and more than three times that of high-income countries.

"It starts to be a difficult situation to manage, and it takes away all their margin for policy," de Croo said.

The former Belgian prime minister said he would spend the week in Bangkok — where world economic policy leaders have gathered since Monday — pushing for advanced economies and multilateral agencies to invest in economic growth, resilience and job creation in the developing world.
ir_summary: UNDP warns of global poverty surge due to energy costs, El Nino, and high interest rates after US-Iran war impacts oil supplies.

title: Returns filing date extended to 31st
text:
ISLAMABAD: The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has extended the deadline for filing income tax returns to October 31.

An official announcement on Thursday said all taxpayers can now file their returns for tax year 2026 by the extended deadline. The deadline, originally set for Sept 30, was first extended by two weeks to Oct 15.

Meanwhile, the FBR received 943,000 new tax returns during the first extension of the filing deadline by Oct 15.

Total returns filed through Oct 14 reached 6.710 million, compared with 4.993m returns filed over the corresponding period last year, an increase of 34.38pc.

Until Sept 30, total returns received were 5.767m, up from 3.980m last year, an increase of 45pc.

As a result, total tax paid on returns up to Oct 14 stood at Rs66.81 billion, about 14.61pc above last year's Rs58.29bn.

Non-salaried filers led the 2026 tax year. Returns filed by non-salaried individuals, a category that covers traders, shopkeepers, professionals, and the self-employed, rose 46.35pc, from 3.038m to 4.446m. This marks a significant shift in the filing of tax returns.

Salaried returns rose by 16.16pc to 2.178 m in tax year 2026 from 1.875m the previous year. Returns from associations of persons, including partnerships, rose 14.64pc to 74,278 in tax year 2026, up from 64,789 in the previous tax year.

The one category that has moved in the other direction is companies. Only 11,089 company returns have been filed so far, down from 14,292 by this date last year, a decline of 22.41pc.

FBR officials describe this decline in corporate returns filings as a matter of timing. Many companies, they say, held back in the expectation that the filing date would be extended further. However, a surge was recorded in tax payments with returns.

The FBR attributes the overall rise in tax return filings to three factors. First, data from banks, property registries, vehicle registration records, and withholding statements are now matched against tax returns to identify people with taxable capacity who have not filed.

The second is a simpler return that enables most salaried individuals and small businesses to file without professional assistance. The third is enforcement: those who fail to file now face restrictions on major economic transactions.
ir_summary: Pakistan's tax authority extends income tax return filing deadline to October 31 and reports increased tax collection.

title: Two firms ink MoU for Rs20bn gas investment
text:
ISLAMABAD: Shaheen Energy (Pvt) Ltd (SEPL) and Anton Oilfield Services Group, China, have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to explore significant investment opportunities in Pakistan's gas sector under the government's 35pc third-party gas sale framework.

Both companies intend to undertake an investment programme of about Rs20 billion over the next three to five years, focusing on Pakistan's policy reforms that have opened new opportunities in the domestic gas market and upstream gas sector (EPC) projects, according to a statement by Shaheen Energy.

Under the amended Pet­­roleum (Exploration & Production) Policy 2012, exploration and production (E&P) companies can sell up to 35pc of their share of pipeline-specification gas to third-party buyers holding a licence from the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority through a competitive process.

The policy amendment was introduced through a statutory regulatory order in 2024. The framework represents a significant shift in Pakistan's gas sector, supporting greater commercial flexibility for eligible gas producers and creating opportunities for private investment in gas processing, transportatio­­­n, and supply infrastructure.

The Karachi-based SEPL is one of the leading ene­rgy companies in the country, engaged in developing and operating low-pressure gas facilities for the processing and utilisation of natural gas and flare gas. The company specialises in gas processing, cle­aning, purificati­on, dehydration and compression, making gas suitable for supply to industrial and commercial consumers.
ir_summary: Chinese and Pakistani firms sign $20 billion gas investment deal under Pakistan's new energy policy reforms.

title: PM rejects LPG auction sans legal cover, policy
text:
ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has rejected a move by the Petroleum Division to auction liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) produced by state-owned entities (SOEs) in the absence of a legal and policy framework.

The prime minister suggested there should be a comprehensive policy change, backed by legal and regulatory framework, before any transaction is executed so that unnecessary controversies were avoided, an official toldDawn.

PM Shehbaz declined to approve any interim measures. As a result, the simultaneous auctions conducted by three major LPG producers in the public sector on Aug 10 would not go ahead, he added.

The approval of the bidding results was estimated to jack up LPG prices by at least 15 per cent on top of higher winter prices. The proposal would have linked the producer price of locally produced LPG to import parity and widened the margins allowed to marketing companies and distributors.

It would have had a net impact of Rs77, 000 per tonne, or around Rs900 for a domestic cylinder of 11.8kg.

A domestic cylinder changes hands at around Rs5,000 against the OGRA's notified maximum of Rs3,296, a premium of roughly Rs1,700, or 52pc. This is mainly due to supply squeeze on two fronts and the authorities' refusal to address the issue.

Land route volumes through Taftan border remain negligible, while LPG totalling over 25,000 tonnes is backed up at Rahimdan, near Gwadar. Each bowser now waits about a month to be decanted and cleared at the Gwadar terminal, a delay industry officials say has pushed freight costs from $100 a tonne to $400.

The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has curtailed imports, leaving Oman as the principal alternative source. Correspondence seen by Dawn suggests that the Foreign Office, at the Petroleum Division's request, had approached Oman for cargoes from OQ Trading, the state-owned supplier.

Insiders suggest that before the petroleum authorities could make a timely decision, OQ Trading instead committed its available volumes to a single private buyer on commercial terms. This is feeding the black market and price escalation in the open market.

Informed sources said the storage at both LPG terminals at Port Qasim was full to capacity, meaning that the shortage was an artificial phenomenon given the fact that stocks should be on the daily reporting dashboard of the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra). Weak enforcement is also a cause, they added.

The sources said police had reported loaded LPG bowsers parked in some areas, creating security and safety risks on highways.

On the instructions of the petroleum division, the three SOEs carried out auctions on Aug 10 simultaneously. The highest bidder offered Rs205 million for supply of a lot over three years. One lot was of five tonnes a day.

The country's total LPG requirement fluctuates between 1.4 and two million tonnes. More than half of it is imported.

Some existing LPG stakeholders, fearing loss of business and market competition, are already in the court against the bidding process on grounds that existing policies and rules provide no such arrangement.

The Petroleum Division and its entities are believed to have held multiple sessions with the Attorney General for Pakistan to push for speedy judicial proceedings.

Under the directives of Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik, the four public sector entities — Oil & Gas Development Company Ltd, Pakistan Petroleum Limited, Pak-Arab Refinery Company and Govt Holdings Pvt Limited — were required to offer standardised lots of five tonnes each on pilot basis to replace "the existing quota-based system".

The signature bonus adds close to 15pc on top of the last price notified by Ogra at around Rs3,296 per 11.8kg cylinder.
ir_summary: Pakistani PM rejects LPG auction without legal framework, halting price increases and requiring policy changes.

title: Sindh woos Chinese investors
text:
SHANGHAI: Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah has made a strong case for Chinese investment in the province, highlighting its strategic location, extensive sea and air connectivity, competitive labour costs and skilled workforce.

Addressing the second Sindh Invest­ment Conference, held in Shanghai after a 12-year hiatus, Mr Shah said the moot would usher in a new era of Chinese investment, job creation, and industrial modernisation in the province.

Mr Shah also presented the Dhabeji Special Economic Zone as a flagship opportunity for Chinese and other international investors seeking a cost-effective base for manufacturing and export-oriented businesses.

The proposed industrial clusters at Dhabeji include automotive and auto parts, light engineering, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, consumer electronics, steel and foundries, warehousing, construction materials, textiles and garments.

The day-long moot was attended by around 400 delegates, including investors, business leaders and representatives of Chinese companies and financial institutions.

The conference featured presentations on major sectors, networking sessions and the signing of 34 memoranda of understanding involving government-to-government (G2G) and business-to-business (B2B) cooperation.

The chief minister said Sindh was ready to become a natural partner for Chinese investors seeking scale, connectivity and government-backed support. He said the provincial government was committed to facilitating foreign investment and ensuring that agreements translated into practical projects.

"Sindh offers a cost-effective environment for investment that compares favourably with many countries around the world," Mr Shah said, emphasising the province's potential to attract foreign direct investment and strengthen international trade partnerships.

He said Sindh combines Pakistan's largest commercial city, two major seaports, extensive industrial capacity, substantial energy and mineral resources, a large agricultural base and several investment platforms linked to the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor.

Speaking to the media after the conference, Mr Shah said the 12-year gap was used effectively to prepare Sindh's infrastructure, policy framework, and workforce to absorb high-value international investments.

Highlighting the tangible outcomes of the five-day visit to China, Mr Shah announced that Sindh government entities and Chinese enterprises have signed 34 memoranda of understanding (MoUs), alongside numerous agreements between private-sector business entities from both sides.

He emphasised that these MoUs are not merely symbolic but are underpinned by rigorous prior groundwork, ensuring their swift translation into operational projects. Major sectors identified for enhanced bilateral cooperation include Thar Coal utilisation, electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing and the establishment of charging stations, renewable energy (wind and solar), modern agriculture, and digital transformation.

Unveiling futuristic economic plans, the chief minister noted immense potential for cooperation in Artificial Intelli­gence, large data processing, and establishing state-of-the-art data centres.

The chief minister said Chinese manufacturers could produce goods in Sindh, use the province's energy and industrial inputs, and transport finished products through Karachi Port and Port Qasim.

He also highlighted Sindh's 350-kilometre coastline, access to major trade routes, and proximity to markets in Central Asia, the Middle East, and Africa.
ir_summary: Sindh Chief Minister promotes Chinese investment in the province at a conference in Shanghai, highlighting economic opportunities and signing MOUs.

title: Roadmap set to boost trade with Malaysia
text:
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan and Malaysia on Friday agreed on a roadmap to deepen trade and investment relations, identifying key areas of cooperation at a business conference.

Malaysian High Commissioner Dato Mohammad Azhar Mazlan, who led the 'Malaysia-Pakistan Business Engagement 2026', said bilateral trade could be increased substantially from $1.5 billion to $5bn through enhanced commercial engagement and greater private sector participation.

He stressed the need to translate the longstanding friendship into stronger trade and investment partnerships, noting Pakistan's importance as a major South Asian trading partner.

He identified artificial intelligence, education, manufacturing and services as promising areas for collaboration, noting that Pakistan's geographical position as a gateway to Central Asian markets and its young population were major strengths.

Referring to opportunities in the edible oil and halal products sectors, he encouraged Pakistani businesses to explore Malaysia, citing Pakistani investment in halal gelatine production there as an example of successful cross-border ventures. He said a win-win approach should remain central to economic engagement.

Minister for Investment Qaiser Ahmed Sheikh said Pakistan and Malaysia shared considerable potential to expand commercial engagement, develop joint ventures and strengthen their presence in regional and global markets.

He identified information technology, artificial intelligence, advanced technology, manufacturing, value-added industries, mining and minerals, agriculture, food processing and halal products as sectors offering substantial potential for joint ventures.

He said Malaysia's technological expertise could complement Pakistan's natural resources, workforce and large consumer market. Pakistan, he added, welcomed high-quality Malaysian investment that contributes to industrial development, technology transfer, employment generation and export growth.
ir_summary: Pakistan and Malaysia agree on a roadmap to boost bilateral trade and investment, targeting growth from $1.5bn to $5bn.

title: Short-term inflation surges 11.38pc
text:
ISLAMABAD: Short-term inflation rose by 11.38 per cent year-on-year in the week ending Oct 15, driven largely by higher food prices, according to official data released by the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics on Friday.

Of the 51 essential items monitored during the week, prices of 23 commodities increased, while seven declined, the data showed. Meanwhile, the prices of 21 items remained unchanged from the previous week.

Short-term inflation has remained in double digits for several consecutive weeks, largely due to persistent increases in petroleum prices.

The Sensitive Price Index (SPI), which tracks short-term inflation, slightly fell 0.04pc week-on-week, reflecting price fluctuations in both food and non-food items.

Unwilling to ease the petroleum levy, the government has continued to raise petrol and diesel prices daily. The surge in energy costs is not only fuelling inflationary pressures but also indirectly boosting sales tax collections through higher prices of goods and services.

This is cost-push inflation, in which rising energy costs are followed by increases in food prices. As a result, households are under pressure from higher consumer prices.

The items whose prices increased the most over the previous week included pulse gram (4.97pc), wheat flour (3.36pc), chicken (3.31pc), eggs (0.99pc), pulse mash (0.98pc), pulse masoor (0.95pc), firewood (0.69pc), shirting (0.58pc), cooked daal (0.55pc), diesel (0.47pc), LPG (0.42pc) and tea prepared (0.28pc).

The items whose prices declined week-on-week included tomatoes (23.05pc), onions (4.90pc), bananas (2.59pc), petrol (0.70pc), rice basmati broken (0.65pc), sugar (0.62pc) and gur (0.36pc).

On an annual basis, the items that recorded the highest price increases included onions (75.19pc), LPG (68.95pc), electricity for Q1 (58.59pc), petrol (49.60pc), diesel (43.98pc), wheat flour (35.13pc), chicken (20.77pc), chilies powder (15.55pc), mutton (14.90pc), beef (12.27pc), bread plain (9.02pc) and tea prepared (8.36pc).

In contrast, tomatoe prices fell by 63.65pc, followed by potatoes (39.93pc), sugar (23.20pc), eggs (19.83pc), salt powder (14.86pc), pulse masoor (8.97pc), gur (8.92pc) and pulse moong (7.83pc).
ir_summary: Pakistan's short-term inflation rose 11.38% due to higher food and energy prices, with government petroleum policies contributing to cost-push inflation.

title: 20 local IT firms attend TechCrunch
text:
WASHINGTON: Pakis­tan showcased about 20 technology companies at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco, seeking to expand its tech industry's international reach, attract investment, and strengthen commercial ties with the US.

Pakistan's Ambassador to the US, Rizwan Saeed Sheikh, urged participating companies to leverage their presence in Silicon Valley to build lasting commercial partnerships and explore investment opportunities in the US market.

He also assured them of the full support of Pakistan's diplomatic missions in the United States for building business connections with American partners, according to a press release from the Embassy of Pakistan in Washington.

The ambassador highlighted the growing capabilities of Pakistan's technology industry and emphasised the importance of strengthening Pakistan-US cooperation in information technology, innovation and digital entrepreneurship.

He encouraged companies to position Pakistan as a competitive, reliable partner in the global digital economy. The Pakistan Pavilion at the three-day event, held from Oct 13 to 15 at Moscone West in San Francisco, featured around 20 tech showcasing their products, innovative solutions across various technology sectors.

During his interaction with company representatives on Thursday, Rizwan Sheikh was briefed on their products and efforts to expand their presence in the US market.

TechCrunch Disrupt is a major technology and start-up conference that brings together early-stage founders, entrepreneurs, software professionals, venture capitalists and industry leaders.
ir_summary: Pakistan showcases 20 tech firms at US conference to boost investment and trade ties with America.

title: ‘Pakistan among 10 states bearing brunt of hunger crisis’
text:
