Trump announced the ban in September on his social media platform, saying CNN, Politico, and MS NOW "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States." The Justice Department has emphasised Trump's contention that the ban is legally justified on national security grounds.

The outlets have said the revocation of their White House passes was unlawful retaliation for their news coverage and accused the Trump administration of manufacturing meritless national security concerns to justify the ban.

The outlets said in a lawsuit that the ban violated the US Constitution's First Amendment protections for freedom of speech and a free press, as well as their rights to due process, meaning fair treatment from the government.

The White House on Sept 24 reinstated the CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists after Kelly decided the ban "likely violated their constitutional due process rights," and order­­ed their access immediately restored.

The judge held a hearing on Oct 8 to hear arguments by the news outlets and the Justice Department over whether to extend the protection for the journalists against being barred from the White House. The Justice Department defended the bans as fair and justified.

"Here we have the unusual situation where the president himself has said he wants to chill speech. He wan­ts to coerce better coverage," Theod­ore Boutrous, an attorney for the outlets, told Kelly during the hearing.

"CNN, MS NOW and Politico eng­aged in apparently indefensible conduct," Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik said. The legal battle is being waged just weeks before the Nov 3 US midterm elections in which Trump's fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Cong­ress. Trump's job approval ratings are at record lows in opinion polls amid concerns over issues such as inflation and the Iran war.
ir_summary: US judge extends White House access for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, ruling Trump's ban likely unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination.

title: Global deforestation slowed last year, except in Congo basin: study
text:
PARIS: Deforestation slowed worldwide last year, but the improvement is unlikely to last as the situation deteriorates in Central Africa and an exceptionally strong El Nino weather pattern intensifies, a new study said on Wednesday.

Seven million hectares of forest — roughly the size of the Republic of Ireland — were permanently destroyed in 2025, a 15-percent drop from the previous year, according to the annual Forest Declaration Assessment.

The slowdown, however, is not enough to keep the world from missing a pledge to end deforestation by 2030, according to the report, which was drafted by a coalition of research groups and non-governmental organisations.

The 2025 figure is "encouraging but so far it's the exception, not a new trajectory", Erin Matson, the study's co-author and lead consultant at advisory group Climate Focus, said in a media briefing. To meet the target, agreed at the United Nations' COP26 climate talks in 2021, deforestation would have to fall by around one million hectares per year.

Clearing forests for agriculture or mining operations remains the leading driver of deforestation. Last year's improvement was due in part to progress in Latin America, with a 33-pc drop in what has historically been the world's deforestation "hot spot", according to the study. The authors pointed particularly to Brazil's deforestation action plan and increased enforcement in the country's Amazon.

Progress in the region, however, "rests heavily on the choices of a sm­­all number of governments and re­m­­ains highly vulnerable" to recent and upcoming elections across the Ama­zon basin. Brazil's left-wing leader, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva — who has vowed to end illegal deforestation by 2030 — faces populist right Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in a runoff presidential election on Oct 25.

Deforestation had surged under the administration of Bolsonaro's father, far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro. Progress could also be threatened in Colombia and Peru, where hard-right presidents were recently elected, according to the experts.

Across the Atlantic in Africa, the situation deteriorated in the Congo basin, where rainforest loss reached 2.4 million hectares — near the same level of deforestation as the Amazon for the first time. "Losing such a size of forest every year is a disaster," said Sam Nguiffo, a lawyer and founder of the Centre for Environment and Development in Cameroon.

"As humanity, we clearly cannot afford that because it will be totally irreversible," he said. Logging for timber or felling trees for agriculture or mining appear to prevail in forest management in Central Africa, Nguiffo said. Deforestation has a "massive impact on the cultural identity and on the livelihood of local and indigenous communities", he said.

"The erosion of the forest, both in size and in number of species, reduces the space available for communities and fuels conflicts," the lawyer added.

El Nino, the warming phase of a natural climate cycle, also threatens progress because its effects include droughts, creating conditions for wildfires. The current El Nino event, which emerged in June, is expected to peak later this year but is already shaping up to be the strongest ever observed. El Nino has been associated with strong drought in Indonesia, where tracts of forest and plantations have been burning in biodiverse Borneo and South Sumatra for months. "If projections of the historically strong 2026-27 El Nino materialise, drought and fire risks will intensify further across tropical forest regions," the deforestation report said.

Matson, of Climate Focus, noted that there was a "huge spike" in tree cover loss during the last "super" El Nino event in 2015-2016.
ir_summary: Global deforestation slowed in 2025 but remains off-track for 2030 targets, with Congo basin worsening and political shifts threatening progress.

title: Trump’s new press secretary faces scrutiny over credentials
text:
WASHINGTON: The White House faced mounting questions on Wednesday over new press secretary Katie Zacharia's legal credentials, after a faltering first day in the job when she gave an inconclusive answer about where she had passed the bar exam.

A US watchdog filed a complaint with the State Bar of California, asking it to investigate whether President Donald Trump's spokeswoman — the public face of the administration — had broken the law by repeatedly presenting herself as a lawyer without a licence.

Campaign for Accountability said Zacharia had described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and listed herself as general counsel for a California-based conservative firm.

"Ms Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility," said the group's executive director, Michelle Kuppersmith. "The State Bar should investigate whether Ms Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials," she added.

Trump described Zacharia as "an attorney" when announcing her appointment last week, but journalists have found no record of her being licensed to practise law in any US state. California's state bar confirmed to media that it had no record of Zacharia holding a licence under either her married or maiden name.

Zacharia, 41, graduated from Pepperdine University's law school in 2011, but obtaining a law degree does not automatically qualify someone to practise law.

Asked by reporters on Tuesday where she had passed the bar exam, Zacharia replied: "When I moved to China," without identifying any jurisdiction where she was licensed.
ir_summary: White House press secretary faces scrutiny over unverified legal credentials and potential misrepresentation as a lawyer.

title: Ukraine accuses US of helping Russia as missiles hit Kyiv
text:
KYIV: Ukraine on Wednesday accused the United States of helping Russia by failing to warn it of incoming missile strikes and hobbling its military response through changes to the Starlink system it uses on the battlefield.

President Volodymyr Zelensky framed the lack of notice about a wave of powerful strikes on Tuesday night and on Wednesday as "completely unjust", and accused Russia of wilfully flouting a supposed "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump.

A senior official in Kyiv confirmed that the United States had in recent days threatened to stop providing intelligence about Russian missile launches that Ukraine uses to thwart attacks. Trump denied doing so on Tuesday.

But they and defence officials also suggested Washington was behind slower speeds reported on some Starlink internet terminals which help Ukraine's military hit Russian-occupied territory and operate interceptor drones.

"It's obvious they (the United States) are helping Russia for some reason," the senior official said. Zelensky adviser Sergiy Beskrestnov said the attacks and Starlink restrictions were more than a coincidence as the network was "the most effective solution" for protecting Ukraine against jet-powered Russian attack drones, which can fly at up to 600 kilometres per hour.

"Through their actions, our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend the country against jet-powered Shahed drones," he wrote on Telegram. Ukrainian defence sources said SpaceX, owned by tech titan Elon Musk, "unilaterally restricted the operation of Starshield terminals… without prior warning", hitting connectivity for its drones. There was no immediate comment from either Musk or SpaceX. But last weekend he backed Trump, who has enraged Western allies by announcing a diesel-supply deal with heavily sanctioned Moscow and blindsided both sides in the nearly five-year conflict by announcing an "energy ceasefire".
ir_summary: Ukraine accuses US of aiding Russia by withholding missile warnings and restricting Starlink military communications during attacks.

title: Lagging behind
text:
THE IMF's latest World Economic Outlook projects Pakistan's economy to grow by 3.5pc in the current fiscal year, while average inflation climbs to 9.9pc. The current account is expected to slip into a deficit of 1pc of GDP. This forecast points to an economy that remains vulnerable despite recent gains in macroeconomic stability.

The economy expanded by 3.6pc last year. Further slowdown matters for a country with a rapidly increasing population, entrenched poverty, and high unemployment. Growth at this pace will hardly raise incomes meaningfully or absorb new entrants into the labour market.

Inflation poses another challenge. After easing to 7.1pc last year, it is forecast to rise sharply, leading to fears of further erosion of purchasing power. For families already squeezed by high energy costs, taxes, and essential expenses, renewed price pressures will undermine any benefits from economic stabilisation. The projected current account deficit signals renewed pressure on foreign exchange earnings.

Higher oil prices and shipping disruptions make imports more expensive. Unless exports grow faster and are more diversified, stronger domestic demand could again widen the external gap. The IMF expects unemployment to decline to 6.5pc in FY27 from 6.9pc the previous year. But, in the absence of stronger growth, which can create a sufficient number of jobs, that is hardly of any comfort. It does not establish whether new jobs will be productive, secure or adequately paid. Nor does it show whether employment is expanding fast enough to keep pace with the working-age population.

The South Asia region is forecast to grow by 6.4pc in 2026. Pakistan's 3.5pc projection places it far below the regional average, highlighting our failure to build a sustained growth engine. The global picture is also distressing. The IMF forecasts global growth of 3.1pc in 2026, rising to 3.4pc in 2027. Investment in AI is supporting activity in some economies. Others face higher energy costs, trade disruptions, and tighter financial conditions. Growth is also becoming increasingly uneven. We must prepare for these pressures rather than assume that stabilisation will deliver prosperity.

The immediate task is to contain inflation and protect vulnerable households without reviving unsustainable subsidies or excessive demand. For that, the government must shift resources towards productive investment, improve the competitiveness of industry, broaden the tax base and expand export capacity. Better education, skills, and employment opportunities are equally important. These changes require consistent policies, not another short-lived cycle of incentives and concessions. The IMF projections expose the cost of postponing structural reform. An economy growing at 3.5pc, with inflation approaching double digits and a weakening external balance, remains vulnerable to the next shock.
ir_summary: IMF projects Pakistan's economic growth at 3.5% with rising inflation and current account deficit, lagging behind regional and global averages.

title: India voter purge
text:
THE purge of millions of voters from India's electoral rolls has sparked widespread demonstrations, spearheaded by young protesters calling for justice. The Cockroach Janta Party is at the forefront of the movement, while more established opposition parties, such as Congress, are also participating actively. The thread uniting these groups is their suspicion that the Indian election commission has been tinkering with the rolls to benefit the ruling BJP.

Earlier this year, the youth-led CJP organised a massive anti-government campaign calling for the resignation of the education minister over exam irregularities. The movement succeeded in ousting the minister, with the youthful energy of its participants catching the BJP government off guard. This time too, India's rulers have responded with brute force, bundling away thousands of protesters, including Rahul Gandhi and CJP leaders, and cutting off access to the iconic Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi.

Around 130m names have been removed from the electoral rolls. The Indian election authorities say the deleted names include voters who have died, relocated, or could not be traced. But the Indian opposition has dismissed this explanation. It is believed that many of the deleted voters were Muslims, as well as those belonging to other marginalised groups.

Moreover, media reports say that the Indian election commissioner — whose resignation is being demanded — ignored objections from within the commission to the deletion of such a large number of voters. Such purging of the rolls is in keeping with the BJP regime's marginalisation of vulnerable groups. It has employed lawfare and dubious means in the past as well to delete Muslim votes; millions have been disenfranchised through the National Register of Citizens.

Earlier, the BJP and its Hindutva cohorts could get away with trampling the rights of Indian Muslims. But now, their shenanigans are not working. It appears that India's other communities are also tired of Hindutva's empty promises and its attempt to remake India in its own image through fair means and foul. The Sangh Parivar has run out of ideas, and its fantasies about a glorious Hindu past will not buy the people bread, or give them jobs. Hopefully, a fairer order can emerge from the tumult, in which all of India's communities are treated equally.
ir_summary: Mass protests in India over the removal of millions of voters from electoral rolls, with opposition alleging bias against minorities.

title: Multan derailment
text:
IN numerous states, including many of Pakistan's neighbours, rail transport is a safe and affordable mode of travel. But in this country, rail journeys can be perilous, as the derailment of the Peshawar-bound Rehman Baba Express near Multan early on Tuesday shows. In fact, derailments and accidents are far too common on our rail network, because for decades, the railways have remained underfunded. At least five people died in the tragedy, which is being blamed on "mechanical failure". The worthy railways minister has said an investigation is under way. There is, of course, much to investigate where the overall state of the rail network is concerned. As per figures in the media, at least 35 train accidents were reported in the first six months of the current year, while in 2025, there were 95 incidents.

The railways authorities say they have been making 'improvements', such as digitalising stations, and providing Wi-Fi. But where overhaul is concerned, especially upgrading signalling equipment and tracks, much needs to be done. Pakistan has a plan (ML-1) to bring its railways into the 21st century; what is missing is much of the funding — billions of dollars are required — as well as the will on part of the state to forge ahead with the modernisation plan. Perhaps officialdom is slothful because train transport is no longer used by the elite. The prime minister recently said he wants to see progress on ML-1; a launch date of January 2027 has been announced. However, it should be remembered that several launch dates for the megaproject have come and gone. To ensure the safety of passengers, and make critical upgrades to the national rail network, the authorities must set realistic timelines, arrange the funding, and start work without delay. A modern passenger and freight rail network can bring considerable economic advantages, while improving connectivity internally and with neighbouring states.
ir_summary: A train derailment in Multan highlights Pakistan's underfunded rail network and delayed modernization plan ML-1.

title: Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan to monitor Ponzi schemes
text:
ISLAMABAD: The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) has approved a Corporate Intelligence Unit (CIU) to identify registered companies suspected of running Ponzi or pyramid schemes, taking deposits or lending without a licence, or operating beyond their approved objectives.

The unit will monitor publicly available information, including news reports, social media and digital advertising, to identify potential violations before complaints are received. Verified leads will be referred to the relevant SECP departments for inquiry or enforcement action. Where appropriate, information may also be shared with agencies such as the FIA, NCCIA, State Bank of Pakistan and NAB.

The CIU is expected to strengthen the SECP's early-warning capacity, support timely regulatory intervention and help prevent further investor losses. By tracking recurring patterns and linking information from multiple public sources, it will also help the commission direct scrutiny towards emerging risks.

SECP Chairman Dr Kabir said that the CIU will strengthen the commission's risk-based surveillance by converting open-source information into verified regulatory leads.

The CIU is being established under Section 20 of the SECP Act 1997, as part of the Chairman's Secretariat.
ir_summary: Pakistan's SECP establishes a Corporate Intelligence Unit to monitor and prevent Ponzi schemes and unlicensed financial activities.

title: Oil gains on renewed supply fears
text:
NEW YORK: Oil prices rose on Wednesday after the Houthis attacked Saudi Aramco's headquarters and Iran said it was deploying new tactics to target ships and keep oil prices high.

Brent crude futures were up 87 cents, or 0.82 per cent, at $106.56 a barrel by 1:25pm ET (1725 GMT). US West Texas Inter­mediate crude gained $1.46, or 1.55pc, to $95.60, touching a three-week high.

Attacks on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-allied Houthis are driving up oil prices, said Phil Flynn, senior analyst with the Price Futures Group. "We're seeing a lot of fear trade today," he added.

Iranian officials declined to detail the new strategy to target ships, but one said Iran began using different offensive tactics about 10 days ago.

Gulf oil flows excluding Iran surged in September to more than 81pc of prewar levels, data showed, led by a recovery in Saudi exports. Iranian exports fell to zero owing to a US blockade.
ir_summary: Oil prices rise due to Houthi attacks on Saudi oil facilities and Iran's new tactics targeting ships.

title: Govt keeps treasury bill returns higher over policy rate
text:
KARACHI: The government kept treasury bill rates almost unchanged in an auction held on Wednesday, but the returns on all tenors of T-bills remained higher than the State Bank's policy rate of 11.5 per cent.

This was the last auction of T-bills before announcement of the next monetary policy on Oct 26. The results showed that the government raised Rs417.6 billion through this auction and another Rs267.9bn through non-competitive bids, making a total of Rs685.5bn.

But investors, mostly banks, were eager to park their maximum liquidity in government papers as the option for domestic lending looks extremely limited.

According to financial experts, investors are shy of taking risks amid the Gulf war and the political uncertainty in the country.

Domestic investors have been hoping over the last three years for initiatives by the government to stimulate the economy. The IMF had forecast a growth rate of 3.5pc for FY27, but the finance minister said on Tuesday he hoped for a 4pc growth.

The absence of domestic investments has created a serious problem for the country while policymakers are unable to bring them back into the economy.

The World Bank says poverty has been rising in the country and 48pc Pakistanis are now living below the poverty line.

"We are trying to protect the money already we have invested. The government has no idea how to stimulate a dormant economy mood," said a businessman in Karachi.

The government relies heavily on bank money and the borrowing size has been increasing each year, piling up a huge domestic debt. The latest auction reflects both the government's needs and banks' eagerness to invest in securities.

The investors' bids were Rs2.6 trillion at this auction — down from Rs2.7tr at the previous one on Oct 1.

The first quarter is already over without fresh borrowing. By the private sector. In FY26 the private sector had borrowed Rs1.4tr while in FY25 it was Rs1tr.

Bankers said most of the amount borrowed by the private sector was meant for working capital; it means no long-term investment.

At the previous auction the largest increase of 75bps was recorded in the benchmark six-month treasury bills, with the rate rising to 12.45pc from 11.70pc in the previous auction held on Sept 16.

At the current auction the six-month T-bills noted a decline of 6bps to 12.39 per cent from 12.45 per cent in the previous auction, still 89 basis points higher than policy rate.

The State Bank kept the return on T-bills almost 99 basis points higher than the interest rate at the previous auction and the same was maintained on Wednesday.
ir_summary: Pakistan's government keeps treasury bill rates above policy rate amid economic uncertainty and high investor demand for safe assets.

title: Ministry seeks cut in wheat seed prices
text:
ISLAMABAD: The Ministry of National Food Security and Research has urged private seed companies to reduce wheat seed prices to make them more affordable for farmers ahead of the Rabi sowing season, which begins in the coming weeks.

National Food Security Minister Rana Tanveer Hussain chaired a meeting on Wednesday with representatives of private seed companies and the National Seed Development and Regulatory Authority (NSDRA) to discuss wheat seed prices and inter-provincial movement.

The meeting focused on facilitating farmers through lower seed costs and uninterrupted supply across provinces, supporting timely wheat sowing and national food security, according to a press release.

Low use of certified wheat seed is a major challenge to wheat production, and the government is promoting climate-resilient, high-yielding and disease-resistant wheat varieties through strengthened research and seed multiplication programmes, the minister observed, while maintaining that enhanced availability and timely supply of quality seed was highly essential.

Timely access to affordable seed is particularly important for small farmers, whose purchasing decisions are affected by the combined costs of seed, fertiliser, irrigation and other agricultural inputs, the minister emphasised.

Mr Hussain directed NSDRA to ensure the smooth inter-provincial movement of wheat seed. Coordination with provincial authorities and seed suppliers will be key to addressing movement-related difficulties and ensuring seed reaches farmers within the appropriate sowing period.

A document on wheat seed position for 2026-27 Rabi crops shows that wheat seed procurement availability is 611,793.06 tonnes, which will fulfil 51 per cent of the total seed requirement of 1,191,555 tonnes.

Wheat seed availability in Punjab is 553,008.75 tonnes (67pc), Sindh 40,873.89 tonnes (23pc), Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 7,458.62 tonnes (7pc), and Balochistan 10,451.80 tonnes (13pc). For Rabi season 2025-26, total seed availability for sowing was 574,329.53 tonnes (51pc).
ir_summary: Pakistan's food ministry urges private companies to reduce wheat seed prices to support farmers and ensure food security.

title: PM slams delay in gemstone projects
text:
ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday expressed displeasure over delays in preparing the pilot project for the gemstones and jewellery sector and the lack of progress on measures to develop the sector.

He directed the relevant authorities to prepare and submit a time-bound action plan on a priority basis.

"Developing the gemstones and jewellery sector is a priority, and no delays will be tolerated," the prime minister said. He called for developing a comprehensive ecosystem for value addition through gemstone mining, cutting and polishing.

"Pakistan incurs losses worth billions of dollars annually due to substandard mining practices and the smuggling of precious stones," he said. He also called for developing a "Brand Pakistan" initiative for gemstones and jewellery, following the example of other countries in the region.

The prime minister directed authorities to formulate a plan to establish centres of excellence early to promote value addition.

The meeting was informed that 4.8 kanals had been transferred for a centre of excellence in Hussainabad, Skardu.

Presiding over a separate meeting, PM Shehbaz said that timely provision of loans to the Apna Ghar housing scheme, SMEs and agriculture was essential for boosting the national economy. He encouraged banks to play an active role in extending loans to these priority sectors to support national development and prosperity.

He said banks whose performance remained unsatisfactory were directed to improve lending to these sectors to qualify for government incentives. The prime minister directed the relevant ministries, secretaries and the State Bank of Pakistan to consult stakeholders from the SME, agriculture and housing finance sectors.

The prime minister also directed that inactive Pakistan Agricultural Storage & Services Corporation Ltd warehouses and silos be operated under a public-private partnership model to enable farmers to safely store their produce.

He appreciated Allied Bank's model of establishing commodity storage warehouses and providing loans to farmers against their stored produce, directing the authorities to expand the initiative with private-sector participation.

PM Shehbaz also welcomed Allied Bank's investment plan for a proposed SME park. Under the Apna Ghar scheme, the briefing said loans worth Rs448 billion had been approved for 75,198 applicants, while Rs76bn had been disbursed to 14,000 people.

Banks have been given a target to extend Rs700bn in loans to finance 125,000 housing units this year.

The total volume of agricultural loans stands at Rs1,352bn, benefiting 3.455 million people, officials said. Targets have been set to increase agricultural lending to Rs1,500bn and the number of beneficiaries to 4.5m by June 2027.
ir_summary: Pakistani PM criticizes delays in gemstone sector development and directs action plan for value addition and mining reforms.

title: Houthis warn of ‘painful’ response as Saudis strike Yemen fuel sites
text:
RIYADH: Saudi Arabia launched strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen on Tuesday, targeting fuel and energy facilities it said were being used to support missile and drone attacks, as the Yemeni group threatened a "harsh and painful" response against Saudi airports, refineries and oil installations.

Hours later, Saudi authorities issued warnings of potential hostile aerial threats in the kingdom's Eastern Province and Riyadh. Residents in the Eastern Province received alerts saying the area faced a "hostile aerial threat" before being told shortly afterwards that the danger had passed.

Loud explosions were heard near Saudi Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran, according to witnesses. There was no immediate confirmation that the facility itself had been struck. The Saudi-led coalition said fragments from an intercepted projectile had fallen on a residential area in Dhahran.

The developments marked a further escalation in the rapidly widening confrontation between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis, who have stepped up missile and drone attacks on the kingdom over the past week.

Earlier on Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had conducted military operations against "vital assets" used by the Houthis to sustain their war effort, Al Jazeera reported.

Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki said the targets included the Al-Sabaha central station in Sanaa, underground fuel reserves and storage tanks, as well as energy facilities in Hodeidah, Sanaa and Dhamar.

The coalition said the sites were being used to supply the Houthis' missile and drone arsenal, posing threats to Saudi Arabia, airports, ports and commercial shipping in the Red Sea.

"The operation aims to neutralise the Houthis' capabilities that threaten the Kingdom, Yemen, the southern Red Sea, and waterways," the coalition said.

Houthi-run Al-Masirah television reported that the Saudi-led coalition had struck a Yemen Petroleum Company facility on the western outskirts of Sanaa.

An AFP correspondent in the Yemeni capital reported hearing an explosion after the coalition had earlier issued an evacuation warning for civilians near the site — its first such order for Sanaa since the war flared up again.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree also said the site had "no military value", while the group warned that any further Saudi strikes would draw retaliation against targets in the kingdom.

The Houthis identified Riyadh's international airport, an oil refinery in the capital and Aramco facilities in eastern Saudi Arabia among potential targets, and renewed warnings to workers to stay away from sites that could be attacked.

The Saudi cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said the kingdom would not allow threats to its security or to freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait.

It warned that the Houthis would "face the consequences of their crimes and repeated attacks" on Saudi airports, holy cities and economic facilities.

Saudi Arabia also faced continuing attacks on Tuesday, with the coalition saying it had intercepted three drones north of Riyadh.

Blasts had also been heard over the Saudi capital late on Monday, when the coalition said it intercepted a Houthi missile and the group claimed another attack on Riyadh airport.

Trump, Erdogan weigh in US President Donald Trump spoke to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday and later told reporters that the Houthis were "behaving very badly".

He also accused the group of trying to drive up oil prices ahead of the Nov 3 US midterm elections and warned that he would "never forget" their attacks on Saudi Arabia.

Trump said he might ask Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to intervene in support of Saudi interests.

Earlier on Tuesday, Erdogan told the Sa­­u­­di crown prince that Ankara would stand by the kingdom, according to the Turkish presidency, though no details were given on any specific new line of support.

Turkiye and Pakistan signed a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia this summer, although Ankara still requires parliamentary approval to implement its commitments under the agreement.

Senior Houthi official Mohammed al-Bukhaiti said the group would target American interests in the region if Washington joined the war.

He said the attacks on Saudi targets were intended to signal to the Saudi leadership that it could no longer wage war in Yemen "from a safe position".
ir_summary: Saudi Arabia strikes Houthi fuel sites in Yemen, prompting threats of retaliation against Saudi oil and airport targets.

title: IMF sees growth at 3.5pc, inflation near 10pc
text:
ISLAMABAD: The Int­e­r­national Monetary Fund (IMF) has projected Paki­stan's economic growth at 3.5 per cent during the current fiscal year, with inflation expected to remain close to double digits, even as global growth is forecast to rebound to 3.4pc in 2027.

In its flagship World Economic Outlook, released at the start of the World Bank-IMF annual meetings in Bangkok, the Fund estimated Pakistan's current account deficit to widen to 1pc of GDP from a surplus of 0.5pc in FY25. Headline inflation is projected to rise to 9.9pc from 7.1pc last year.

However, the Washi­ngton-based lending age­ncy projected Pakistan's unemployment rate to dec­l­ine to 6.5pc this year compared to 6.9pc last year and 7.1pc a year earlier. The IMF, which concluded its review of Pakistan's economic situation last week, did not explain the projected decline in unemployment despite the rising population and its other economic forecasts, including higher inflation and a widening current account deficit.

The Fund's growth projections are significantly lower than the government's 4pc target for the current year and the 3.8pc forecast by the World Bank last month. Its estimated 3.5pc growth rate for Pakistan is slightly lower than the 3.6pc recorded last year but higher than the 3.2pc in FY25.

Saying global economic activity had proved resilient despite multiple challenges, the international lender projected global growth to slow to 3.1pc in 2026 before rebounding to 3.4pc in 2027. Global headline inflation is projected to rise notably to 4.7pc in 2026 before easing to 4.1pc in 2027, it added.

The IMF attributed global economic resilience to the technology upturn, buffers and adaptations that helped mitigate the damage from geopolitics-driven disruptions.

"In less than seven years, the global economy has been subjected to an exceptional sequence of events. The pandemic and the ensuing disruptions to global supply chains; the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, with the consequent sharp increases in the prices of energy and other commodities; and significant changes in trade barriers and trading relations have tested the resilience of households, firms, financial markets and governments," it said.

"Individually, each of these major developments would have been considered unlikely. Their confluence over such a short period of time is even more extraordinary. Yet, desp­ite this barrage of shocks, the global economy has held up," the IMF said.

It added that labour markets had remained unexpectedly strong, financial systems had broadly withstood the shocks and the sharpest monetary tightening in half a century, while inflation had receded from its peaks in many economies, although it remained persistent in some cases.

The IMF warned that energy-importing economies like Pakistan, which have limited links to the technology value chain, face the most difficult outlook. However, the margins of adjustment that have helped sustain resilience are not limitless and risks are skewed to the downside, it said.

Further escalation in conflicts, a reassessment of expectations surrounding artificial intelligence, renewed trade tensions and fiscal vulnerabilities could weaken growth. On the upside, stronger AI investment and productivity gains, or a sustained easing of geopolitical and trade tensions, could support growth.

The Fund advised its members that fiscal frameworks must deliver better results in dealing with disruptive shocks and build policy space through revenue measures. During cost-of-living crises, governments should preserve price signals and rely primarily on temporary, targeted income support for the most vulnerable, it said.

The stable global aggregate masks a reallocation of growth across economies. Countries with limited direct exposure to the war shock and strong participation in the technology uptu­­rn are seeing activity hold up or stre­n­­gthen. Energy exporters outside the immediate conflict zone are benefiting from favourable terms of trade.

Conversely, energy-importing economies with little connection to the technology value chain face the most difficult combination of higher import costs and exchange rate pressures, weaker real incomes, more constrained fiscal space and fewer offsetting demand impulses.

Many low-income and vulnerable countries belong to this latter group, increasing the risk that recent shocks will widen income gaps across and within countries.

The IMF projected world trade volume growth to slow in 2026 and stabilise in 2027, reflecting the drag from tariffs, adjustments in production chains and continued strength in technology-related trade.

A day earlier, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb told Reuters that the government expected the economy to grow by more than 4pc this fiscal year despite elevated oil prices. He also said the government was looking to privatise five to six entities during the year, potentially raising more than $1 billion.
ir_summary: IMF projects Pakistan's economic growth at 3.5% with inflation near 10% in its World Economic Outlook report.

title: Opposition slams, govt defends KP emergency in parliament
text:
ISLAMABAD: Senators on Tuesday debated the legitimacy of the federal government's decision to impose emergency rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, with the opposition questioning its constitutionality and the government defending the extraordinary measure as a last resort.

The National Assembly, however, was adjourned after a brief sitting due to the death of a lawmaker earlier this month, but the political crisis in KP remained the highlight of the day, even during the short proceedings.

Speaking in the upper house of parliament, PTI Parliamentary Leader Barrister Ali Zafar said what was happening in KP was not merely an administrative decision but a test of Pakistan's Constitution. "The Constitution must be our shield in a crisis, not a casualty of the crisis. The question is: are we using the Constitution to protect Pakistan, or are we using an emergency to change the political order of Pakistan?" he said.

In response to the allegations against the PTI, Mr Zafar said no political party or Pakistani wanted terrorism to flourish and that terrorism must be defeated with full strength. "But we must defeat terrorism without allowing the fight against terrorism to become a fight against constitutional democracy," he said.

He said Article 232 was an emergency power, not a political weapon, and Article 234 provided for extraordinary arrangements intended for extraordinary circumstances. Their existence did not mean they could be exercised without limits, he said.

"The government must demonstrate that constitutional conditions have genuinely been met, that the action is necessary and proportionate, and that every applicable procedure has been followed. The existence of an emergency power does not place its exercise above the Constitution," he said.

"This is a political crisis disguised as a security solution," Mr Zafar said, pointing to the timing amid intense political confrontation and a breakdown in dialogue between the federal government and the PTI. "You cannot restore public confidence by making people believe that their elected mandate can be taken away in the name of security."

He warned that the issue concerned provincial autonomy, federalism, elected representation, fundamental rights and the balance between the federation and its units.

Calling on the Senate not to become a rubber stamp, he said parliament, which represents the federation and gives every province an equal voice, must examine legal grounds, demand evidence and scrutinise necessity and proportionality.

Meanwhile, Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar said the federal cabinet "rightly decided" last week that the process of political reconciliation with the opposition PTI was over. He stressed that the PPP and PML-N had both made efforts to reach a point of understanding with the PTI, but failed. "They said they would talk about it, then consulted with their chief minister, and after that, virtually, they refused," he said.

He added, "Political reconciliation can be secured when other things are … equal. Other things have gone in a very bad, very wrong direction in this country and particularly in the province."

Regarding arguments that terrorism was also pre­valent in Balochistan, he highlighted that the Balo­c­histan government was "fully on board" with fighting terrorism. The deputy premier added that when Maulana Fazlur Rahman of the JUI-F came to play his part in breaking the deadlock in negotiations, "thi­ngs had gone far beyond".

Speaking in the house, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi claimed the Constitution was not violated in the imposition of the emergency and the government acted strictly as per the procedures. "The PML-N and PPP sat together and examined every clause to ensure that no provision was violated," he said, adding that the decision was not easy.

Mr Naqvi said the option of emergency or governor's rule was available even on Nov 26 and earlier, but the government exercised restraint and contacted the PTI leadership, including Barrister Gohar, on Oct 10, asking him to suggest amendments to para 4 of the draft. "Had that agreement been reached, this step would not have been taken," he said.

He said the government made six amendments in the draft, which was sent to the chief minister, who forwarded it to Murad Saeed, after which the matter was sabotaged. "If they did not have authority, they should have said so earlier."

Another opposition leader and PTI ally, Allama Raja Nasir Abbas, termed Oct 11, when emergency and governor's rule were imposed, "a black day". The senator questioned why emergency was imp­osed only in KP if the system had collapsed, when the situation in Balochistan was equally dangerous.

He said an agreement had been reached on political issues and differences arose over attempts to link security with political issues. He warned that unnecessary violence created hatred against the state and urged immediate withdrawal of the decision.

The National Assembly, however, did not debate the emergency decision and its session was adjourned in accordance with parliamentary norms, which mandate that proceedings on the first day be confined to prayers if a lawmaker has passed away.

PTI leader Barrister Gohar Ali Khan insisted on a speech to share his views on the KP rule, but was not allowed by the National Assembly speaker. PPP MNA Naveed Qamar asked Barrister Gohar to speak on the floor of the house on Wednesday, while Speaker Ayaz Sadiq quipped that the PTI had already been offered a chance during the talks.

"We tried to give you a lot in dialogue, but you (PTI) were not ready to take what we had offered," the speaker quipped bef­ore turning off the mic. "Political discussion will be allowed tomorrow," he added. Later, opposition MNAs staged a protest outside the Parliament House.

At the outset, Speaker Ayaz Sadiq administered the oath of membership to PML-N's Malik Munir Iqb­al Channar, who won the Bah­awalpur polls last mon­th held to fill the seat of his late father Malik Muha­m­mad Iqbal Channar.
ir_summary: Pakistani parliament debates government's imposition of emergency rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa amid opposition's constitutional challenges.

title: PM vows no leniency for hoarders
text:
ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said on Tuesday that wheat was available in abundant quantities to meet domestic needs, while vowing no leniency for hoarders, according to the Prime Minister's Office.

Presiding over the first National Agricul­tural and Food Security Council (NAFSC) meeting, the prime minister said that wheat was available in abundant quantities to meet domestic needs.

"No leniency will be shown to those hoarding wheat," the PMO quoted PM Shehbaz as saying. "It is essential to determine the fair price of wheat before sowing so that farmers receive appropriate compensation for their labour," the prime minister said.

"We want farmers to get the fair price for wheat and for consumers to have affordable wheat," he added.

The prime minister stated that the decision regarding the price of wheat would be made in consultation with the provinces.

"The consultation with the provinces will be completed soon, and the price of wheat will be announced shortly," he said.

The prime minister termed agriculture the "backbone of the national economy" and said it could set the country's economy on the path to growth in the short term.

Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, Sindh Food Minister Makhdoom Mehboob uz Zaman, and relevant senior officials also participated in the meeting, according to the statement.

During the meeting, the prime minister commended CM Maryam for taking commendable steps such as farmers' development, aquaculture, shrimp farming, and providing direct subsidies to farmers through the Kisan Card.

The Sindh chief minister was also "working day and night for the development of farmers and providing them with facilities", PM Shehbaz said.

The prime minister noted that the livestock sector also had vast potential to increase national exports, noting that measures were being taken to boost exports of Pakistani halal meat.

He said the federal government would "provide all kinds of support to the provinces for the development of agriculture".

"Providing fertilisers, quality seeds, modern machinery, and equipment and technical capabilities for better water utilisation to farmers at low cost is the top priority," the prime minister said.

He said that ensuring fair prices to farmers for their crops, particularly small- and medium-scale farmers, was a priority as well.

The Punjab chief minister and Sindh food minister shed light on the measures taken by the provincial governments for the development of farmers in their provinces, the PMO said.

It said that the briefings were also given at the meeting on measures for the development of agriculture in Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Azad Jammu and Kashmir, and Gilgit-Baltistan.
ir_summary: Pakistani PM vows no leniency for wheat hoarders and announces price consultation with provinces to support farmers and consumers.

title: ‘Emergency applies to all of KP, not just 12 districts’
text:
ISLAMABAD: The emergency proclamation issued under Article 232 applies to all of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, not just the 12 terror-stricken districts of the province, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said on Tuesday.

Addressing a press conference alongside his cabinet colleague Attaullah Tarar, the law minister said that for those 12 districts, a special mechanism had been introduced.

"Under the chief executive, extra measures have been taken; a dedicated secretariat has been established which will be providing assistance to those districts," he said.

At the outset of the press briefing, the law minister noted that the province in the recent past had witnessed a hike in terrorist incidents, noting a "195 per cent" rise, with 8,600 terrorist attacks recorded in 2024-2026 compared to 2,900 in 2020-2024.

He emphasised that it was essential that counterterrorism efforts taken by federal and provincial agencies be "harmonised", adding that such an approach was standard practice globally.

"All these arrangements are made to run the country in a way that people feel safe," the law minister remarked, adding that the "non-serious" attitude of the PTI-led KP government "has now ceased to exist".

He recalled that the PTI, allegedly using government resources, "launched an onslaught on the capital". However, at the time, the imposition of governor's rule and emergency did not come under discussion.

Describing the situation on the ground in the province, the law minister said: "The KP police were under attack, armed forces deployed in the province were under attack […] innocent people lost their lives."

"You cannot shut your eyes after receiving such reports and seeing this rise in terrorist activity," Azam added.

Recalling the events leading up to the federal government's decision, the law minister said the government had held "constant engagement" with the provincial authorities.

"Unfortunately, their response was somewhat different. Maybe their politics were more important to them than having the national interest at heart," he said.

The information minister claimed that the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had "welcomed" the federal government's move to impose governor's rule and emergency in the province, saying the measures had given them "hope".

"Had the people of KP supported the pro-terrorist stance of the PTI government, you would have seen millions on the streets," he said.

The information minister, during the presser, reiterated that the federal government did not have a political agenda against the PTI-led provincial government; instead, it was pursuing "a unified policy on counterterrorism".

"You cannot have a government in the country that sympathises with terrorists, supports terrorism or has a policy that enables terrorists to carry out their operational actions," he said.

He questioned how one country could have two separate counterterrorism policies.

"As the [law] minister explained, the framers of the constitution included these clauses (232 and 234) for a time like this," citing a "complete breakdown" of law and order in KP.
ir_summary: Pakistan's law minister states that a state of emergency applies to all of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province due to terrorism, not just 12 districts.

title: Israeli army wounds two in Ramallah raid
text:
RAMALLAH: Israeli army fire wounded two Palestinians on Tuesday during a raid in the city of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, according to the Palestinian health ministry.

A hospital in the city received "a young man with a serious gunshot wound to the lower back and a 14-year-old with a live bullet wound to the upper thigh, in addition to numerous cases of suffocation, as a result of the (Israeli army) assault on Ramallah", the ministry said.

The army raided the former headquarters of the Addameer Prisoner Support and Human Rights Association, seizing documents and furniture, according to journalists who witnessed and filmed the scene.

Israel had closed the organisation's office in August 2022 along with six other Palestinian NGOs and civil society groups after designating them "terrorist organisations". Photos and video footage on Tuesday showed Israeli soldiers moving furniture, office equipment, and folders out of the office and onto a trailer attached to a military vehicle.

The army also reaffixed its order for the organisation's closure on the front door of the premises. Israeli forces were deployed in the neighbourhood for nearly four hours, fired tear gas and stun grenades toward a group of reporters, and wounded four of them, according to journalists and eyewitnesses. In a separate incident on Tuesday, four Palestinians from the same family were injured after settlers stormed their home in the village of Talfit, south of Nablus in the northern West Bank, according to a medical source and a family member.

Youssef Abu Aisheh, 43, said that settlers knocked on his door presenting themselves as soldiers, then entered his home and assaulted him, his wife, and their seven children.

"They banged on the door violently and said they were soldiers, and when I opened the door I was shocked to find they were settlers wearing jeans, vests, and black masks, and carrying clubs," he said. As a result of the assault, his daughter suffered a broken leg, his wife a deep head wound, while he and another daughter were bruised, Abu Aisheh said, adding that the Israeli police did not respond to his request for help.
ir_summary: Israeli army raid in Ramallah wounds Palestinians and seizes documents from a human rights organization previously designated as terrorist.

title: UNDP seeks investment, jobs as aid flows decline
text:
BANGKOK: The United Nations Development Programme on Tuesday announced new initiatives to help attract investors and jobs to developing countries, which are being rocked by crises outside their control amid a sharp drop in official development aid.

UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo said the agency was increasing its cooperation with the World Bank, and forging new ties to the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the European Investment Bank, other financial institutions and private investors, to advance the investment and jobs agenda.

Developing countries needed to undertake reforms to improve governance, improve the rule of law and boost domestic revenues, but progress on that front had been slowed by a series of crises since the Covid pandemic, De Croo told Reuters.

"The way development is being financed is changing, and that's a good thing, but we need to create some space for those countries to be able to implement those reforms," De Croo said on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok, Thailand.

De Croo said the crises facing developing countries were worse in some aspects than the Covid crisis of 2020-2021, but it was premature to be talking about debt relief measures.

Domestic central banks and regional institutions would need to address liquidity needs in countries struggling with high energy costs, rising interest rates and the worst El Nino weather effect since 1950. Only then could the issue of solvency be addressed, he said.

Countries had been shielding their populations from the energy price shock caused by the war in the Middle East through fuel subsidies and other measures, but at a huge cost, and the coming super El Nino posed another threat.

"The alarm lights are at least on orange, and if this continues for a few more months, countries will come into trouble," he said, adding that UNDP was working with 46 countries to develop targeted subsidies that were less costly.

Many countries were already pulling back from such measures as fiscal buffers ran dry, and no quick end to the war in the Middle East appeared in sight, De Croo said. If it dragged on, there was a risk that Gulf countries and others that had maintained support would curb their aid as well, he said.

"We need to find a way to stop (the war), at least to get again safe access to the Gulf region … and it's the same in Ukraine," he said. "At some point wars need to end."

The new UNDP investment and jobs initiatives came amid warnings about a huge job gap facing developing countries, with some 1.2 billion young people set to enter the workforce over the next decade but only 400 million jobs in sight.

One will focus on work to improve investment policies and regulations, develop specific projects and pipelines and move projects to implementation. The other will look for sectors with strong job-creation potential, align skills with employer demand and address barriers to business investment and hiring.

UNDP said it already had pilot initiatives underway in Nepal, Yemen, Haiti, Lebanon and Ghana as part of its World Bank partnership, and was also working with Italy's Generali on expanding insurance coverage for developing countries.

This was crucial, De Croo said, noting that natural catastrophes in Asia caused $65 billion in economic losses in 2025, of which only $5bn was insured.

"What insurance is doing is managing risk," he said. "We see quite some margin in using insurance systems in a world that is becoming more turbulent than ever to try to manage that risk and help countries to become investable."
ir_summary: UNDP announces initiatives to attract investment and jobs to developing countries amid declining aid and multiple crises.

title: Demonstrations backing France’s protesting students gather strength
text:
PARIS: Tens of thousands of people joined rallies across France on Tuesday to support protesting high school students, boosting a movement that poses a major challenge to President Emmanuel Macron as his term in office winds down.

Some 161,500 people turned out, according to the interior ministry — more than double the 71,500 it gave for the last nationwide demonstrations on Thursday last week. Unions helping organise Tuesday's rallies put the countrywide turnout at 480,000.

The numbers suggested snowballing street opposition to the government just six months before France votes for a successor to Macron, who is completing his maximum second mandate. On Saturday, national demonstrations against the spiralling cost of living are to take place, and unions and student groups see the two protest currents fusing together.

The agitation comes as Macron's centrist government struggles to get a cost-cutting budget through parliament, in the teeth of worsening debt that has spooked the bond market. Although most of Tuesday's demonstrations were peaceful, violence occurred on the sidelines of one of two marches in Paris, where the interior ministry said 41,500 people participated.

Journalists saw some cars set on fire and police fired tear gas as masked youths tried to erect barricades across roads and threw objects. Tear gas was also fired during a demonstration in Lyon. Among those taking part in a demonstration in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis was Swedish activist Greta Thunberg. She said she was there because "our future is being robbed".

University students were prominent in Tuesday's demonstrations, alongside teachers and union leaders. They were also backed by far-left opposition France Unbowed (LFI) party, whose chief, presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Melenchon, was seen among crowds in Paris.

Thousands also marched in the cities of Nantes, Lyon, Lens, Strasbourg, Toulouse, Bordeaux and Marseille, according to police and reporters. "We stand in solidarity with the high schools that are worse off. We need real measures and proper dialogue, not repression," said 16-year-old Emeline, outside a Marseille school.

"We're here because we really feel we're not being heard by the government," said Nina, 17. The student movement sprang up last month, with teenagers at France's lycees — high schools for those aged 15 to 18 — blocking the entrances to many schools to demand better classroom conditions.

Perceived heavy-handed reactions from police against the students drove many to join Tuesday's demonstrations. One teen lost his hand when he picked up a police stun grenade during the protests, while another lost an eye, and another teeth when an officer fired a teargas canister in his face.

Police have opened internal investigations into 34 allegations of violence against demonstrators. Some 147 teaching staff have been injured in the protests, the education ministry said.

"We're not giving up the fight, whether it's for the high school students who were hit with a harsh crackdown, or for denouncing police violence," said Patricia, a 20-year-old university student in Paris who did not give her last name.

Some Indian tourists who wandered into the Paris demonstration said they were unnerved. "Initially we were terrified," said Snehil Jain, a 45-year-old visiting Paris for a week with his wife. "We had seen the media images of violence around these protests. But then we saw it was a peaceful protest, so we were OK then." France's education ministry said 214 schools, mostly high schools, were closed on Tuesday.

University student union l'Union Etudiante reported 90pc of universities had closed nationwide to show support. French students say they are determined to press their demands over absent teachers, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded schedules and other grievances.

They have dismissed a government pledge — made after last week's demonstrations — to send 3,000 substitute teachers to the 114 worst-affected schools. "We are continuing the blockades. We are not budging," said Naouel, a high school student in Brest. She said she hoped the protests would continue after the half-term holidays, in late October.

Mariolino, a 16-year-old in Nantes, concurred. "Those who think the anger will disappear with the holidays just don't get it," he said. On Monday, Macron had urged restraint from protesters, saying the issues "deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect".
ir_summary: Mass protests in France against government policies gain momentum with student and union support ahead of elections.

title: Britain’s spy chief accuses Iran, Russia of hybrid campaigns
text:
LONDON: Iran is stepping up attempts to hit harder targets such as military sites in Britain and Russia is increasing its hybrid warfare against Ukraine's allies, the UK's domestic spy chief said on Tuesday. In his annual speech on wide-ranging threats to Britain, MI5 Director General Ken McCallum also said the greatest concern about the misuse of AI was terrorists being able to develop bioweapons or even create new pathogens.

McCallum said state threats had quadrupled over the last decade, and his organisation now devoted more resources to the issue than during the Cold War. On Monday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Tehran was "highly likely" behind a suspected plot against RAF Fairford, an airbase used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran. It prompted a security alert and led to US President Trump withdrawing planes from the air base.

Tehran has rejected accusations of involvement in the Fairford incident or any other accusations of malign activity in Britain where the authorities have for a number of years accused it of being involved in plots and attempted assassinations against dissidents and Israeli and Jewish targets.

Russia also denies involvement in hostile acts in Britain and other Western countries, but McCallum said it remained the "aggressor number one".

McCallum echoed comments from other European spy agencies that Russia was using tactics just short of conventional conflict, citing the attempted drone attack on a cargo plane at a German airport and a cyber attack on Polish energy infrastructure.

"It's no accident that Russian aggressors are trying to unsettle other European homelands at a time when their military progress in Ukraine is minimal and horrifically costly."

Russia has rejected Germany's accusations over the incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August as "entirely fabricated".

Speaking about AI, McCallum said the technology was "supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders" and terrorists were exploiting it to improve reconnaissance and attack methodologies.

"Not yet realised — the misuse case to which I'd attach greatest weight — is AI's potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons," he said, adding it was the area on which he and his colleagues were "particularly focused". "These risks are real."
ir_summary: UK spy chief accuses Iran and Russia of hybrid warfare campaigns and increased state threats against Britain and its allies.

title: Narrative confusion
text:
AS the information minister on Tuesday proclaimed that the people of KP had "welcomed" the imposition of governor's rule and emergency in the province, he seemed to be forgetting that citizens had also distributed sweets and celebrated when the late Gen Pervez Musharraf overthrew Nawaz Sharif's government almost to the day, 27 years ago.

The parallel is not exact: one was a military coup, the other a constitutional provision invoked by an elected government. Yet, the lesson holds. Public approval, however genuine, did not legitimise the removal of an elected government then, and it cannot by itself justify the removal of an elected government in KP now. If anything, the minister's remarks are a reminder of how rarely Pakistan's political class draws the obvious lessons from its own history.

There are two official versions of why the KP government has been dismissed. On Sunday, the interior minister was far more circumspect than the information minister while providing the state's rationale, insisting that the decision was "not political" and "only security-related". He had been negotiating with the PTI till the eleventh hour, trying to avoid imposing governor's rule and emergency on the province, he said. "Our issue was entirely terrorism-related, and we want[ed] to take you on board on it," he asserted, addressing the opposition. The information minister, on the other hand, alleged the PTI had an "unholy alliance with terrorists". Which of those two narratives, offered from the same platform, was true? If a political party was colluding with terrorists, why was the state negotiating and not making arrests based on the 'evidence' the information minister claimed to possess? The disconnect suggests that the government has yet to settle on a coherent justification for a decision of this gravity.

Meanwhile, KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi has said his advisory council will take its policies from Islamabad. Why not from the people of KP, who will be most affected by them? Perhaps unwittingly, the governor has sent the clearest possible signal that KP's mandate is being held in abeyance. What the government in the centre and the governor's new set-up in KP need to realise is that their words are not reaching only the leaders of a rival party, but also being heard by all those who helped elect those individuals to office. If winning the confidence of the people of KP is not a priority at this stage, it ought to be. Governor's rule is, by constitutional design, a temporary measure. The centre must say clearly how long it intends it to last, what it hopes to achieve in that time, and how the province's elected mandate will be restored. Anything less will only confirm the impression that this was never solely about security.
ir_summary: Pakistan's government gives conflicting justifications for imposing governor's rule in KP province, citing both security concerns and political allegations.

title: El Niño’s long reach
text:
THE extraordinary El Niño gathering strength in the Pacific could make 2026 the hottest year on record, with 2027 hotter still. According to the EU's Copernicus climate service, sea temperatures in a Pacific region reached a record high in September. US forecasters expect the phenomenon, which changes weather patterns worldwide, to remain strong into early next year. For Pakistan, its effects could stretch across several seasons. El Niño can influence the western weather systems that bring winter rain and snow to the northern mountains, while it has often been linked with weaker monsoons in South Asia. The coming winter's snowfall will be important: snow stored in the mountains helps feed the Indus and its tributaries as temperatures rise. Heavy winter rain, if it replaces snowfall, could leave less water stored for the hotter months. Too little accumulation could reduce the water available to farms in spring and summer. A weaker monsoon in 2027 would put additional pressure on reservoirs and irrigation supplies. At the same time, a warmer year would mean greater demand for water and electricity.

Much will depend on how these changes affect the country's water supplies and crops. Wheat growers depend on winter rainfall and irrigation, while rice and cotton farmers rely heavily on summer water supplies. A shortage at the wrong time could cut yields, hurt rural incomes and push up food prices. That would affect families struggling with household expenses and add to the import bill if production falls short. Nor would farmers be the only ones affected: reduced river flows could constrain hydropower generation just as hotter weather drives up demand for electricity. Pakistan, therefore, needs a thorough assessment of what El Niño could mean for the months ahead. The Met Office should provide clear, regularly updated guidance on winter precipitation and the outlook for the next monsoon. Water authorities must use it to plan reservoir releases and irrigation allocations, while agricultural departments should help farmers choose crops and planting dates suited to changing conditions. These decisions cannot wait until fields are dry or prices start rising. El Niño begins in a distant ocean, but its possible effects on Pakistan's water, harvests and economy are close to home. The country has advance warning of a difficult period; it should make that warning useful.
ir_summary: El Niño's potential impact on Pakistan's weather, water supply, agriculture, and energy is analyzed, urging government assessment.

title: Deeper poverty
text:
PAKISTAN'S poverty crisis is far deeper than official indicators suggest. While the government celebrates economic stabilisation, almost four in every 10 Pakistanis suffer from deprivation in health, education, and living standards.

The latest UNDP figures put multidimensional poverty at 38.3pc of the population against 19.3pc for South Asia. We are worse off than nearby countries — poverty affects 16.4pc of India's and 14.9pc of Bangladesh's population. These estimates are based on surveys from different years, however, and should not be treated as a strictly contemporaneous ranking. Still, the comparison is an indictment of our development priorities.

That Pakistan's multidimensional poverty rate is almost twice the regional average is not simply a reflection of low incomes. The index captures deficiencies in nutrition, child health, schooling, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, and other necessities. A family may earn enough to remain above an income-based poverty line and still lack access to these essentials. The intensity of deprivation for the multidimensionally poor is 51.7pc. Another 12.9pc of the population is vulnerable to such poverty.

This means millions more risk falling into acute deprivation when faced with illness, joblessness, rising food prices, or climate-related disasters. Our poor performance exposes the limits of an economic strategy focused primarily on containing inflation, accumulating foreign exchange reserves and meeting fiscal targets.

Though necessary, they cannot substitute for growth and development. An economy cannot sustain higher productivity when children miss school, malnutrition damages their development, and poor healthcare pushes households into financial distress. Economic stability should be judged by whether it improves people's lives, not merely by whether the balance-of-payments holds or the budget deficit narrows.

Pakistan's widening development gap with India and Bangladesh is a warning that stability without investment in people will leave poverty entrenched.
ir_summary: Pakistan's multidimensional poverty rate is 38.3%, nearly double South Asia's average, highlighting failures in development priorities.

title: Nervous selling drags index below 165,000
text:
KARACHI: Amid political turmoil following the imposition of governor's rule and an emergency in PTI-ruled Khyber Pakh­tunkhwa, equity investors remained unsettled on Tuesday by the uncertain outlook. Economic concerns persisted despite the finance minister's optimism that GDP growth would exceed four per cent this fiscal year, even with the oil shock.

The Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) continued its downward trend, extending overnight losses as nervous investors offloaded positions. The selling pushed the benchmark KSE-100 index below the key resistance level of 165,000.

Topline Securities Ltd said the index fell 347.97 points, or 0.21 per cent, to close at 164,776.44. The benchmark remained range-bound throughout the session, reflecting cautious investor sentiment and persistent selling pressure on index-heavy stocks.

Investor sentiment is likely to remain cautious amid ongoing market volatility. Near-term market direction will hinge on developments in key economic indicators, institutional activity, and investor positioning. Selective opportunities may arise in fundamentally sound stocks, while a prudent investment approach remains advisable.

Pakistan Telecom­muni­cation Company, United Bank, Habib Bank, Lucky Cement and Mari Ener­gies emerged as the major laggards, collectively wiping out 343 points and weighing on overall market performance.

Investor participation improved as trading volume rose 5.72pc to 384 million shares, while traded value dipped 9.67pc to Rs13.1bn.

Ali Najib, Deputy Head of Trading at Arif Habib Ltd, said the PSX recorded a mixed, volatile session, opening higher after yesterday's sell-off and climbing to an intraday high of 166,071. However, profit-taking at higher levels curtailed the recovery, pushing the benchmark into negative territory and resulting in a lower close.

On the sectoral front, auto sales (cars, LCVs, vans and jeeps) fell 3pc month-on-month and 12pc year-on-year to 15,100 units in September. Nevertheless, cumulative sales in 1QFY27 rose 19pc to 50,500 units.

Analysts expect the market to remain volatile amid domestic political uncertainty. Selective value buying may offset further downside risks. Investors should remain cautious, prioritise fundamentally strong stocks, and avoid aggressive positions until sentiment stabilises.
ir_summary: Pakistan's stock market falls amid political turmoil and economic uncertainty, with the KSE-100 index dropping below 165,000.

title: Pakistani youth face job crisis
text:
ISLAMABAD: Only seven per cent of Pakistan's youth have access to formal technical and vocational training against the regional average of 22pc, and the World Bank estimates that this skill gap costs Pakistan $31.5 billion annually in lost productivity and unrealised export potential.

"How to boost youth employment in Pakistan for the age of AI," is a topic that is part of the World Economic Forum's annual meeting of Global Future Leaders, which opened in Dubai on Tuesday. Pakistan provides a case study in efforts to bridge the current gap between education and employment.

The annual meeting gives a new generation of leaders a platform to shape the future by jointly creating bold opportunities in a volatile world, while building the capacity to withstand setbacks and respond to the unthinkable.

Among youth aged 15 to 29, nearly a third are NEET (not in education, employment, or training). For young women, that share climbs past half.

The problem is not that young Pakistanis are not working hard enough. It is the infrastructure needed to connect talent to opportunity — structured mentorship, career guidance, industry networks, honest labour market signals — that was never built in most of the country.

Nationally, graduate unemployment at 18.3pc exceeds the overall unemployment rate of 14.7pc across all education levels. Statistically, the people who studied hardest are the most likely to be left waiting. This is not a talent problem. According to Pakistan's case study article, it is an architectural problem.

In Pakistan, a university degree has become the beginning of a job search, not the end of one. According to Gallup Pakistan's analysis of the Pakistan Labour Force Survey 2024-25, graduate unemployment among young Pakistanis aged 20-24 stands at 32.8pc. Nearly one in three graduates in this age group is unemployed — not because they lack capability, but because the system they graduated into was never designed to absorb them.
ir_summary: Pakistan faces a youth unemployment crisis with high graduate joblessness and a large skills gap costing billions annually.

title: Exporters seek govt support to stem decline
text:
ISLAMABAD: Textile and clothing exporters have urged the government to introduce structural reforms and provide temporary financial support to arrest the sector's downturn and protect Pakistan's share in international markets amid mounting global competition.

The proposals were laid out at a high-level meeting, chaired by Commerce Secretary Jawad Paul, on Tuesday. The meeting reviewed challenges facing the textile industry and possible policy interventions to restore export competitiveness.

A source told Dawn that issue-based subcommittees had been constituted to examine the industry's concerns and submit recommendations within 15 days.

At the outset, exporters called for structural reforms to address the rising cost of production and at the same time, they sought immediate relief through a six to eight per cent drawback of local taxes and levies (DLTL) on total export sales, conditional upon achieving a 10pc growth in exports.

The exporters said the proposed incentive would help sustain production, encourage higher exports and prevent further erosion of the country's market share under increasingly difficult international trading conditions.

The meeting was attended, among others, by officials from the ministries of finance, power, petroleum, mines and minerals, the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR), the State Bank, and the Punjab Industries Department.

Among the industry representatives were Pakistan Textile Exporters Association Patron Khurram Mukhtar and Chairman Reehan Naseem, Pakistan Hosiery Manufacturers and Exporters Association (PHMA) Chairman Syed Zia Alamdar, Pakistan Textile Council (PTC) Chairman Fawad Anwar, and All Pakistan Textile Mills Association representatives Rehman Naseem and Aamer Fayyaz.

A major concern raised during the discussions was the industrial electricity tariff, particularly the burden of cross-subsidies that exporters said continued to undermine their competitiveness.

Industry representatives highlighted a discrepancy of Rs56 billion in power tariff calculations, of which the Power Planning and Monitoring Company (PPMC) acknowledged Rs26bn.

It was decided that the matter would now be taken up with the Power Division during a meeting scheduled for Friday (Oct 16). The commerce ministry was asked to submit recommendations to the prime minister for a final decision.

The exporters' representatives questioned the methodology used to calculate gas tariffs, particularly the treatment of unaccounted for gas losses, which they said added to industrial energy costs.

Another major issue concerned anomalies in the Export Finance Scheme (EFS), including differences in rates, inadequate allocation of funds to the corporate sector and the failure of certain commercial banks to implement the prescribed fixed financing rate of 4.5pc.

The industry representatives sought corrective measures to ensure that export financing remained accessible at competitive rates, particularly at a time when exporters were facing rising production costs and weakening demand in overseas markets.

The meeting dwelt at length on delays in tax refunds and other taxation issues involving the FBR, which exporters said had heightened liquidity pressures and constrained their ability to finance export orders.

On labour-related expenses, the industry representatives informed the meeting that the overall human resource cost had reached $270 per worker, placing an additional burden on manufacturers.
