Near-term attention will remain on oil prices, foreign flows, and institutional participation, with 170k serving as the key psychological level.
ir_summary: Pakistan's stock market rebounds on optimism about IMF loan talks and potential $1.2 billion disbursement.

title: PM orders winter gas load plan amid LNG shortages
text:
ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday directed the relevant authorities to prepare a comprehensive plan for gas load management and take all necessary measures to ensure uninterrupted gas imports during the winter season, given the regional situation.

The premier issued these instructions while chairing a meeting, said the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) in a statement.

"The prime minister directed officials to develop a comprehensive gas load management plan, take necessary measures in advance, launch a public awareness campaign on its implementation, and ensure uninterrupted gas imports in light of the current regional situation," the PMO said.

The participants were informed that domestic consumers would be given priority for the supply of locally produced gas while RLNG would be prioritised for power generation and industries, it said.

The meeting took place as the authorities struggle to finalise the liquefied natural gas (LNG) import plan for the upcoming three winter months — December to February — amid a challenging supply situation stemming from the US-Iran conflict.

Renewed hostilities in the Middle East have resulted in disruption of major oil and gas supply routes — the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — and caused fuel prices to rise.

Against this backdrop, gas companies and the Petroleum Division had sought at least 22 import cargoes for the three-month period, but the task force on energy, led by Lt-Gen Zafar Iqbal, has promised no more than 10-12 cargoes of around 100 million cubic feet each on a best-effort basis, using all diplomatic and logistical channels.

The plan will be presented to the prime minister for approval, given the involvement of around $100m per spot cargo and the requirement for consent from the Ministry of Finance and the State Bank of Pakistan.

Later, the premier reviewed affairs of the National Highway Authority (NHA), including ongoing development work on national highways, motorways and expressways.

PM Shehbaz directed that all ongoing NHA projects undergo third-party audit. He also ordered the authorities to formulate a strategy for constructing national highways, motorways and expressways under public-private partnerships.
ir_summary: Pakistani PM orders gas import and load management plan due to regional conflict disrupting LNG supplies.

title: Pakistan drives regional rise in poverty levels
text:
ISLAMABAD: Projecting Pakistan's economic growth at 3.8 per cent and fiscal deficit at 3.5pc for the current fiscal year, the World Bank on Tuesday said the country was home to almost half of the extremely poor population in the entire Middle East, North Africa and Afghanistan-Pakistan (Menaap) region.

"Menaap is the only region in the world in which poverty remains above pre-pandemic levels and continues to rise. Pakistan accounts for nearly half of the region's extreme poor," the Washington-based lending agency said in its Economic Outlook ahead of the IMF-WB annual meetings next week.

A prolonged slowdown in tourism, construction and related services could reduce labour demand and weaken income flows to labour-sending economies, particularly Pakistan and parts of the Levant, it added.

It estimated GDP growth would increase from 3.2pc in FY25 to 3.7pc in FY26 and 3.8pc in FY27, as services, manufacturing and livestock production remain resilient despite rising import costs. Higher commodity and transport costs are expected to put pressure on inflation and external balances, but continued strength in domestic activity is expected to outweigh these pressures.

The bank estimated the current account deficit at 0.1pc in FY2026, increasing significantly to 0.8pc in FY2027, while the fiscal deficit was estimated at 2.6pc in FY2026, rising to 3.5pc in FY2027.

It reported that food insecurity remained particularly acute in the occupied West Bank and Gaza and the Republic of Yemen, with significant pressures also evident in Afghanistan, Djibouti, Lebanon and Pakistan.

A stronger-than-usual El Niño weather pattern predicted for late 2026 could further amplify food-price pressures and hurt the poor. Pakistan is directly exposed through changing monsoon conditions, it said.

The burden of poverty was highly concentrated in the region.

"Pakistan accounts for about 48pc of the people in the region living below the $3.00 per day poverty line. Afghanistan, the Syrian Arab Republic and the Republic of Yemen together account for another 47pc," it said.

The most recent estimates show poverty rates at the $3.00-per-day line approached or exceeded 20pc in Djibouti, Pakistan, Syria and the Republic of Yemen. In 2024, 14.3pc of the Menaap region's population lived on less than $3.00 a day, compared with 10.4pc globally, while 26.9pc lived on less than $4.20 a day, compared with 18.9pc worldwide.

"The increase was driven primarily by a rise in poverty in Pakistan, where the poverty rate rose by 6.4 percentage points at the $3.00-per-day line and 3.2 percentage points at the $4.20-per-day line between 2018/19 and 2024/25, following a succession of adverse shocks, including the Covid-19 pandemic, the devastating 2022 floods, a macroeconomic crisis marked by high inflation and currency depreciation, and a prolonged period of economic adjustment that weakened real household incomes and employment opportunities."

Economic losses stemming from the US-Iran conflict are also concentrated in the region, but their ultimate scale remains highly uncertain and will depend on how the conflict evolves.

Under the baseline assumption that disruptions persist through the end of 2026 without sustained further escalation, the region is projected to contract by 2.1pc in 2026, after growing 3.3pc in 2025.

Oil-importing countries — Djibouti, the Arab Republic of Egypt, Jordan, Morocco, Pakistan and Tunisia — remain exposed through economic channels, including rising inflationary pressures from higher oil and other commodity prices, loss of fiscal space, a decline in remittances from the Gulf economies and increased borrowing costs, mainly because of higher insurance risk premiums as the conflict persists.
ir_summary: World Bank reports Pakistan accounts for nearly half of extreme poverty in the Middle East and North Africa region.

title: FBR allows late returns without surcharge
text:
ISLAMABAD: The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has proposed new rules allowing individuals who file their income tax returns after the due date or extended deadline to be included in the Active Taxpayers' List (ATL) without paying the prescribed surcharge.

The concession, however, will be subject to the condition that the individual undertakes not to purchase, acquire or otherwise obtain ownership or beneficial interest in any property for six months from the date of furnishing the undertaking through the FBR's Inland Revenue Information System (IRIS) portal.

The new rules were issued on Tuesday through SRO1690 of the Income Tax, as draft amendments to the Income Tax Rules 2002. FBR sought feedback from all stakeholders within one week before finalising them.

Under the proposed rule 81B, a new rule (2B) is proposed that provides that an individual who files an income tax return for the latest tax year after the due date or the extended deadline will be eligible for inclusion in the ATL without payment of the surcharge if the taxpayer submits an undertaking through the FBR's IRIS portal.

However, the concession comes with a significant restriction. The taxpayer will have to undertake that he or she will not purchase, acquire or otherwise obtain ownership or beneficial interest in any property for six months.

The six-month restriction will begin from the date appearing on the electronic acknowledgement generated by IRIS after successful submission of the newly prescribed Form ATL-U.

The proposed rules also give the FBR powers to verify whether a taxpayer has complied with the undertaking. The FBR may use information available under the Income Tax Ordinance as well as information received from any authority, agency, registry, financial institution or other lawful source.

If information available with the tax authorities shows that an individual acquired ownership or beneficial interest in a property during the six- month period, the taxpayer will first be provided an electronic opportunity of being heard.

governed by the existing provisions applicable to late filers.

The FBR has also proposed a new undertaking Form ATL-U for taxpayers seeking to avail themselves of the facility. The form will require the individual's name, CNIC or NTN, tax year, date of filing the return, IRIS acknowledgement or reference number and the date on which the undertaking is furnished. IRIS will electronically verify the undertaking.
ir_summary: Pakistan's tax authority proposes allowing late tax filers to avoid surcharges if they agree not to buy property for six months.

title: Moscow moot ends sans joint statement
text:
ISLAMABAD: The eighth edition of the Moscow Format regional consultations on Afghanistan on Monday ended without a joint communique, mainly because of disagreements between Pakistani and Afghan delegations in what was possibly the first instance in the series where participants failed to agree on a joint statement.

Russian presidential envoy for Afghanistan Zamir Kabulov said Moscow regretted that the participants could not agree on the final document.

"When drafting the final joint statement, we encountered one problem, that problem was that our Afghan and Pakistani colleagues didn't see eye to eye," he said.

The Moscow meeting brought together special envoys and senior officials from Afghanistan, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, with Belarus and Egypt attending as guests. The format dates back to 2016 -17 and has emerged as one of the main regional diplomatic tracks on Afghanistan.

The failure to agree on a joint statement underscored how the worsening Pakistan-Afghanistan dispute is now complicating wider regional efforts to build consensus on Afghanistan.

The tense relations between Islamabad and Kabul were among the key issues discussed at the meeting, with the dispute over terrorism and counterterrorism language ultimately preventing the adoption of the joint document.

Mr Kabulov said the Afghan side objected to references that placed Afghanistan in a terrorist context.

Pakistan's special envoy for Afghanistan, Moha­mmad Sadiq, told the meeting that Islamabad wanted peace and stability in the region and had pursued political and diplomatic engagement with the Taliban leadership to address terrorism emanating from Afghan soil.

"Pakistan desires peace and stability in the region and has remained patiently engaged in political and diplomatic efforts aimed at addressing the menace of terrorism emanating from Afghan soil. However, it is unfortunate that Pakistan's numerous goodwill gestures and highly responsible appr­oach were misconstrued, resulting in increased terrorist attacks from Afghan soil, with the active support and backing of the Taliban Regime," he said.

Afghan Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi, meanwhile, criticised Pakistan's statements and actions towards Afghanistan and Afghans, accusing Islamabad of using military pressure, refugees, students and transit routes as instruments of leverage.

At the same time, he insisted that the problems affecting relations bet­ween the two neighbours could be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy.

Russia offered to help de-escalate the dispute, although Kabulov stressed that resolving bilateral disputes was not the purpose of the Moscow Format.

"Russia is ready to assist in ending this conflict in any possible, permissible way either on its own or in partnership with our other partners provided that both sides make such a request. We are ready to provide the maximum possible assistance," he said.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, who opened the meeting, endorsed the performance of the Taliban authorities while warning against any attempt by Nato to establish military infrastructure in Afghanistan or neighbouring countries.

He backed assistance to Kabul and said strengthening Afghanistan's counterterrorism capacity served regional interests.

Meanwhile, the Inter­national Criminal Court on Monday unsealed arrest warrants for two Afghan ministers accused of committing crimes against humanity through the Taliban government's restrictions on women and girls, AFP reported.

The warrants, for Habibullah Agha, minister of education, and Neda Mohammad Nadeem, minister of higher education, were issued in September 2025 but remained under seal until Monday.

The two officials are accused of gender-based persecution linked to policies that have barred girls from attending school beyond primary level and excluded women from higher education following the Taliban's return to power in August 2021.

The two warrants against the ministers were issued after the ICC, in July 2025, authorised warrants for Afghanistan's Supreme Taliban Leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and Supreme Court President Abdul Hakim Haqqani, parts of which have been made public.

Both Agha and Nadeem were instrumental in imposing the supreme leader's vision of Afghanistan.

In a sharp reaction to the ICC warrants, a Taliban spokesman condemned the ICC position on the arrest of Afghan leaders.
ir_summary: Moscow Format talks on Afghanistan ended without a joint statement due to Pakistan-Afghanistan disagreements over terrorism language.

title: IMF talks likely to clear way for $1.2bn disbursement
text:
ISLAMABAD: Pakis­tan's ongoing talks with a visiting staff mission of the International Monet­ary Fund (IMF) are set to conclude on a positive note later this week, paving the way for the disbursement of about $1.2 billion under two concurrent progra­mmes — the $7bn Exten­ded Fund Facility (EFF) and the $1.4bn Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF).

Informed sources said the two sides were now finalising the Memor­andum of Econ­omic and Fiscal Policies (MEFP) after covering the substantive parameters of the biannual review.

Following the completion of the draft exchanges, the staff mission, led by Ms Iva Petrova, is expected to conclude its visit in the next couple of days, official sources said. There were no new demands from the Fund, except for makeup adjustments to bridge past slippages. The revenue target remains unchanged, with a greater focus on achieving the half-yearly target following robust collection in the first quarter, which exceeded the target.

The development comes as the authorities struggle to finalise the liquefied natural gas (LNG) import plan for the upcoming three winter months — December to February — amid a challenging supply situation stemming from the US-Iran conflict.

The gas companies and the petroleum division had sought at least 22 import cargoes for the three-month period, but the task force on energy, led by Lt Gen Zafar Iqbal, has promised no more than 10-12 cargoes of around 100 million cubic feet each on a best-effort basis, using all diplomatic and logistical channels.

The plan will be presented to the prime minister for approval, given the involvement of around $100m per spot cargo and the requirement for consent from the Ministry of Finance and the State Bank of Pakistan.

The matter has assumed greater importance because the LNG import plan will affect the current account targets agreed upon by the Ministry of Finance and the IMF. Sources, however, indicated that actual LNG imports may not exceed seven to eight cargoes over the three winter months, given prevailing market conditions, which would bring the outcome closer to the Ministry of Finance's desired level.

The two sides have agreed to expedite groundwork for targeted subsidies in the gas sector through the social protection programme to contain gas-sector circular debt and move BISP-based subsidies for the poorest consumers in the power sector into the implementation phase, starting January next year following the introduction of the revised base tariff.

The distribution companies have already filed tariff petitions during the course of the talks to demonstrate their preparedness to the IMF team, the sources said.

The government has assured the Fund of plans to reduce cross-subsidies from the industrial sector and contain gas-sector debt, which has now reached Rs3.6 trillion and continues to rise. This includes principal payables of around Rs1.8 trillion and almost an equivalent amount in accrued interest and late-payment surcharges.

The gas companies have reported that the introduction of a protected category for domestic consumers, involving gas prices of Rs200-350 per mmBtu, has aggravated the pricing gap and, consequently, increased circular debt. Only four of the 12 consumer slabs covered the cost of gas supply during the winter months, while the remaining eight remained below breakeven rates for around eight months despite the imposition of substantial fixed charges.

Although these measures are not being defined as prior actions, the authorities may have to take a few steps between the conclusion of the ongoing IMF talks and the scheduling of the Fund's Executive Board meeting to ensure smooth processing of Pakistan's case for the disbursement of $1.2bn and seek waivers for a couple of unavoidable slippages that had already occurred against the end-June 2026 targets.

An IMF structural benchmark committed by the government requires a major policy reform by end-January 2027 to replace the budgeted tariff-differential subsidy and cross-subsidy system with a targeted, budgeted subsidy framework for low-income consumers through BISP.

The World Bank is assisting the government in linking power consumers to the National Socio-Economic Registry. The government has undertaken to complete the technical linkage, along with validity checks, by end-November to determine eligibility criteria.

The IMF is now also pushing for greater transparency in the Inland Freight Equalisation Margin (IFEM), which facilitates uniform petroleum pricing across the country.
ir_summary: Pakistan and IMF finalize talks for $1.2 billion loan disbursement under economic programs.

title: Talks futile without Imran’s advice, asserts PTI
text:
ISLAMABAD: As the government reiterated that its doors were open for a dialogue with all political parties, the PTI on Monday said reconciliation with the ruling coalition was not possible without the involvement of jailed party chief Imran Khan.

Addressing a press conference at the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa House in the federal capital, PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja said only Imran Khan was able to bridge the gulf "developed between the state and the nation".

"Imran Khan is very important for us and we had every right to seek his opinion, but it was not allowed," Mr Raja said about the recent talks with the government.

The PTI leader said another reason for the failure of the talks was that the government was not willing to pursue a collective strategy against terrorism. "We were being pushed to support the government over every action being taken regarding terrorism in KP," he said, adding that the PTI had demanded that the government respect the recommendations and opinions of a jirga held by the KP Assembly, in which political parties and stakeholders had participated.

"We were told that a unanimous strategy against terrorism would not be developed and it would not be included in the agreement," he said, adding that the government had deliberately complicated the situation.

Federal Parliamentary Secretary for Information and Broadcasting Barrister Danyal Chaudhry said the government firmly believed in reconciliation and made serious efforts to resolve matters through dialogue and negotiation. The PTI sabotaged the negotiation process, he alleged.

Flanked by Prime Minister's Coordinator Ikhtiar Wali Khan, Barrister Danyal said the government engaged the PTI with complete sincerity and made every effort to resolve matters amicably.

"The government is ready to take all political forces along and believes in resolving political differences democratically through dialogue and reconciliation," he said, noting that the PTI lacked clear leadership on negotiations.

On the performance of the PTI government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, he said serious questions had been raised over the past 15 years regarding governance and law and order in the province. "Corruption flourished in KP while basic facilities and administrative improvements remained elusive," he claimed.

Minister for Kashmir Affairs and Gilgit-Baltistan Amir Muqam, however, said the government's delegation had suggested that both sides "be on the same page" about terrorism.
ir_summary: PTI insists talks with government are impossible without jailed leader Imran Khan's involvement and criticizes anti-terrorism strategy.

title: Makkah accord nations agree to deploy rapid force
text:
ISLAMABAD: Members of the Makkah defence pact announced their intention to begin rapid force deployment, aimed at enhancing Saudi Arabia's "readiness, military integration, and the collective capacity to confront and counter threats".

The announcement came as the Riyadh-backed Yemeni government claimed recapturing the key Red Sea port of Mocha, amid its bid to retake control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.

Meanwhile, fighting between the government forces and Houthi militia raged in other parts of the country.

Government forces advanced rapidly along the coast with heavy Saudi air support to seize key positions in the Dhubab area on the narrowest point of the strait, a vital oil route whose seizure by the Iran-backed Houthis last month sent shockwaves through energy markets.

The offensive came against the backdrop of a meeting of the Makkah Defence Alliance in Riyadh, which convened in the Saudi capital to take stock of the Houthi attacks on the kingdom.

Military spokesman Lt Col Majid Abdullah al-Nuzayli said the pro-government forces had "successfully taken control of Bab al-Mandeb". In a series of statements, he said that government forces also took control of Dhubab airport and cut off the road between Dhubab and Mocha. Hundreds of Houthi fighters have been surrounded in the Dhubab area, he said, adding that some Houthi fighters later fled by boat via the sea.

The government offensive was announced on Sunday to recapture territory, with Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi swearing to fight "until the country is liberated from the grip of the terrorist militia".

Saudi Arabia, which arms and trains Yemeni government forces, is backing the military campaign with air power and has sought logistical help from allies to push back the Houthis, restore free traffic in the Red Sea, and end the group's attacks on its territory. Riyadh said on Monday it had attacked hundreds of targets in Yemen to provide air cover for the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and Yemeni ground forces.

"100 fighter jets participated at dawn today in Operation 'Dawn of Yemen'," Saudi-led coalition spokesman Major Gen Turki al-Maliki wrote on X, using the name for the new offensive announced on Sunday.

The Houthi-run health ministry said two people had been killed and seven wounded in strikes on Sanhan and Sa'wan districts in Sanaa province. The renewed fighting has worsened a humanitarian crisis in Yemen, with the UN migration agency saying on Monday that some 184,000 people had now been displaced since the war resumed.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland that Saudi Arabia has a right to defend itself against attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels, Al Jazeera reported.

"Obviously the Saudis have come under Houthi attack … and they have a right to defend themselves", he said, adding that neither Riyadh nor Yemen's internationally recognised government was "in favour of [Houthi] control in that territory". Mr Rubio also stressed that the US intended to honour the security agreement it had with Saudi Arabia.

While the war has raged on several frontlines in Yemen, the heaviest fighting has been in the southwest, both in the coastal area near the strait and in the hills around Taiz, where the Houthis have been battling to surround government forces. Last week Houthi attacks damaged a culvert on the Taiz-Aden road, making it impassable. On Sunday night, the fighters made new advances into the town of al-Turbah, sitting atop a high promontory on the road, five government military sources said, though another government source denied this.

A Houthi-run news agency on Monday cited a military source as saying the group had driven government forces from the al-Mawasit district of Taiz province, reaching the home of Alimi, head of Yemen's interim presidential council. Taiz, nestled among Yemen's southern highlands, has been on the frontlines since early in the civil war, often under Houthi shell and sniper fire.

A Houthi attack on the Saudi energy infrastructure damaged the East-West pipeline, AFP reported. "A pumping station east of Riyadh in Khurais. It wasn't targeted before. There was big damage and the pipeline stopped again," the report, citing a source, said. The information came a day after the Iran-backed Houthis said they targeted sites in Saudi Arabia belonging to state oil giant Aramco, including infrastructure in Khurais. The East-West pipeline has been targeted multiple times after war erupted across the Middle East following US-Israeli strikes on Iran. In September, it remained shut for almost 11 days.

A government source denied the oil pipeline halted operations.

Meanwhile in Riyadh, members of the Makkah Defence Alliance affirmed that the alliance embodied a firm commitment to collective defence and a unified position in confronting threats, the Foreign Office said on Monday.

The committee decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom, in accordance with the approved arrangements and the national legislation of the parties.

The members affirmed that the security of each member was an integral part of the collective security of the three countries, and that translating the Makkah defence pact into practical measures demonstrated the credibility of the commitment to collective defence, the statement added. It also strengthened the effectiveness of deterrence, and reaffirmed the unity and determination of the three countries to defend their security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, in accordance with the provisions of the agreement.

The parties also condemned in the strongest terms the attempted targeting of Makkah and Madinah, as well as the continuing attacks targeting cities and civilian and economic facilities in the Kingdom, reaffirming their unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the Kingdom's security and territorial integrity.

As part of the institutional development of the Makkah Alliance for Defence, the committee decided to appoint retired Lt Gen Nauman Mahmood as the first secretary general for a three-year term. Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif and army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir represented Paki­stan at the meeting.

Multiple vessels were struck by unknown projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz on October 4 and October 3, while another tanker was forced to turn back after a warning by the Iranian Guards. An AFP report citing the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) said a tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz inbound was hailed by the IRGC and instructed to turn back, or the vessel would be targeted. "The master of the tanker has confirmed that they have complied with the instruction," the UKMTO said, adding that the ship was entering the strait near the Omani coastline.
ir_summary: Makkah defence pact nations agree to deploy rapid force to counter threats amid Yemen conflict and Houthi attacks.

title: Spain’s PM calls snap election after housing bill defeat
text:
MADRID: Spain's Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday called a snap election for Nov 29, after parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government amid nationwide protests.

The defeat on Friday was just the latest political setback for Sanchez, one of the few left-leaning government leaders still in power in Europe. "To do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people," Sanchez said in a televised address, adding that his aim was "to secure a much broader, progressive majority in parliament".

The next general election was scheduled to take place by August 2027. His announcement came after tens of thousands of people marched in Madrid and other cities on Saturday demanding action on housing affordability.

The government's proposed measures, which included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants, were voted down by opposition parties in Spain's parliament.

The defeat infuriated the protesters and underscored the difficulties Sanchez's minority coalition government faces in passing legislation. The protests were fuelled by the eviction last month of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid flat where she had lived for decades.

Hundreds of demonstrators have occupied a tent camp in central Madrid for more than a week, demanding housing reforms. One of them, 19-year-old student Sara Prieto Aparicio, said that she believed that calling the snap election "was the best thing to do". "There is a big mobilisation by citizens and I think this favours elections," she said.

"This wave of indignation is unstoppable and we are not going to stop," Alicia del Rio, a spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants' Union, one of the protest leaders, said while renewing a call for a general strike. Recent opinion polls have generally put the main opposition conservative Popular Party (PP) ahead of the Socialists.

The PP would likely need to partner with the far-right Vox to form a government however. Making housing the central campaign issue "could mobilise left-leaning voters", said Federico Santi, a Europe analyst at political risk consultancy Eurasia Group.

He said an early election could help limit further erosion of support for the Socialists, amid resurgent inflation, legislative deadlock and corruption scandals. Housing has become one of Spain's main political issues as supply lags demand.
ir_summary: Spain's PM calls snap election after parliament rejects his housing bill amid nationwide protests.

title: Intense heat puts births in jeopardy, UN tells climate talks
text:
NADI: Extreme heat is increasingly linked to problems such as premature births or underweight babies, the UN climate chief warned on Monday as Fiji hosted talks ahead of a major summit.

This week's meetings in the city of Nadi and on the atoll nation of Tuvalu are aimed at drawing the world's attention to life on the frontline of climate change in the Pacific.

They are a precursor to the larger UN-sponsored global climate summit — known as COP31 — to be held in Turkiye next month.

Highlighting the need for urgent action, United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell cited a new survey showing more than two-thirds of health professionals across five continents had seen complications caused by intense heat in the past five years.

"Climate-driven extreme heat during pregnancy is increasingly linked to premature birth, stillbirth, low birth weight, and maternal complications," he said.

The Plan International charity said in a separate report on Monday that climate disasters were also increasing the risk of child marriage and teen pregnancies, in part through their impact on the health and education services on which girls depend.

The South Pacific is among the most vulnerable regions in the world to global warming — from rising sea waters jeopardising homes to increasing temperatures causing coral bleaching. Fiji's climate minister Lynda Tabuya called for commitments from developed nations to a "just transition", with support for "countries in the world that suffer the most".

A UN report released in August found developing countries needed $310 billion-$365 billion to adapt, yet had only $26 billion in adaptation finance available in 2023. "We rely on and we appeal to countries to commit to climate finance," Tabuya said. Australia — the head of this year's climate negotiations and a major coal exporter — faces accusations of hypocrisy. Its sales of the fossil fuel have boomed on the back of demand caused by the Middle East conflict.

Tabuya told journalists there had been "frank discussion" on Monday with Australian counterpart Chris Bowen and Pacific officials. "Yes, we have sentiments expressed from certain countries," she said, when asked if she backed calls from other Pacific leaders for Australia to halt expansion of coal and gas projects.

"But for the Pacific, it's important at this pre-COP that we find common ground. There will be things that we disagree on, but we can agree to disagree," Tabuya said.

Also high on the agenda is a push by Pacific leaders for the world to stick to a target of limiting global warming to 1.5C and give more attention to the impact on oceans.

"Keeping 1.5 alive means hope — hope for Tuvalu, hope for Kiribati, hope for small island atolls around the world," Bowen told journalists.

"We can actually come to this conversation and say, 'as a fossil-fuel exporting nation, we can bring something different to the table'," he said. Sea levels are also rising at a record pace, driven by warming oceans and glacier melt, according to the August UN report.
ir_summary: UN climate chief warns of heat-related birth complications at Pacific climate talks, urging finance for vulnerable nations.

title: Flydubai co-pilot wanted to crash plane into Israeli airport: officials
text:
JERUSALEM/WASHINGTON: The flydubai co-pilot who stabbed his captain in a suspected attempt to crash the plane has told UAE interrogators he planned the attack before he was hired by the Dubai state-owned airline, according to two Israeli officials with knowledge of the probe.

A third source briefed on the UAE probe said the co-pilot, an Omani national, had planned to crash flight into Ben-Gurion airport near Tel Aviv. He had also operated a flight to Tel Aviv earlier this year and intended to hijack and crash the plane then, but opted not to, the source added.

It was not immediately clear why the co-pilot changed his mind on that previous flight, although the co-pilot is thought to have known someone onboard.

The co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073, which had been bound for Israel from Dubai, attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said, calling the incident a "terrorist attack". Two sources have said the co-pilot is an Omani national named Hamam al-Hammami. Israeli officials have not named the co-pilot but have said he is from Oman. UAE authorities and flydubai have not publicly disclosed the co-pilot's identity. Al-Hammami is in UAE custody.

US Vice President JD Vance said on Monday he has not seen anything conclusive yet on an Iranian role in the flydubai incident. Vance spoke to reporters before leaving on a flight to Alaska. The two Israeli officials said the co-pilot told interrogators that he had applied for a job at Dubai state-owned flydubai after searching for airlines that fly to Tel Aviv.
ir_summary: Flydubai co-pilot attempted to crash plane into Israeli airport in a terrorist attack, according to UAE and Israeli officials.

title: Farming reform
text:
THE Kissan Board Pakistan has demanded that agriculture receive at least 10pc of the federal and provincial budgets to lower input costs and address recurring deficits.

The farmers' body also wants support prices of Rs5,000 per 40kg for wheat and Rs700 for sugarcane, citing declining profitability. It has criticised urea shortages, high electricity bills, weak fruit sector returns, and the Pak-Afghan border closure, warning of protests if their demands are not met. Their case for enhanced budgetary allocations deserves consideration. The sector contributes about 22pc of GDP and supports nearly 60pc of the population, but receives only 2-3pc of allocations. However, money alone will not fix matters. Nor should a larger allocation become another excuse for inefficient price subsidies. Pakistan has spent decades trying to support farmers through administered prices, input subsidies and other interventions. This has distorted markets, encouraged inefficient production and benefited better-connected producers more than small farmers.

Public investment should, instead, address structural weaknesses that depress farm productivity. Water management, irrigation efficiency, farm-to-market roads, storage, research, extension services and better seed technology need sustained investment. Mechanisation must become a central priority. Shared machinery services, and affordable financing can help spread mechanisation without imposing a massive capital burden on farmers. The aim should be to lower production costs, while raising yields and quality. That requires modernisation, not perpetual protection from market forces. Farmers cannot become globally competitive if they face unpredictable trade policies, distorted input markets, poor access to finance, unreliable power and water supply, and arbitrary official intervention in crop markets. Policy must encourage farmers to respond to prices and market demand rather than to official announcements.

Pakistan also needs to look beyond the farm gate. A stronger downstream processing industry can reduce post-harvest losses, add value to farm output and create export opportunities. Better cold storage, grading, packaging, processing, and logistics are essential, and can help stabilise markets when production falls by allowing stocks to be preserved. This matters because agriculture is treated as a production problem when it is really a value-chain issue. Producing more wheat, fruit, vegetables, sugarcane or rice means little if large quantities are wasted, farmers receive poor returns, and consumers face shortages or sudden price spikes. Farmers, therefore, are right to demand greater public investment. But the test should not be the size of the allocation. It should be where the money goes and what it achieves. Agriculture needs investment, but not another round of costly interventions. It needs infrastructure, technology, mechanisation, processing, markets, and policies that make farming competitive rather than dependent on the state's largesse.
ir_summary: Pakistani farmers demand higher budget allocations and support prices, calling for agricultural reforms to address structural issues and improve competitiveness.

title: Mass surveillance
text:
THE new National Cybercrime Investigation Agency chief, Ali Nasir Rizvi, has adopted a "zero-tolerance policy against fake news and anti-state propaganda", according to the agency.

Troublingly, neither 'fake news' nor 'anti-state propaganda' has a clear, legal meaning, and the fact that these terms are now centrepieces in the NCCIA's policy gives rise to concerns about what the state's priorities truly are. The authority's mandate includes protecting citizens from fraud, harassment, blackmail, and financial scams. It recently shut down several fraudulent call centres, showing it can deliver well on those responsibilities. Monitoring and policing opinion are something else altogether.

Further, the fact that the NCCIA has established 'cyber patrolling units' in every region is alarming. Why is the authority engaging in mass public surveillance? What is being monitored, for what purpose, and under what legal authority? Who will be providing oversight, and how will citizens be protected from excessive surveillance? Since the DG has promised merit and transparency, he should satisfy the public in this regard.

It is worth pointing out here that these special units for surveillance sit atop the 2025 Peca amendments, which criminalised spreading 'false' information, amid strong protests from journalists and rights groups. The timing of the announcement also comes amidst a deadlock between the government and the opposition over protests announced by the latter.

In such a charged political environment, the message would seem to be that dissent, not disinformation, is the actual target. It is hoped that the NCCIA will act with restraint and transparency to avoid cementing that perception. The authority must avoid politicising its work.

Misinformation and disinformation do real harm; the answer to them is fast, credible official communication, improved media literacy, and platform accountability, not prosecution and lawfare. The state must build trust with the public if it wishes to defeat what it calls 'fake news' and 'propaganda'.
ir_summary: Pakistan's cybercrime agency adopts zero-tolerance policy against fake news and anti-state propaganda amid concerns over mass surveillance and political dissent.

title: Services exports surge 29pc
text:
ISLAMABAD: Services exports grew by a robust 28.89 per cent year on year in the first two months of 2026-27, largely driven by higher earnings from information technology.

According to official data compiled by the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS), services exports have continued to expand, maintaining uninterrupted growth since the start of FY27, in contrast to mixed trends in goods shipments.

In absolute terms, services exports totalled $1.81 billion in July-August FY27, up from $1.41bn in the corresponding months of last year. In August, services exports rose 28.97pc to $873.01 million, from $676.91m in the corresponding month last year. Telecomm­unications, computer and information services have driven growth since the beginning of the fiscal year.

According to data compiled by the State Bank of Pakistan, exports of telecommunications, computer and information services grew 17.36pc to $811m in 2MFY27 from $691m a year ago.

Exports of other business services surged 38.62pc to $420m in 2MFY27, from $303m in the same period last year. Similarly, exports of transport services increased by 35.87pc to $178m from $131m a year earlier.

However, exports of travel services surged 146.66pc to $222m from $90m in 2MFY26.

At the same time, services imports rose 9.77pc to $2.37bn in 2MFY27, from $2.16bn in the corresponding period last year. In August, services imports rose 2.53pc to $1.15bn, from $1.13bn a year ago.
ir_summary: Pakistan's services exports grew 29% in early FY27, driven by IT and telecommunications, while imports also increased.

title: Nine parties prequalify for Gepco
text:
ISLAMABAD: The Pri­v­a­tisation Commission board has approved the prequalification of nine parties interested in acqui­ring Gujranwala Electric Power Company (Gepco).

The board meeting, held on Monday and chaired by Adviser to the Prime Minister on Privatisation Muhammad Ali, was informed that it had received 11 expressions of interest (EoIs) for acquiring 51 per cent to 100pc shareholding, along with management control.

After evaluating the submissions against the approved prequalification criteria, the financial adviser recommended nine interested parties for prequalification and progression to the next stage of the transaction.

The prequalified parties include three Turkish energy companies, alongside leading Pakistani business groups and investment consortia, reflecting continued domestic and international investor interest in Pakistan's electricity distribution sector.

The nine prequalified parties will now proceed to the next stage of the transaction under the approved process, including access to the Virtual Data Room (VDR) for detailed buy-side due diligence, a press release said.
ir_summary: Pakistan's Privatisation Commission approves nine parties to bid for acquiring majority stake in Gujranwala Electric Power Company.

title: Govt concedes marginal power tariff surges
text:
ISLAMABAD: After months of reluctance, the Power Division finally conceded on Monday that the marginal power price had significantly incre­ased 'due to regional war' and the subsidised rates to a select industrial category had burdened other consumer categories.

This came at a public hearing convened by the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra), whose case officers reported that the average power supply cost now stood at Rs32 per unit, compared with Rs22.98 per unit offered to industrial consumers on Dece­mber 10 last year under the Incremental Consum­ption Package.

The Power Division team led by additional secretary Mehfooz Bhatti and Naveed Qaiser, however, warned that its retrospective correction from June 9, as demanded by wider in­dustrial consumers thro­ugh interventions, would need to be legally examined.

The government team generally appeared on the back foot, as Mr Bhatti said the incremental package was announced after almost a year of hard work on industry demand, but nobody could have anticipated a 'war scene' that changed 'economic fundamentals'.

Not only the industrial representatives Rehan Javed, Amir Shaikh, Arif Bilwani and Tanveer Barry but also Nepra members Amina Ahmad, Ghulamullah Shaikh and Maqsood Anwar wondered why the government team had not applied for review of the package on completion of the mandatory six-month period and why it did not work out the latest or average marginal cost.

Rehan Javed protested that he had been highlighting the fault since February through 48 emails and multiple representations at monthly public hearings, but both the power division and Nepra had turned a deaf ear.

He said the package rate was frozen at Rs22.98, while the cost averaged Rs34.26 per unit.

As a result, other consumers paid about Rs11.28 per unit, cross-subsidising fewer industrial consumers who benefited from the below-cost rate.

Mr Rehan and Mr Shaikh made a strong case for suspending the incremental package and its readjustments to consumers with effect from June 9, when the review was legally due.
ir_summary: Pakistan's Power Division admits electricity tariff increases due to regional war and cross-subsidization issues at a regulatory hearing.

title: Power sector losses drag state-owned entities' profits
text:
ISLAMABAD: The aggregate profitability of the state-owned entities (SOEs) contracted by 30 per cent in the first half of FY26 as their overall performance deteriorated across seven core areas, increasing fiscal and material macroeconomic risks to the sovereign state of Pakistan.

According to the July-December 2025 SOEs Monitoring Report, released on Monday by the Ministry of Finance, the power sector remains the weakest performer, but the aggregate loss profile of loss-making SOEs is estimated at about Rs2.8 billion per day, while fiscal support through subsidies, grants, loans, and equity injections has reached nearly Rs6.6bn per day. Power sector circular debt increased by Rs374bn, driven by inefficiencies and poor recoveries.

This is "equivalent to approximately 11pc of total federal budgetary receipts (on the six-month period)", the MoF deplored, adding that "this persistent fiscal burden continues to crowd out developmental expenditure, compress fiscal flexibility, and weaken sovereign fiscal buffers".

The broader SOE balance sheet also remains highly leveraged, with debt exposures exceeding Rs10tr, including about Rs2.5tr in foreign currency-denominated liabilities or Foreign Relent Loans (FRLs), exposing the sovereign to elevated exchange rate pass-through risk, refinancing pressure, imported sensitivity, and external account volatility.

Collectively, these risks indicate that Pakistan's SOE sector is no longer merely a governance challenge, but a high-impact sovereign balance sheet vulnerability with direct implications for fiscal sustainability, sovereign creditworthiness, debt dynamics, external financing dependence, and long-term macroeconomic stability.

In the first core area of aggregate profitability and losses, the report noted that the situation deteriorated. "During the first half of FY26 (July-December 2025), the SOEs experienced a mild contraction in financial performance. Aggregate profits declined by 7pc, dropping from Rs457.2bn in HY2025 to Rs423.3bn in HY2026". On the loss front, cumulative losses across SOEs remained broadly stable, edging down marginally from Rs342.9bn in HY2025 to Rs342.8bn in HY2026.

"Combined, these movements resulted in a net adjusted profit of Rs80.5bn for HY2026, representing a 30pc contraction from the Rs114.3bn net aggregate profit recorded in HY2025", the Central Monitoring Unit (CMU) of the MoF said.

Despite a marginal consolidated profit, the report said the narrowing spread between profits and losses signalled rising fiscal and operational pressures within the federal SOE portfolio. On the second parameter of the aggregate balance sheet, the report noted a modest contraction across key financial indicators. Total equity declined by 3pc, falling from Rs6.629tr in HY2025 to Rs6.407tr in HY2026. Liabilities also edged lower, down 1pc from Rs31.092tr to Rs30.7tr.

As a result, total assets contracted by 2pc, declining from Rs37.721tr in HY2025 to Rs37.107tr in HY2026, underscoring a modest weakening in the overall financial position of the SOE sector.

"However, the reduction in equity alongside elevated leverage levels continues to expose the portfolio to heightened fiscal and refinancing risk, particularly in capital-intensive sectors such as power, infrastructure, and transport".

The dominance of a handful of SOEs in driving aggregate profitability highlights a material concentration risk within the federal portfolio. A substantial portion of overall earnings remains dependent upon the Oil & Gas and financial sectors, thereby exposing the broader SOE ecosystem to commodity price volatility, exchange-rate movements, regulatory adjustments, and macroeconomic cyclicality.
ir_summary: Pakistan's state-owned entities' profits fell 30% due to power sector losses, increasing fiscal risks and sovereign debt exposure.

title: Major assault on Houthis as Riyadh moot begins
text:
ISTANBUL: Yemen's internationally-recognised Saudi-backed government on Sunday launched a major military campaign to recapture territory held by the Houthis, just a day before Riyadh hosts an emergency meeting of the Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia leaders under the Makkah agreement.

The announcement for the major military offensive, aimed at retaking all areas under Houthi control, came from the head of Yemen's presidential council, Rashad al-Alimi.

Pakistan's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said earlier on Friday that a meeting of Makkah Def­ence Alliance's Strategic Poli­tical Defence Committee (SPDC) would focus on the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis showed no signs of abating over the weekend, with the Houthis saying the kingdom had launched dozens of strikes on Yemen's capital Sanaa after which they attacked an Aramco facility with ballistic missiles and drones in south of Riyadh.

The foes have traded strikes since the Houthis seized all of Yemen's Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandab strait in a lightning offensive.

On Sunday, the Houthis also cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government's interim capital Aden, according to four security sources.

Just hours later, Yemen's presidential council head said, "I announce today the start of military operations to retake the remaining territories of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory." He called on all the armed forces to begin carrying out their assigned missions, in accordance with the approved plans, until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthis.

Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around Taiz province has killed more than 70 people over the past day. Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 troops were killed — 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj — while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.

The Houthis, formally known as Ansar Allah, have controlled Yemen's capital Sanaa and large parts of the northwest, where most of the population lives, since 2014. They have withstood a series of attacks over the years by Saudi Arabia, the UAE and their Western allies.

The movement launched a surprise offensive last month which captured the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and some 150km of coast on the Red Sea in a matter of weeks, giving the Houthis new leverage over the international shipping route. That advance also opened a new front in the US-Israeli war launched in February against Iran, to which Tehran's responses included choking oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, to the other side of the Arabian Peninsula.

Alimi said the decision to launch the counteroffensive came after all chances of de-escalating the conflict had been exhausted. He thanked Saudi Arabia for its support and called on Yemen's regional allies and international partners to support the Yemen forces and institutions.

Regional and western officials had told Reuters earlier this week that Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies were planning to launch an assault on the Houthis, with the Saudis leading aerial combat and Yemeni forces fighting on the ground.

The US is already providing intelligence to support Riyadh's operations in Yemen, while some regional and European nations are providing mainly defensive military aid to the kingdom, six people with knowledge of the Saudi preparations told Reuters.

Meanwhile, the foreign ministers of Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia would meet in Riyadh on Monday to discuss the developing situation.

According to Mr Dar, this was an emergency meeting which would focus on the Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia, as the previous meeting of foreign ministers in New York had done. The committee would meet again as planned after "the end of October or beginning of November".

"The meeting will address recent developments in the region and the stage reached in the Alliance's institutionalisation efforts," the Turkish foreign ministry said. It said Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Defence Minister Yasar Guler and Chief of the General Staff Gen Selcuk Bayraktaroglu would attend the meeting of the pact's strategic political and defence committee, along with officials from Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.
ir_summary: Yemen's Saudi-backed government launches major military offensive against Houthis amid regional diplomatic meetings on security.

title: PTI embarks on planned protest march
text:
PESHAWAR/LAKKI MARWAT: A day after rele­asing the five-day plan for the protest march, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on Sunday launched the march from Lakki Marwat after reaching the city by helicopter to lead the protest.

The PTI decided to embark on the march after talks with the federal government failed for multiple reasons, particularly over the counterterrorism policy.

Addressing the participants, CM Afridi said the PTI's negotiating committee had gone to Islamabad to lower the political temperature, but those making decisions behind closed doors had sabotaged the talks.

"They wanted their will to prevail in KP, but I declared that only Imran Khan's vision and policies would be implemented here. We do not accept any policy that is not in the interest of the people of KP and the Pakhtuns," he claimed. Both sides blame each other for the collapse of talks.

The chief minister declared: "We are not 'yes-men'; we are soldiers of Imran Khan, and we will carry forward his policies." He repeatedly asked the crowd whether it supported a military operation, asking those opposed to it to raise their hands. He questioned the policy being followed to tackle terrorism, saying: "What kind of policy is this, where terrorism has persisted for 22 years?"

Sunday night, the convoy had entered Karak district and reached Hamidan Chowk.

Former CM Ali Amin Gandapur, who was leading PTI workers from Dera Ismail Khan to Lakki Marwat, took a U-turn from Yarik because of road blockades and the prevailing law and order situation.

Addressing the workers at Yarik, he noted that Section 144 had been imposed in the area for three days and that the party leadership had clearly directed workers not to damage public property or engage in any activity that could worsen the situation.

Mr Gandapur told the workers that the return should not be viewed as a withdrawal from the protest movement, but as a temporary decision based on the prevailing circumstances, the safety of the workers and the instructions of the party leadership. He emphasised that the law and order situation did not warrant keeping a large number of workers at the site overnight.

He also told the workers that they could remain at Yarik if they wanted to, but he could not violate the instructions by party leadership. However, some workers expressed disagreement with the decision to take the convoy back. They said they wanted to stay and continue their participation in the protest for as long as the movement continued.

Mr Gandapur expressed displeasure over their position and urged them to take the situation on the ground into account. "TikTok-type talk" should not be made here, he told the workers, stressing that decisions had to be based on the situation on the ground. He then persuaded the workers to return, following which the convoy left Yarik for D.I. Khan.

According to the plan shared by the KP CM on X, PTI supporters from Tank, Dera Ismail Khan, South and North Waziristan and Bannu will join the march from Lakki Marwat's Gandi Chowk on Oct 4. The caravan will halt for the night near Karak, from where people will depart at 12:30pm the next day and stay overnight near Kohat. At 12pm on Oct 6, protesters from Kohat, Hangu, Kurram, and Orakzai will join the convoy, which will move towards Peshawar.

The caravan will depart from Budh Bair in Peshawar on Oct 7 afternoon. "The remaining constituencies of Peshawar will join us at Kohat Road Bridge and the Motorway Toll Plaza. And we will spend the night near Charsadda Interchange," the KP CM said. They would then depart the Charsadda Interchange at 12:30pm on Oct 8 after people from Charsadda and Mohmand join them.

Refraining from detailing the final leg of the trip to the federal capital, CM Afridi said the people "of entire KP" would gather at Khairabad in Nowshera on Oct 8 and spend the night there. "The next phase will be announced there." Ahead of the march, movement on several roads in KP had been banned under Sec­­tion 144, which was imposed in D.I. Khan, Hangu, Tank, and Upper and Lower South Waziristan.

Afridi assailed for using 'state helicopter'

A special helipad was prepared near Maidadkhel for the CM and a video shared on social media earlier showed a crowd of PTI workers gathered around it as KP's CM touched down. A video shared by the PTI on its X account showed Afridi's convoy surrounded by a large crowd of supporters. Information Minister Attaullah Tarar criticised Afridi for using a "state helicopter for a political march". Calling the use of the helicopter a "violation of the Islamabad High Court's orders", he wrote on X, referring to a recent ruling that directed provincial governments to ensure that no government resources or machinery were used to facilitate any march or gathering.
ir_summary: PTI launches protest march in KP over failed talks with federal government on counterterrorism policy.

title: Inter­national Labour Organ­isation top official due tomorrow on four-day visit
text:
ISLAMABAD: The Dir­e­ctor-General of Inter­national Labour Organ­isation (ILO), Gilbert F. Houngbo, will pay a four-day official visit to Pakis­tan from Oct 6 to strengthen the ILO's longstanding partnership with Pakistan and its tripartite constituents and advance shared priorities for decent work and social justice.

During his visit, Mr Houngbo will hold meetings with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, President Asif Ali Zardari and Min­ister for Overseas Pakist­anis and Human Resource Development Chaudhry Salik Hussain.

He will also meet the chief ministers of Sindh and Punjab during visits to Karachi and Lahore.

A key highlight of the visit will be the 75th anniversary of the Employers' Federation of Pakistan (EFP) in Karachi, which Mr Houngbo will attend.

The ILO Director-General will also travel to the Gadani ship recycling yards where he will see ILO-supported work to promote safer and more sustainable ship recycling.

According to ILO Pakis­tan, the visit of Mr Hou­ngbo will provide an oppo­r­tunity to engage with stakeholders on improving occupational safety and health, working conditions and environmental practices in the sector. In Lahore, Mr Houngbo will meet workers' representatives and visit Millat Tractors.
ir_summary: ILO Director-General visits Pakistan to discuss labor rights, meet officials, and promote decent work and safety standards.

title: Situationer: Can Afridi strike a balance between agitation & governance?
text:
WHILE the PTI focuses on political mobilisation to secure Imran Khan's release, the province it is charged with governing continues to face acute security pressures.

At present, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa remains the bastion of PTI's political power. With the provincial government in its hands, the party enjoys a degree of security that allows it operational space and maneuverability.

In the ongoing political contest, KP provides PTI with a crucial fallback option; a platform from which it can continue to function and regroup.

But the province has also borne the brunt of terrorist attacks, mostly blamed on the proscribed Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), who Islamabad accuses of using Afghan soil to stage their assaults.

Since the outfit renewed its attacks following the breakdown of a 'ceasefire deal' in Nov 2022, security forces have conducted several targeted intelligence-based operations along the north-western border, though the PTI-led provincial administration has opposed such actions at times.

Data from the Centre for Research and Security Studies' (CRSS) Annual Security Report 2025 indicated a nationwide rise in fatalities from 2,555 in 2024 to 3,417 in 2025, a 34 per cent increase. KP alone accounted for 711 of these deaths, an 82pc share of the national rise.

"In light of these facts and figures, the question that comes to mind is why the majority of terror incidents take place in KP," military spokesperson Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry asked at a recent press conference.

"The primary reason for this is the politically conducive environment provided [to terrorists], and the political-terror nexus that is flourishing in the province," he had claimed at the time.

The province's chief executive, Sohail Afridi, has been the focal point of such claims.

The federal government has repeatedly criticised the provincial administration over worsening law and order, and accused it of not coordinating with the Centre. For his part, CM Afridi has publicly criticised military operations against terrorist groups in KP, and indicated the party's preference to negotiate with Afghanistan.

The chief minister claims the deteriorating security environment is the result of a failed foreign policy, pursued over the last 22 years.

"If a policy is not delivering results and is continuously failing, there is a need to change it," he said during a recent visit to Kohat, in the wake of a suicide bombing that claimed the lives of several security personnel.

Simultaneously, Afridi has been charged with spearheading the protest movement by none other than Imran Khan himself, and has made multiple trips to Islamabad to meet the incarcerated PTI founder, albeit without much success.

He has also taken the lead in coordinating the party's nationwide "street movement", efforts that culminated in the present protest, following a series of delays and postponements.

Professor Faizullah Jan, a journalism professor at the University of Peshawar, said, "I think Afridi has been selected because he is hard-headed like Murad Saeed, indebted to Imran for everything, and being 'anti-establishment.' Because of his young age and a lack of experience (in governance and politics), he is unlikely to be a threat to party leadership, unlike Pervez Khattak, Mehmood Khan, and Gandapur."

Critics argue that his focus on agitation, especially at a time when the province faces escalating security threats and growing political pressure, has intensified questions about the PTI-led government's ability to govern effectively.

Coming to mainstream politics from the Insaf Students Federation (ISF), Afridi maintains a natural connection with the youth and claims to operate on the same wavelength as them. As a former special assistant for communication and works to his predecessor, Ali Amin Gandapur, he had previously demonstrated his abilities as a firebrand speaker, effectively articulating the party's narrative.

His approach to political mobilisation is, therefore, inseparable from the broader PTI strategy, which is central to understanding the province's current state of unrest.

For his administration, the challenge is not merely resisting pressure from the Centre, but demonstrating that governance can proceed even amid political mobilisation.

"Despite the KP chief minister's combative mood, they (provincial government) want a working relationship [with the federal government]," Ahmed Bilal Mehboob of the Pakistan Institute of Legislative Development and Transparency (Pildat) told Dawn.

"Imposing governor's rule will cause more agitation," he added. "Both the KP and federal governments need to coexist."

His detractors would have you believe that this is not possible.

Describing the PTI's rule, KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi says the party has been unable to balance political agitation with its administrative responsibilities, and has neglected issues such as terrorism, corruption and problems faced by medical staff and university faculty, among other issues.

"They don't pay attention to these provincial issues; they only care about agitation and the march to Islamabad and what people are saying about them on social media, so they can one-up each other," the governor says. "There are three or four groups within them (the PTI) which do not agree with each other."

Mr Kundi said that whenever he speaks with the president, prime minister or interior minister, he informs them that the provincial government "is not seriously monitoring the law and order situation".

"They do not attend the funerals of army officers and personnel and these people want to go off to Islamabad. There are a lot of issues," he says.

But how does the PPP leader - whose own party has spearheaded protests against the Centre in recent months - justify his criticism when another party opts for a similar course of action?

Giving examples of PPP and Jamaat-i-Islami protests in recent months, Mr Kundi notes that this political agitation was largely peaceful.

"We marched from Karachi to Islamabad with Bilawal sahib without incident," he recalled. "But when the PTI protests, they spread chaos. You can see it even now; the CM is making statements about what he will do when he gets to Islamabad. He wants chaos."

But even Mr Kundi, who has been making a case for imposing governor's rule in the province for quite some time now, does not believe that this option can be exercised lightly.

In his view, governor's rule is a "constitutional option", which should only be treated as "a last resort" for when the situation in the province severely deteriorates.

"The president and prime minister sit down with institutions and assess the situation. If they find that it is necessary to use governor's rule to resolve the situation in the province, they can impose it," he explained, recalling that the option had been used in the past as well.

So, what is really at stake here? According to Riccardo Valle, a research analyst tracking militancy across South and Central Asia and co-founder of The Khorasan Diary, local grievances, the absence of the state and poor governance were detrimental to the broader security environment where counter-terrorism policy is enacted, limiting its effectiveness.

On the other hand, he noted that constant pressure from militants against security forces poses a major hindrance to any comprehensive effort by the government to address social and economic issues, as security issues prevent the solving of the matter.

When asked what policies the KP government could implement to counter terrorists, Mr Valle noted that it "cannot become the sole issue or responsibility of a single province".

Friction between the provincial administration and the Centre could "ultimately benefit militant groups, who can exploit confusion and disagreement both from a narrative-building perspective as well as by increasing pressure on security forces," he said.

Asked about why the KP government is so opposed to military operations, he noted that operations brought mixed results, citing the 2009 Operation Rah-i-Nijat and 2014's Operation Zarb-i-Azb.

"While these operations displaced militants and led to effective control of territories, they also caused collateral damage, internal displacement and profound social [and] economic issues," Valle explained.

"Today, the asymmetric warfare adopted by militant organisations in KP further complicates the efficacy of any such military operation, possibly exacerbating the conflict and alienating local communities," he added.
ir_summary: PTI-led KP government faces security challenges and federal criticism over terrorism and governance amid political tensions.

title: Steep fuel price rise close to midterms forces one-third of US states to cut taxes
text:
WASHINGTON: A steep rise in fuel prices close to the November midterm elections has forced about one-third of US states to cut fuel taxes or ease diesel restrictions, as officials seek to limit the impact of the war with Iran on consumers.

With voters already concerned about the cost of living, the surge in gasoline and diesel prices has created an immediate political problem for governors and state lawmakers. The price at the pump is one of the most visible ways in which the war is affecting Americans' daily lives.

According to the latest AAA Fuel Prices report, overall gasoline prices remain the highest they have ever been for this time of year. AAA said the national average dropped nearly seven cents in the week ending Oct 1 to $4.41 a gallon, following a record-setting September in which the monthly average reached $4.33 — 50 cents higher than the previous September record set in 2023.

AAA has attributed the continuing price pressure to volatility in crude-oil markets linked to the conflict in the Middle East and instability in shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Ohio is among the states responding most directly. Its lawmakers on Wednesday approved a 90-day suspension of state gasoline and diesel taxes, winning broad bipartisan support. The measure was signed by Governor Mike DeWine.

Several states have moved during the past week to reduce fuel costs, while others have delayed tax increases or relaxed rules affecting certain fuel users. Ohio's move also illustrates the political sensitivity of the issue.

Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, told Fox Business that elevated gasoline prices before the November elections could give Republicans the "same fate" Democrats experienced in the 2022 midterms, when gasoline prices reached an average of about $5 a gallon.

Republicans currently hold both chambers of Congress and are defending those majorities in the November elections. High fuel prices could therefore become an electoral liability as voters remain focused on the cost of living.

Georgia has resumed a 30-day suspension of its motor-fuel tax. Indiana has extended an existing fuel-tax holiday and eased rules governing tax-exempt diesel. Utah has reduced its state gasoline tax by six cents a gallon through the end of the year.

Illinois and Kentucky have delayed or frozen scheduled increases in their motor-fuel taxes, preventing further increases at a time when motorists are already paying more.

California has adopted a different approach, allowing an early switch to a cheaper winter-blend gasoline in an effort to increase supplies and lower prices. The measures also reflect pressure on farmers and transport operators, for whom fuel costs can quickly translate into higher costs for food and other goods. Alabama, Arkansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Nebraska, North Carolina, North Dakota, Oklahoma and Texas have temporarily relaxed restrictions or enforcement involving dyed diesel, a tax-exempt fuel normally reserved for agricultural, commercial and other specified uses.

Texas is providing fuel-related relief, but its measures are largely limited to commercial and agricultural diesel rather than gasoline used by ordinary motorists.

For state governments, cutting fuel taxes carries a cost of its own. Motor-fuel taxes provide revenue for roads and other transportation infrastructure, and suspending them can leave governments with less money for those programmes.

There is also uncertainty over how quickly a tax reduction reaches consumers. A temporary tax holiday does not necessarily translate into an equivalent reduction at every pump because fuel already in the supply chain may have been taxed before the suspension takes effect.

The measures target different parts of the fuel market, but they share a common purpose: to provide relief to motorists, farmers and businesses facing unusually high energy costs.

Federal lawmakers have floated proposals for a nationwide gasoline-tax holiday, but no broad federal suspension has been enacted. The response has instead largely been left to the states, creating a patchwork of relief measures.

New York has not suspended its state fuel taxes in response to the latest price surge. Its officials have instead focused on other forms of household relief, including efforts to negotiate a freeze in National Grid gas rates to limit higher home-heating costs.

Virginia, Maryland and the District of Columbia are also not currently offering state-level gasoline-tax breaks, although proposals are being debated in some jurisdictions.

The political consequences will vary from state to state. Where fuel taxes have been suspended or reduced, incumbents can point to immediate measures aimed at lowering costs. Elsewhere, officials face questions about why similar relief has not been provided.

For Democrats, the issue provides an opportunity to criticise the administration over the economic consequences of the Iran war. Republicans, meanwhile, face pressure in states they govern to show that they can protect consumers from higher fuel costs.
ir_summary: US states cut fuel taxes due to price surge from Middle East conflict ahead of midterm elections.

title: UK Green party adopts ‘Zionism is racism’ policy
text:
LONDON: The UK's left-wing Green party voted on Sunday to define Zionism as racism at the party's annual conference, drawing sharp backlash from three British Jewish groups, the ruling Labour Party and Israel's government.

Members of the Green party, which has five MPs in Britain's 650-seat parliament and which enjoyed a boost in recent local and special elections, backed the motion at the party's conference, with 1,022 votes in favour and 813 against.

According to the motion, Zionism would be "treated as any other form of racism" and the party supports the establishment of a "single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine".

"This has been a serious and deeply felt debate within our membership," a Green spokesperson said. The Greens have enjoyed a surge in popularity under the charismatic leadership of Zack Polanski, attracting voters dissatisfied with the centre-left Labour government's stance on the Israel-Hamas war.

However, Polanski's popularity has taken a hit in recent months, polls show, following several missteps. "This motion would make the Green Party the first electorally significant UK political party in living memory to adopt what appears to be an overtly antisemitic political platform," three Jewish community groups said in a letter to the party ahead of the vote.

"We also emphasised the implications for the safety and welfare of all British Jews," the heads of the Board of Deputies, Community Security Trust and Jewish Leadership Council warned.

Israel's president, Isaac Herzog, called the Green party's decision "a disgrace".

"Zionism is the national liberation movement of the Jewish people, and it forms the basis for the Jewish people's right to a state and a national home in the Land of Israel," Herzog said on X.

Bridget Phillipson, chair of the ruling Labour Party and Minister for Women and Equalities, also condemned the Green Party's conference decision.

"It is shameful to vote against a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine and to condemn the vast majority of British Jews and Jews around the world as racist for supporting Israel's right to exist," she said in a party statement.

The motion laid bare divisions in the party with Polanski — who is currently running to become an MP in former prime minister Keir Starmer's London constituency — skipping the vote.

Despite at least three out of five Green MPs opposing the motion, Polanski said earlier this week that the "displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people" was "clearly racism".

United Nations investigators have accused Israel of committing "genocide" in the war in Gaza, a finding that Israel has rejected.
ir_summary: UK Green Party votes to define Zionism as racism, sparking backlash from Jewish groups and Israel.

title: Bangladesh’s rivers of ‘plastic’
text:
The use of single-use plastic started in Bangladesh in the 1980s. In about half a century, the Buriganga, Dhaka's lifeline, has become choked with plastic waste.

The country generates around 3,000 tonnes of plastic waste every day, according to a 2022 study by the Environment and Social Development Organisation (ESDO). Experts say production has since increased significantly.

Much of this waste ends up in the country's river system, clogging waterways, endangering aquatic life and posing a public health risk through microplastics in food. Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET), the polymer used in bottles and food packaging, takes an estimated 450 years to break down, quietly leaching microplastics and chemicals into the environment and contaminating food.

A 2025 study titled "Health risk assessment of microplastics contamination in the daily diet of South Asian countries" found microplastics were significantly more common in fish caught from the Buriganga than in fish from the Bay of Bengal.
