"The allegations by the Afghan Taliban regime linking Pakistan with the alleged violence in Nuristan are frivolous, baseless and devoid of any truth," said a post on the information ministry's 'fact-check' account on X.

The statement came after Afghanistan's defence ministry alleged that Pakistan-backed individuals had crossed the border and were involved in the reported violence.

According to Reuters, the Afghan Taliban claimed to have killed and wounded several fighters who allegedly crossed into the eastern province of Nuristan. The Taliban account alleged that this group included fighters allied with the militant Islamic State-Khorasan outfit.

"Pakistan categorically rejects the fabricated claims of involvement by its security forces or intelligence agencies in any internal clashes in Nuristan or elsewhere in Afghanistan, including allegations of recruiting or training former Afghan security personnel or facilitating Daesh or any other terrorist group operating in Afghanistan," the information ministry said.

It pointed out that "not a shred of evidence has been produced to substantiate Pakistan's involvement; no identities, documents, communications, forensic evidence or independent verification".

The ministry noted that an alleged video "being peddled on social media to support this false claim only shows a few unarmed individuals who are not even properly dressed or equipped were arrested in what seems to be a pre-planned video shoot by Afghan Taliban regime, well known for lies and fabricated claims".

"Instead of externalising responsibility for its internal security challenges through fanciful allegations, the Afghan Taliban regime should take credible and verifiable action against terrorist organisations operating from its territory and fulfil its commitments that Afghan soil will not be used for terrorism against Pakistan or any other country."

The statement further said it was "particularly ironic for the Afghan Taliban regime to accuse Pakistan of supporting terrorism while terrorist organisations operating from Afghanistan continue to pose a direct threat to Pakistan and regional security".

The ministry highlighted that the presence and activities of "terrorist groups of all types inside Afghanistan are well documented", including in successive reports of the United Nations and other neutral international organisations.

"Attempts to manufacture a Pakistani connection cannot obscure the reality that these terrorist groups continue to find sanctuary and [a] permissive environment for growth in Afghan territory," it asserted.

"Such claims by this non-inclusive, non-representative Taliban regime are also reflective of lies to externalise internal dissent and oppression of women, children and minorities," the ministry said.
ir_summary: Pakistan military reports killing over 70 terrorists in Balochistan operations and rejects Afghan claims of cross-border involvement.

title: IMF talks to unlock next $1.2bn set to begin today
text:
ISLAMABAD: Formal negotiations between the government and a visiting International Monetary Fund (IMF) staff mission for the fourth review of the $7 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and the third review of the Resilience Support Faci­lity (RSF) are expected to begin today (Monday).

Official sources said the mission, led by Iva Petrova, would stay for almost two weeks, until the first week of October, to conduct the fourth review of the EFF and the third review of the RSF.

Pakistan is currently under a 37-month IMF programme aimed at stabilising the economy through fiscal discipline, structural reforms and measures to support long-term growth.

Upon successful completion of the reviews, Pakistan will be eligible for the disbursement of about $1 billion (760 million Special Drawing Rights) under the EFF and another $200m under the RSF by the end of Novem­ber or early December, a total of $1.2bn.

Meanwhile, Adviser to the Finance Minister Khurram Schehzad clarified on Sunday that the government was not buying any aircraft for Pakis­tan International Airlines (PIA), which was privatised through an auction in December last year.

"The government is neither buying aircraft for a privatised PIA, nor has it announced any sovereign guarantee of taxpayer-funded loan for doing so," Mr Schehzad posted on X following claims on social media that a minister was arranging and negotiating sovereign-linked financing for the jets.

The claims came after a recent meeting between Finance Minister Aurangzeb and Chairman of the US Export-Import (Exim) Bank John Jovanovich on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

The finance ministry said the two discussed the Reko Diq mining project and funding opportunities for procuring an aircraft for PIA.

The finance minister shared PIA's interest in Boeing's 787 Dreamliners and "sought support for a financing package covering aircraft and engines". However, Mr Schehzad pointed out in his post that the US Exim's "mandate, like export credit agencies elsewhere, is to support its country's exports and jobs".

"Boeing aircraft are US exports. US Exim provides financing support to foreign purchasers of US-manufactured aircraft, including airlines, through established financing structures," he added.

"US Exim's own framework provides for asset-backed aircraft financing, where financing can be secured against the aircraft itself and credit assessed on the airline/lessee and/or guarantor, if any. A sovereign guarantee is therefore not an automatic requirement."

He added that Mr Aurangzeb's discussions with US Exim were not confined to PIA. They covered potential financing across aviation, refinery upgrades and Reko Diq as part of a much broader Pakistan-US economic engagement.
ir_summary: Pakistan begins IMF talks for $1.2 billion loan disbursement under economic stabilization program.

title: US, Iran may return to table within days over Hormuz
text:
WASHINGTON/TEHRAN: The Uni­ted States and Iran are expected to hold talks this week, said President Donald Trump after he rejected a proposal by Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East and a return to the conditions in the ceasefire deal that fell apart a few months ago.

President Trump told Axios that his negotiators would engage their Iranian counterpart over the next few days apparently to break the stalemate over Hormuz.

Iran announced a peace proposal last week at the UN General Assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted to the Americans via Qatari mediators. It called for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Lebanon, and a return to the conditions in the ceasefire deal that fell apart a few months ago. That agreement called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran has never closed the door to diplomacy but it would not capitulate. "Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met," Mr Araghchi posted on social media.

"Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock."

President Trump, however, said Iranians were losing badly, which was the reason they wanted to make a deal to open the strait. "They want to make a deal and I think that's fine. I like making a deal too."

His ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, accused Tehran of demanding too much in exchange for a return to the negotiating table.

"This was, I think, a pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable. To ask for the release of the blockade, the sanctions, international sanctions and access to billions in assets, just to talk," he told NBC News in an interview broadcast Sunday.

The Wall Street Journal first reported that Trump had rejected the Iranian proposal, citing unnamed US officials. It said Trump was privately sceptical that Iran would meet his demands and had told his staff that he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely after the November US midterm elections.

Despite Trump's public statements, mediators facilitating Tehran's talks with Washington have not officially relayed a US rejection of the plan, the Iranian top diplomat said. "We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them," Mr Araghchi noted.

At the same time, Iran's armed forces said they were prepared for any renewed US attacks. Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia warned that the US would suffer greater damage if it launched another attack on his country.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed on Sunday to have seized an American submarine drone on Sunday in the strategic Strait of Hormuz. They said that the drone was "operating in the Strait of Hormuz for espionage purposes", identifying the model as a Remus 600 autonomous underwater vehicle that was "now in the hands of the force's specialists for data recovery".

Separately, Iranian Army Commander-in-Chief Amir Hatami said the war was at a critical and decisive stage, adding that Tehran would not accept a situation in which it was unable to trade while foreign powers used the region's strategic waterways. "If Iran cannot trade, if Iran cannot live, no one will be able to trade or live," he added.
ir_summary: US and Iran may hold talks soon over reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Middle East ceasefire conditions.

title: Expanding surveillance
text:
PUNJAB'S decision to extend its digital surveillance network should be appreciated. However, the question is what the government does with the vast amount of data it is collecting. The expansion to 98 tehsils will take the network well beyond its existing urban footprint. The present network uses systems such as automatic vehicle registration-plate recognition, facial recognition, video analytics and crime-pattern analysis. The potential benefits are considerable. Properly integrated surveillance can improve police response, help identify suspects and stolen vehicles, provide digital evidence, map crime patterns and allow scarce policing resources to be deployed effectively. It can also improve traffic management and response to women's safety and crime reporting. But cameras alone do not make cities safer.

The government appears to be expanding the hardware much faster than it is developing the institutional capacity to turn data into intelligence. This is where the project needs greater attention. Punjab is generating an enormous stream of potentially valuable data from cameras, emergency calls, traffic systems, police records and other digital platforms. However, there is little public evidence that this information is being systematically combined and analysed to understand the causes, patterns and geography of crime. The reported 70pc reduction in serious crime is encouraging, but such claims need independent verification. A fall in reported incidents in areas covered by cameras is not, by itself, proof that surveillance caused the decline. The larger opportunity lies in using the network as a public safety intelligence system rather than treating it primarily as a surveillance project. Data should be integrated with police investigation, prosecution and court outcomes. This could help explain why cases fail, where investigations break down and which policing interventions work. There is another requirement: safeguards. As surveillance expands into union councils and public spaces, rules governing access, retention, sharing and use of personal data become essential. Facial recognition and other AI tools should not become a licence for indiscriminate monitoring. Access to sensitive data must be logged and audited, with penalties for misuse. The technology can improve policing, but only if the authorities develop the analytical capacity, accountability and institutional discipline needed to extract its full value.
ir_summary: Punjab government expands digital surveillance network with concerns about data use and institutional capacity.

title: 16 killed in relentless Russia, Ukraine strikes
text:
KYIV: Russian and Ukrainian strikes killed at least 16 people over the last 24 hours, both countries said on Saturday, with the war still raging in its fifth year.

Both Moscow and Kyiv have stepped up attacks after the deadliest summer since 2022 — the year Russia launched its invasion, starting Europe's worst war since World War Two.

US-led talks to end fighting have not led to a breakthrough and the Kremlin has repeatedly said it intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine. Kyiv said Russian strikes had killed at least six people — in northeastern Sumy, in Zaporizhzhia and in the Dnipropetrovsk region, where a 17-year-old girl was among the victims.

And in Kyiv, several people were wounded a day after a day-time Russian attack killed seven people. Moscow has intensified strikes on the capital as the city prepares for another winter of war.

Russia said Ukrainian strikes had killed four people in its Krasnodar and Belgorod regions. Vladimir Saldo, appointed by Moscow to lead occupational authorities in the Kherson region, said a Ukrainian drone had hit a cafe in the village of Askaniya-Nova, near Crimea, Friday evening.

"Under the rubble, rescuers found the bodies of two young girls — born in 2004 and 2006," he said on Telegram, adding that a man had also been killed in the same area.

Moscow-appointed official Yevgeny Balitsky said night-time Ukrainian strikes killed three more people in the occupied part of the Zaporizhzhia region. United Nations officials have warned about the increasing numbers of civilian victims in the war.

At the UN General Assembly this week, US President Donald Trump once again said that a deal between Moscow and Kyiv to end the war was "going to happen". For many observers however, that prospect appeared distant.

Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky said Saturday that Russia was "escalating every single day". In Kyiv's Solomianskyi district, residents of a typical Soviet-era apartment block hit by a Russian drone were cleaning up their building — already worried about what might come next.

Oleksandr Gorlachov, 43, had gone to his allotment plot outside the city. Early Saturday morning however, he was woken up by a video call from his elderly parents — who are both deaf — and rushed back to help.

"I watched as my mother is standing there in her nightgown, my father in his underwear, outside the building in tears… and there are flames, everything is burning," he said.

"The apartment is completely smashed up." His mother, he said, is a seamstress. "Her sewing machine was there. She was in tears because it's broken now.

"So, well, it's a tragedy. But in my family everyone is alive and for that I thank God," he said. With mounting Russian attacks on the capital, his family is in "constant stress" and he tries to distract himself by planting tomatoes.

"They don't have enough land," he said, mocking Russia — the world's largest country. "They want to simply wipe out our nation."

Despite Russia making life in Kyiv increasingly tough, Gorlachov said he "wasn't going anywhere". But fellow resident Anastasiia Grygorovych — woken up when her window "fell on me" — had already fled her home-town of Gorlivka, now occupied by Russia. Now she was considering leaving Ukraine altogether.
ir_summary: Russian and Ukrainian strikes killed at least 16 people in 24 hours as the war continues with intensified attacks.

title: Rs16bn bank-funded remittance reward scheme unveiled
text:
KARACHI: State Bank Governor Jameel Ahmad on Friday launched the Pasban Remittance Reward Scheme, under which the banking industry will offer Rs16 billion in annual cash prizes to recipients of home remittances sent through formal channels, with no cost to the national exchequer.

The scheme, launched under the auspices of the Pakistan Banks Association (PBA) and developed under the patronage of the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP), is aimed at encouraging overseas Pakistanis to send money through formal banking channels. It will distribute Rs4bn in prizes every quarter to 2,521 winners, or more than 10,000 winners annually.

Each quarterly draw will offer one top prize of Rs100 million, 20 prizes of Rs25m each, 100 prizes of Rs10m and 2,400 prizes of Rs1m.

The scheme rewards the person receiving the remittance in Pakistan instead of the sender abroad. Partici­pation is automatic and free, with no application, registration, ticket purchase or minimum-balance requirement.

To qualify, a beneficiary must receive home remittances equivalent to at least $100 into an eligible bank account or wallet in each of the three months of a quarter.

The number of entries increases with the value of each qualifying remittance. For example, a $260 remittance earns three entries, while $1,000 earns 10. There is no upper limit on the number of entries that an eligible account can earn.

However, cash collected over the counter will not qualify, as the remittance must be credited directly to an eligible account or wallet. Roshan Digital Account inflows and remittances credited to foreign-currency accounts are also excluded.

The first qualifying period will run from Oct 1 to Dec 31, 2026, and the first draw is scheduled for Jan 15, 2027.

Prizes other than the top award will be distributed through regional pools, with 50 per cent allocated to remittances originating from the Gulf Cooperation Council countries, 15pc each to the United Kingdom and Europe, and 10pc each to North America and other countries.

The Rs100m first prize will be open to eligible beneficiaries regardless of the country from which the remittance was sent.

Speaking at the launch ceremony, the SBP governor said workers' remittances were the backbone of millions of families, helping meet household expenses and supporting education, healthcare and investment.

Mr Ahmad said Pakistan's external account position had improved substantially and SBP's foreign exchange rese­rves have jumped to $21.4bn from below $3bn in February 2023.

He said the strengthening of foreign exchange buffers had been driven primarily by purchases from the market rather than accumulation of external debt.

Meanwhile, workers' remittances reached a record $41.6bn in FY26 compared to $21.7bn in FY19, nearly doubling over the period.

Mr Ahmad said the government and SBP had over the years introduced various Home Remittance Incentive Schemes to encourage the use of formal channels. As those programmes expanded and their cost increased, the authorities began moving towards "a more sustainable, market-oriented model" funded in coordination with the banking industry.

He said Pasban represented another step in that transition and would help maintain the attractiveness of formal remittance channels while recognising the contribution of overseas Pakistanis.

The scheme's terms and conditions state that Pasban builds on systems previously used for the Sohni Dharti Remittance Programme, which has been discontinued. Pasban is a separate scheme and points or rewards accumulated under Sohni Dharti will not be transferred to it.

PBA Chief Executive and Secretary General Muneer Kamal said Pasban built on a remitter incentive funded by banks since July 2026, taking the banking industry's annual commitment towards remittance-related support to close to Rs100bn.

The draw process will be operated by 1LINK through an algorithm-based random selection system without manual intervention, while the entry-generation and draw systems will be independently audited.

Prize money will be placed in escrow at the National Bank of Pakistan before each draw. Winners will be contacted by their banks and results will also be announced publicly without disclosing personal details.

After verification, prizes will be credited in rupees to the winning accounts and applicable withholding tax will be deducted at source.
ir_summary: Pakistan's central bank launches a $16 billion cash prize scheme to incentivize formal remittances from overseas Pakistanis.

title: Makkah defence pact chiefs hold urgent talks in Riyadh
text:
ISLAMABAD: The military chiefs of Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia met in Riyadh on Friday for urgently convened talks under the Makkah Joint Def­ence Agreement as the kingdom faced a sharp escalation in missile and drone attacks by Yemen's Ansar Allah movement.

The meeting followed a decision by the foreign ministers of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye in New York on Thursday to convene the chiefs of staff and examine ways of supporting the kingdom under the trilateral defence pact.

No further details on the discussions or any decisions reached were immediately released.

It was reported earlier that Pakistan's Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkiye's Chief of General Staff Gen Selçuk Bayraktaroglu would meet Saudi Chief of General Staff Gen Fayyadh bin Hamed Al-Ruwaili in Riyadh.

A plane from Nur Khan Airbase carrying the Pakistani delegation landed in Riyadh shortly after 2pm on Friday, according to a source. However, there was no immediate official statement from the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR).

Meanwhile, the Turkish Defence Ministry explicitly said Gen Bayrak­taroglu would travel to Saudi Arabia on Friday to attend the meeting of the chiefs of general staff under the Makkah Defence Alliance.

The Pakistani Foreign Office said the ministers at their meeting in New York reviewed progress towards establishing the General Secretariat, committees and working groups under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement and preparations for beginning their work.

"The ministers also discussed plans to convene an urgent meeting of the chiefs of staff of the three countries to explore ways to assist the Kingdom under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, which stipulates that an attack against any one of its parties shall be considered an attack against all parties," the Foreign Office said.

The Saudi foreign ministry gave a similar account, saying the meeting had addressed preparations for an "urgent session" of the three countries' chiefs of staff to "explore measures supporting the Kingdom" under the agreement. The Turkish defence ministry also echoed this understanding.

The meeting was the first gathering of the three military chiefs since the alliance came under an immediate test, with Ansar Allah attacks reaching Saudi territory and prompting Riyadh to seek support from its partners.

The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement was signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye in Makkah on Aug 7 and the first meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee was subsequently held in Istanbul on Aug 31, where the three countries agreed to establish a permanent secretariat in Riyadh and decided that Pakistan would provide the secretary general for its first three-year term.

Pakistan appointed retired Lt Gen Nauman Mahmood as the alliance's first secretary general on Wednesday, taking another step towards putting the institutional structure of the pact in place.

The New York ministerial meeting indicated that the three governments wanted the military chiefs to examine practical options. Therefore, the Riyadh meeting was expected to begin that process, although any decision on specific deployments or military assistance would depend on the Saudi requirement and the agreement reached by the three sides.

The Ansar Allah fighters have in recent days stepped up missile and drone attacks against Saudi territory, including attacks involving Riyadh, Taif and Yanbu, while Saudi authorities have reported interceptions of ballistic missiles. The escalation has also affected civilian and economic facilities and prompted particular concern after missiles were claimed to be directed towards the vicinity of the holy city of Makkah.

The three commanders were expected to exchange assessments of the evolving threat, including the nature and scale of Ansar Allah missile and drone capability, the vulnerability of Saudi territory and critical infrastructure and the level of support Riyadh may require from Pakistan and Turkiye.

Turkiye has already signalled its willingness to address Saudi military requirements, with Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan saying last week that Ankara was ready to help with "military needs, especially on some technical issues". Pakistan has also repeatedly affirmed its commitment to the agreement.
ir_summary: Military chiefs of Pakistan, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia meet in Riyadh to discuss defense cooperation amid Yemeni attacks on Saudi Arabia.

title: Gulf waterways must remain open, PM tells UN
text:
NEW YORK: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Friday called for the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab to be kept open, telling the United Nations General Asse­mbly that the two waterways were vital to the world economy and must not be turned into flashpoi­nts, as he pressed Pakistan's mediation between Washington and Tehran as a path to de-escalation.

"The Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab are arteries of the global economy. They must remain open, connecting nations, not becoming chokepoints of confrontation," he said.

Addressing the 81st session of the UNGA, the premier highlighted the loss of lives, economic suffering and pressure on critical maritime routes caused by the conflict in the Middle East, particularly around the Strait of Hormuz.

"At this critical moment, Paki­stan chose to act swiftly. Through concerted efforts, Pakistan bro­ught Washington and Tehran under one roof in Islamabad," he said, referring to diplomatic efforts that culminated in the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding between the United States and Iran in June.

Pakistan has continued to present the Islamabad MoU as a framework for de-escalation and renewed diplomacy.

"Amid the roar of missiles, drones and guns, the voice for diplomacy must echo even louder and stronger," the premier stated.

The United Nations secretary general has expressed support for Pakistan's mediation efforts bet­ween Iran and the United States.

Responding to a question about Pakistan's continuing role as a go-between and PM Shehbaz's meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, a UN spokesperson said the secretary general had been "very clear in expressing his support and his gratitude for the mediation efforts led by Pakistan".

The spokesperson said the effo­rts had led to the Islamabad understanding, which, in a different context, had helped create "a moment, a period of calm" in the region.

The understanding had also facilitated the movement of essential supplies, the spokesperson said, noting that "energy and food and other items were flowing more easily through the Strait of Hormuz."

Asked about reports of continuing discussions following the prime minister's meeting with the Iranian president and the prospects for further progress, the spokesperson said the UN was aware of the developments.

"We've seen reports of various discussions going on," the spokesperson said. "And we hope that they will bear fruit."

PM Shehbaz also condemned "in the strongest possible terms" recent attacks by the Houthis against Saudi Arabia, calling them "deplorable" and expressing Pakis­tan's complete solidarity with the kingdom.

He highlighted the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement signed by Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia as a reflection of Pakistan's commitment to peace.

"This alliance is not directed against any country; it is a collective commitment for defence, stability and peace in the region, and nothing more," he stressed.

The premier restated Pakistan's support for Palestine, expressing concern over Israeli actions in Gaza and the West Bank as well as continuing hostilities involving Lebanon and Syria.

In particular, he said the forcible eviction of Palestinians in the West Bank "clearly reflects Israel's genocidal agenda".

"Pakistan believes that the only just and lasting solution is the creation of an independent, sovereign, viable and contiguous State of Palestine, based on pre-1967 borders, with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital," he reaffirmed.

Turning to South Asia, PM Shehbaz reiterated that any attempt by India to divert Pakistan's share of water would be treated as an "act of war".

"Water must never be weaponised. Riv­ers should nourish nations, not divide them. Therefore, any attempt to stop, imp­ede or divert Pakistan's share of the waters will be treated as an act of war. India must make no mistake about it," he said.

He said India's unilateral decision to hold the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance since last year's conflict had no legal basis, noting that New Delhi's claims and actions regarding the treaty had been rejected by UN experts as well as by the Permanent Court of Arbitration, leaving Pakistan "vindica­ted beyond any doubt". He called the Indus river system the "lifeblood" of the region.

The premier, who opened his address by saying "the pursuit of peace is among the noblest of human endeavours", also recalled last year's conflict with India, which was triggered by a terror attack in Pahalgam that New Delhi blamed on Islamabad, an allegation Pakistan denied.

"Our brave and valiant armed forces, under the courageous leadership of Field Marshal Asim Munir, responded with precision and professionalism," he said.

He once again praised US President Do­­nald Trump's "resolute and visionary lea­dership" in brokering a ceasefire between the two countries in May 2025, stressing that it saved "hundreds of millions of lives".

"Who knows the extent of devastation that could have taken place had President Trump not stepped in at this critical moment with clarity of thought and action?" he said. "We must therefore ensure that South Asia never reaches this precipice ever again."

This, however, required a fair resolution of the Kashmir dispute, the premier said.

"For eight decades, the Kashmiri people have waited for the United Nations to fulfil its solemn commitment of a free and impartial plebiscite," he said.

He said Kashmiris had endured illegal occupation, arbitrary detention, extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, sexual violence and collective punishment for generations, and declared that Pakistan would continue to extend its full diplomatic, political and moral support to them until they were granted their right to self-determination, terming Kashmir "Pakistan's jugular vein".
ir_summary: Pakistani PM calls for keeping Gulf waterways open and promotes Pakistan's mediation between US and Iran at UN General Assembly.

title: 3 Iraqi airports suspend flights from Iran
text:
BAGHDAD: Iraq's Erbil and Sulaimaniya airports suspended Iranian flights starting on Friday, two sources said, after other Iraqi airports took the same step earlier in the week.

The move means that according to sources and state media, flights to and from Iran are suspended from all four Iraqi airports at which they were operating Baghdad, Najaf, Erbil and Sulaimaniya.

Iraq's state news agency reported the suspension at Najaf International Airport earlier on Friday. Two separate sources said earlier in the week that Iraq ordered its civil aviation authority to halt Iranian flights to Baghdad airport from Wednesday. The sources said at the time that the government was discussing diverting Iranian flights from Baghdad to Najaf.

Washington had annou­nced it would impose sanctions on any global companies doing business with Iranian airlines after Sept 23, with the aim of grounding Iran's entire civilian fleet worldwide.

The United Arab Emirates, the Middle East's biggest travel hub, also said on Thursday it was suspending all flights by Iranian airlines to and from the country until further notice.

Iraq's Najaf airport, a top destination for Shia pilgrims, suspended all Iranian flights on Friday, enforcing US sanctions and leaving travellers scrambling for solutions.

Airport director Hussein Muhanna said that "all flights were halted between Iran and Najaf airport following a directive from the prime minister's office to the governor" of Najaf.

"All Iraqi airports, including in Kurdistan, have enforced the ban," a government source said.

The airport in the holy city of Najaf, south of Baghdad, is a major hub for Iranian flights and their main destination in Iraq.

They mainly carry Iraqi Shia pilgrims to Iran's holy cities or Iranians visiting sacred sites in Iraq. The flights also serve Iraqi students studying in Iran, and patients seeking medical treatment there.

Haidar Mansour, 50, was hoping to travel to Iran this month for a kidney transplant after three years of undergoing dialysis.

"People's lives are at risk," Mansour said. "I cannot even walk in the street, it is impossible for me to travel by land." Instead of a flight lasting only a few hours, passengers will have now to take a land journey of at least 12 hours, depending on the destination.

Across the border, Iraqi doctoral student Assad Jabbar is stranded in Qom after being turned back at the airport from his Friday flight home. His only option is the longer land route, but taxis and buses are already "pac­ked and prices are rising", he said.
ir_summary: Iraq suspends all flights from Iran at four airports to comply with US sanctions on Iranian airlines.

title: Ireland’s Gaza stance spills from Eurovision into football
text:
DUBLIN: No Irish supporters in the stadium, no home match in Ireland and no pundits or Irish commentary on television: the country's strong support for the Palestinian cause is increasingly reshaping its sporting and cultural calendar.

Ireland face Israel in football's Nations League in Hungary on Sunday before a designated Irish "home" game in Serbia on October 4, amid protests and calls for a boycott over Israel's war in Gaza.

Sunday's match comes days after national broadcaster RTE confirmed Ireland would again boycott the Eurovision Song Contest next year because of Israel's participation.

But contractual obligations mean it must show the football matches. The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) has, meanwhile, declined its ticket allocation for Irish supporters for Sunday's fixture.

The game is being staged in Debrecen, Hungary, because Israel cannot currently host international matches, while the reverse fixture was shifted from Dublin to Backa Topola, Serbia, and will be played behind closed doors.

"It is highly unusual for a state broadcaster to show a major international match while stripping away punditry" and the other usual elements, said Neil O'Boyle, an associate professor at Dublin City University specialising in sport and media.

RTE faced "a unique dilemma", he said, between its contractual obligations and "intense pushback from the Irish public and some of its own staff". "The 'silent' broadcast is intended as a kind of moral compromise," he said.

Ireland has long been a strong supporter of the Palestinian cause, with sympathy often linked to the country's own history of British rule. Research published this year by political scientist Liam Kneafsey and colleague Miceal Canavan found Ireland a clear outlier in western Europe.

Their study, based on a representative survey conducted in late 2023, found 53 percent of Irish adults sympathised more with Palestinians and 11 percent with Israel, compared with around 27pc pro-Palestinian sympathy in the next-highest western European country.

"Ireland's history of colonisation, partition and displacement gives people a ready-made template for understanding a distant and complex conflict," Kneafsey said.

Such attitudes were "rooted in history and identity, not just a reaction to headlines", he added. Dublin formally recognised a Palestinian state in 2024 alongside Spain and Norway, and has repeatedly criticised Israel's conduct in Gaza.

More than 160 Irish sportspeople have signed a letter urging the national team to boycott the football games, while protests have targeted the FAI and players.

Manager Heimir Hallgrimsson has acknowledged players are uncomfortable about the fixtures, saying: "We're not playing with genocide. We're playing against genocide." Israel's football federation accused him of "stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy", remarks Taoiseach (prime minister) Micheal Martin on Tuesday called "unacceptable".

Amnesty International Ireland's executive director, Stephen Bowen, said UEFA should have suspended Israel, arguing that Israeli clubs operating in occupied Palestinian territory breached football's rules. "It shocks the conscience that Ireland has to play these fixtures," he said.

"Upset and outrage here in Ireland at these matches is palpable." But former Irish justice minister Alan Shatter strongly rejected the boycott campaign. "It's a scandal that a group of obsessed political activists have created a situation where our home game is now taking place behind closed doors in Serbia," he said.

Shatter said the FAI should have staged the fixture in Dublin with police protection and accused campaigners of placing players under unacceptable pressure. The FAI itself requested last year that UEFA suspend Israel but received insufficient support from European football's governing body. It says refusing to play could bring sporting and financial sanctions.

Israel strongly rejects allegations that its conduct in Gaza amounts to genocide. It launched war on Gaza in response to a Hamas attack inside Israel on October 7, 2023, that resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to a tally based on official Israeli figures.

Its bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza has killed more than 73,900 people there, according to the occupied Palestinian territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
ir_summary: Ireland boycotts sports events and alters broadcasts due to its strong pro-Palestinian stance amid Israel's war in Gaza.

title: Pope Leo warns UN risks becoming ‘charade’
text:
PARIS: Pope Leo said on Friday that the United Nations and other multilateral groups were in crisis, warning in a speech at the Paris headquarters of the UN culture and education body, Unesco, that international dialogue risked becoming a "charade".

The first US pope, speaking on a visit to France as a tense UN General Assem­bly unfolded in New York, also decried world leaders who disrespected the rule of law, without naming individuals.

"Instead of respecting the law, those in power invoke it when it serves their interests and disregard it when it restrains them, treating even justice itself as though it were a commodity to be bought and sold," said the pontiff.

The UN and other multilateral groups "are experiencing a crisis of effectiveness", he said. "Dialogue is seen as an obstacle to action rather than a resource for peace, a charade rather than an opportunity to seek the common good together." Leo, who became pope in May 2025, drew the ire of US President Donald Trump earlier in the year after criticising the Iran war.

This year's UN General Assembly, ending on Monday, has been the scene of heated arguments. In a speech on Tuesday, Trump threatened to annihilate Iran if it did not agree terms to end the war. On Thursday, dozens of delegates left the assembly hall as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke. Trump announced in 2025 that the US would withdraw from Unesco.

Leo is on a whirlwind four-day, three-city visit to France, where he is seeking to repair the Church's standing there after abuse scandals sparked nationwide shock.

The pope, who has made sounding the alarm about the risks of AI a central part of his 16-month papacy, put the issue at the heart of his visit to France.
ir_summary: Pope Leo criticizes the UN and multilateralism as ineffective, warning international dialogue risks becoming a charade.

title: Spanish city bans burqa, niqab in public spaces
text:
BARCELONA: The Spa­nish city of Lleida on Frid­ay approved a ban on full-face coverings in most public spaces in a rare step targeting the Muslim burqa and niqab in the country.

Unlike European neighbours such as France, Portugal or Belgium, Spain has no national legislation banning or restricting the use of the garments worn by some Muslim women.

A provincial capital of around 150,000 people in the northeastern region of Catalonia, around 150 kilometres west of Barcelona, Lleida banned full-face veils in some public spaces in 2010, in a first for Spain. But the Spanish Supreme Court nullified the measure in 2013 following a long legal challenge by a Muslim association.

The court ruled that the ban infringed on religious freedom and transgressed the powers of a local authority, also cancelling similar measures adopted in other municipalities.

A meeting of Lleida's city parliament on Friday voted 16-11 to modify a municipal law that was drawn up with the aim of avoiding similar legal pitfalls. The measure includes a ban on "remaining in or moving through public spaces with items or elements that totally cover the face", without explicitly mentioning the burqa or the niqab.
ir_summary: A Spanish city bans full-face coverings in public spaces, targeting Muslim veils after a previous ban was overturned by the Supreme Court.

title: Amnesty calls for abolition of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement
text:
WASHINGTON: Am­­n­esty International called for the abolition of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which is tasked with leading Donald Trump's anti-immigrant crackdown in a report released on Thursday.

The report, titled "We Had Whistles, They Had Guns," documents widespread human rights violations during ICE's large-scale operations, the rights watchdog said.

The release comes less than a week after a Venezuelan migrant, Wilber Garces Perez, was shot and wounded by an ICE agent in Austin, Texas, reigniting anger in the US over the immigration authorities' methods.

In January, the deaths of two Americans, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both 37, who were shot by federal agents in Minneapolis, sparked outrage across the country.

"Masked and armed federal agents attacking people in the streets with impunity doesn't make our communities safer — it puts everyone in danger," Nadia Daar, director of Amnesty International USA, warned in the report.

The report is based on more than 150 testimonies gathered between March and June in four major cities where ICE concentrated its activities, Amnesty said.

"ICE is fundamentally broken and cannot be fixed," Daar wrote.

"For the US government to have an immigration enforcement system that complies with international human rights law and standards, ICE needs to be abolished and we need to start over."

racist, xenophobic, and false rhetoric, with the aim of detaining and deporting as many migrants, asylum seekers, and refugees as possible from the United States."

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comment.
ir_summary: Amnesty International calls for abolishing US Immigration and Customs Enforcement over human rights violations in immigration enforcement.

title: Disposable humans
text:
DESCENDING into dirt, disease and uncertainty for a living is inhuman. Sanitation workers — the pillars of urban hygiene — often perish as poisonous gases fill their lungs. In eight months, 26 have died across the country. Karachi recorded eight losses, with 18 in Punjab. None of the workers were Muslim. In Pakistan, discrimination takes many forms. Among its most shameful manifestations have been job advertisements for sewerage management and garbage disposal. These have humiliated scores of underprivileged citizens with their 'only Christians and Hindus may apply' criteria — a practice banned by the Islamabad High Court. The Amnesty International and the Centre for Law & Justice report last year also highlighted the bigotry that stigmatises an essential service and creates social marginalisation. The call to do away with this practice at the recent Citizens Commission for Equality and Human Rights conference in Karachi deserves support. Compensation cannot persist as an escape for the government.

The situation has remained unchanged for years. The lack of protective gear and no health cover or stable employment mean we are normalising 'disposability' of vulnerable segments. The government is obligated under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and domestic labour laws to provide safe working conditions for the people. Manual scavenging violates fundamental freedoms and strips away human dignity, besides exposing the state's utter disregard for its constitutional duties. In an age when modern machinery makes urban hygiene possible, why should individuals be made to risk their health and lives by descending into gutters? Those in power must be made to answer for the illness, harm and deaths inflicted on those who live on the fringes of society. Sadly, the deaths of workers who risk life and limb to make our environment livable are a reminder of our lost humanity.
ir_summary: Article criticizes Pakistan's government for unsafe conditions and discrimination against non-Muslim sanitation workers, violating human rights.

title: Reducing the burden
text:
PAKISTAN'S students do not need voluminous textbooks especially in the early stages; they need better learning. The Punjab government's decision to revise the curriculum from pre-primary to Grade 5, reduce textbook volume by 25pc, and shift students away from rote learning is therefore a welcome step. The current education system has confused the amount of content covered with learning. Crowded textbooks and examination practices have compelled children to memorise the text rather than understand the concepts, ask questions or apply knowledge. Reducing the syllabus can help correct this imbalance by giving teachers more time to explain and engage students. The proposed emphasis on learning outcomes is particularly important. Children should be able to demonstrate what they have understood, not simply reproduce what they have read. But this will require changes beyond the textbooks. Examinations must test comprehension, reasoning and application if schools are expected to teach those skills.

This makes teacher training crucial to reform. Cambridge has been involved in reviewing the curriculum against international curricula and it is also expected to help train teachers. The government has proposed dedicating Saturdays to teacher training. These measures can work only if the training is practical and sustained. Yet another round of workshops and certificates will not change classroom behaviour. Teachers need support in lesson planning, assessment, classroom management and teaching children with different learning abilities. Moreover, teacher and student mental health counselling and a ban on corporal punishment will make schools safer, and replace fear and humiliation with healthier discipline. At the same time, the government should not overload the framework. AI education has merit, but primary schools must first secure reading, writing and maths. Implementation will determine whether the reform succeeds. Teachers should understand the purpose of the changes; textbooks must reflect them properly, and examinations should reinforce the new learning goals. The government will also need mechanisms to monitor classrooms rather than merely inspect whether new books have reached schools. The reduction in textbook volume is therefore useful, but it is not the reform's most important feature. The significance of this step should lie in recognising that children learn better when education moves from content coverage to actual comprehension.
ir_summary: Punjab government reforms education by reducing textbook volume and shifting from rote learning to comprehension-based outcomes.

title: Pakistan emerges as transit hub: minister
text:
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan is seeking to strengthen regional connectivity and position itself as a key transit hub for trade between Central Asia, China and the South Caucasus, Communications Minister Abdul Aleem Khan said on Friday.

Speaking at a high-level panel at the Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in Baku, the minister said Pakistan was pursuing fiscal discipline and austerity to withstand global economic uncertainty, including higher fuel and maritime freight costs and disruptions to traditional trade routes.

He said Pakistan was also seeking to act as a neutral diplomatic venue and constructive mediator in regional conflicts to help ease tensions and maintain trade flows. Mr Khan said Pakistan's deep-sea ports — Karachi, Port Qasim and Gwadar — remained operational and could serve as alternative gateways for regional commerce.

"Karachi Port Trust handled more than 54.68 million tonnes of cargo in the previous fiscal year," he said.

Improved regional connectivity is transforming Pakistan into an important trade hub, as the country emerges as a key maritime gateway for Central Asian states, he said.

He highlighted motorway projects including the M-6, M-10 and MNJC as key trade routes linking Pakistan with western China and Central Asia.

The minister also pointed to transport arrangements with Azerbaijan, including 1,500 annual reciprocal permits, which he said would strengthen links between Pakistani ports, the South Caucasus and the Trans-Caspian Middle Corridor.
ir_summary: Pakistan aims to become a regional transit hub for trade between Central Asia, China, and the South Caucasus, says minister.

title: Short-term inflation surges on costly food, energy
text:
ISLAMABAD: Short-term inflation, measured by the Sensitive Price Index (SPI), surged by 11.92 per cent year-on-year for the week ending Sept 24, mainly due to higher food prices, according to official data released on Friday.

On a week-on-week basis, the index rose by 0.99pc, according to the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics.

Short-term inflation has recorded double-digit growth over the past few weeks due to persistent increases in petroleum prices. Unwilling to reduce the petroleum development levy (PDL), the government is steadily raising petrol and diesel prices daily, barring a few negligible downward revisions. The rising energy prices are indirectly contributing to higher sales tax collection.

At the same time, an unprecedented increase in transportation costs has also been reflected in the prices of essential food items, including onions, tomatoes and other vegetables.

The SPI has now risen for the 74th consecutive week.

The items, whose prices increased the most over the previous week included electricity for Q1 (18.76pc), eggs (2.02pc), garlic (1.57pc), LPG (1.55pc), pulse masoor (0.75pc), chicken (0.72pc), washing soap (0.59pc), pulse gram (0.34pc), mutton (0.31pc), beef (0.30pc), curd (0.27pc), milk fresh (0.14pc) and wheat flour (0.11pc).

The items whose prices saw a decline week-on-week included tomatoes (13.45pc), potatoes (8.33pc), bananas (5.66pc), onions (2.42pc), diesel (1.57pc), salt powdered (0.90pc), petrol (0.34pc), sugar (0.23pc), mustard oil (0.04pc) and gur (0.01pc).

However, on an annual basis, the items whose prices increased the most were onions (115.98pc), LPG (63.97pc), electricity for Q1 (58.59pc), diesel (51.80pc), petrol (47.49pc), wheat flour (32.41pc), gents sponge chappal (16.69pc), chilli powder (16.37pc), mutton (15.75pc), beef (13.22pc), firewood (10.72pc), bread plain (8.96pc), shirting (8.38pc), washing soap (8.36pc) and milk fresh (8.10pc).

In contrast, the prices of potatoes dropped 39.21pc, followed by sugar (21.14pc), tomatoes (19.81pc), eggs (18.40pc), salt powder (14.73pc), pulse gram (11.65pc), pulse masoor (10.47pc), pulse moong (7.89pc), gur (7.30pc), rice IRRI-6/9 (3.28pc), garlic (3.03pc), chicken (2.51pc) and rice basmati broken (0.33pc).

The index, comprising 51 items collected from 50 markets in 17 cities, is computed weekly to assess the prices of essential commodities and services at shorter intervals.

Data showed that the prices of 20 items increased, 10 decreased, and 21 remained stable compared to the previous week.
ir_summary: Pakistan's short-term inflation rose 11.92% due to high food and energy prices, driven by government petroleum policies.

title: Almost 10,000 traders join tax scheme
text:
ISLAMABAD: Nearly 10,000 shopkeepers registered under the Asan Tax Scheme (ATS) in its first month, State Minister for Finance and Railways Bilal Azhar Kayani said on Friday.

Data on shopkeeper registrations under the tax net was presented at a meeting chaired by Mr Kayani. The meeting reviewed progress in implementing the scheme and was attended by traders' representatives Ajmal Baloch and Kashif Chaudhry.

An official announcement said 9,806 shopkeepers joined ATS within one month of its launch and were at various stages of filing their tax returns.

The meeting was informed that 1,929 of those registered were joining the tax system for the first time, while 428 shopkeepers had already filed their returns. Shopkeepers from both small and major cities had filed returns.

The state minister directed the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) to immediately address technical objections raised by shopkeepers and lawyers regarding the scheme's implementation.

He also directed the authorities to provide FBR plates to shopkeepers who had filed their returns at the earliest. "The ATS is a unique facility designed specifically for shopkeepers and not available to any other business segment," Mr Kayani said.

He expressed hope that more shopkeepers would join the scheme, saying there was no reason for them to remain non-filers after launch of this ATS.
ir_summary: Pakistan's tax authority reports nearly 10,000 shopkeepers registered under the Asan Tax Scheme in its first month.

title: Nepra proposes higher grid-sharing charges
text:
ISLAMABAD: The National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) is seeking higher charges for grid sharing, dedicated transformers, feeders and grid stations, as well as temporary disconnections and reconnections for high-rise buildings and industrial consumers, as part of proposed changes to the Consumer Service Manual (CSM).

Under the proposed amendments to power companies' CSM, Nepra would also suggest removing the requirement for electric vehicle charging stations (EVCSs) as the government has already liberalised EVCS margins, allowing market players to determine their sale margins.

The regulator has asked interested stakeholders to submit their written comments on the proposed changes within 30 days, ending Oct 25.

Nepra has proposed five major changes to the CSM.

First, for multi-storey buildings, including those comprising residential units, the proposed CSM envisages that any building requiring a dedicated transformer of more than 500kVA capacity shall be liable to pay grid-sharing charges. At present, a building of ground plus three storeys is not considered a high-rise and as such, no grid-sharing charges are applicable.

Next, the distribution companies (Discos) would be allowed to provide multiple industrial, commercial or bulk supply connections to new consumers or extend load for existing industrial consumers, up to three feeders, with a maximum consolidated threshold of 15MW at the same premises and under the same tariff category, subject to technical feasibility and availability of capacity at the existing grid station.

Consumers would pay 100 per cent of grid-sharing charges, including transmission charges. This means a consumer would pay Rs8.948 million per MW and 100pc of the cost of land, or Rs0.855m per MW, proportionate to the load. These charges would apply to load exceeding 5MW.

For load above 15MW, a dedicated grid station and associated transmission line would be required. If a consumer applies for a load extension above 15MW and is subsequently provided a connection from a dedicated grid station, the charges already paid by the consumer, including grid-sharing charges, transmission-line charges and the cost of land, would be refunded.

At present, a dedicated transformer and 11kV distribution feeder of up to 5MW are allowed. Under the proposed third change, a dedicated transformer, 11kV feeder and rehabilitation charges would apply to connections of up to 1MW.

Similar arrangements would apply to loads above 1MW and up to 2.5MW on the basis of actual rehabilitation charges. The Discos would be required to ensure that 11kV feeders are not compromised, while the cost of meeting technical parameters would be borne by the consumer.

The fourth amendment proposes that before expiry of the period allowed for temporary disconnection, the consumer shall approach the Disco for reconnection.

However, if the consumer does not apply for reconnection, the connection shall be deemed to have been reconnected and charges shall apply upon expiry of the temporary disconnection period.

There shall be no restriction on obtaining multiple temporary disconnections, but for a subsequent temporary disconnection, the consumer would be required to pay fixed charges and other applicable charges for at least one month before applying for the next temporary disconnection.

Under the fifth amendment, Discos are proposed to charge detection bills for a maximum period of 12 months for all registered consumers in cases involving the use of bogus meters, load-profile freezing, manipulation of billing meters through software, reversal of meter readings through Bluetooth devices and security breaches of billing meters.

In such cases, the detection bill would be charged on the basis of load rather than future or previous consumption. However, for domestic consumers, the period covered by the detection bill would be confined to six months.
ir_summary: Pakistan's power regulator proposes higher grid-sharing charges and new rules for industrial and high-rise building electricity connections.

title: Govt working on 174 IMF-sought tweaks, NA panel told
text:
ISLAMABAD: The government on Thursday said the International Monetary Fund (IMF) was seeking about 174 amendments to various laws to improve governance in the financial sector, state-owned enterprises, foreign remittances, climate change and local currency integration as part of its two ongoing programmes worth $8.4 billion.

"There are a total of 174 amendments the IMF wants to be passed," Finance Secretary Imdadullah Bosal told the National Assembly Standing Committee on Finance and Revenue, presided over by Syed Naveed Qamar.

He said the government was working on the amendments, which would be placed before parliament for approval.

The statement came ahead of formal negotiations with a visiting IMF staff mission for the fourth review of the $7bn Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and the third review of the Resilience Support Facility (RSF), beginning on Monday.

A day earlier, IMF Mana­ging Director Kristalina Geor­gieva — who met PM Shehbaz Sharif on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly — appreciated the country's performance under its programme and praised the government's efforts for economic stabilisation, which she noted were yielding tangible results.

Mr Bosal said changes to the Sovereign Wealth Fund (SWF) law were also part of the discussions. He said the IMF had been clearly told that the proposed amendments would be presented to parliament, but their approval remained parliament's prerogative.

The SWF, covering five maj­or blue-chip companies, incl­u­ding OGDCL and Pakistan State Oil, has been a critical debating point of discussion as the IMF wants their governance and financial reporting standards to be brought at par with those applicable to other state-owned enterprises.

The SWF group was created as a prospective investment vehicle for government-owned entities from Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE, but little progress has been made.

Mr Bosal said the government was also holding discussions with the IMF on remittances, which were critical to Pakistan's external stability. He said efforts were needed to address costly payment-system impediments, while the IMF had strongly opposed subsidies for facilitating remi­ttances. Such subsidies, which had previously crossed Rs120bn, have already been withdrawn.

He said changes to the sugar policy were also among the benchmarks for the IMF review and that the federal government had circulated a draft policy for liberalisation. Three provinces had agreed to the policy, while one had raised reservations that needed to be addressed.

Committee Chairman Nav­eed Qamar questioned the government's strategy for power distribution companies (Dis­cos), particularly the fate of loss-making entities. "You will give away the profitable Dis­cos, but what will happen to the remaining ones?" he asked.

The panel stressed that economic reforms should be underpinned by a coherent, transparent and sustainable strategy, particularly where their implementation could impose additional costs on consumers, businesses and productive sectors of the economy.

Mr Qamar said fiscal consolidation should be accompanied by measures to promote investment, exports, employment and sustainable economic growth.

Members emphasised that assessment of the IMF programme should not remain confined to formal compliance with prescribed benchmarks but should also determine whether reforms were translating into measurable economic and social outcomes.

The committee sought clearer information on implementation timelines, outstanding commitments, effectiveness of public expenditure and the implications of various reforms for citizens, businesses and taxpayers.

The finance secretary reported that approximately $4.5bn had been disbursed by the IMF and three programme reviews had been completed.

He said the programmes were supporting balance-of-payments needs and macroeconomic stability while requiring reforms relating to revenue mobilisation, debt sustainability, fiscal consolidation, taxation, the energy sector, SOE governance and trade liberalisation.

The committee was informed that key programme commitments included parliamentary consideration of supplementary expenditure beyond approved budgets, restrictions on new tax amnesties and preferential tax treatment, energy-sector reforms and implementation of the National Fiscal Pact with the provinces.

The panel also examined the retailer tax-registration scheme, with members questioning its limited initial participation and seeking a measurable assessment of its effectiveness.

The committee called for an evaluation covering the number of registrations, revenue generated, compliance outcomes and whether the scheme's existing design required further adjustment.

It stressed that the finance ministry should assess the scheme's performance over a defined period and hold implementing authorities accountable against clearly stated objectives.

Members also sought detailed data on industrial captive-power users that had shifted to the national grid and asked for clarification about the implications for gas and petroleum consumption and circular debt.

They said implementation of energy-sector reforms should be assessed against actual operational, financial and economic outcomes.

The committee also reviewed the governance framework for state-owned enterprises and the reporting relationship between government-owned entities, their respective line ministries and the finance division.

Officials said reporting lines had been clarified and proposed amendments were aimed at strengthening boards, improving governance and enhancing investment discipline within the Sovereign Wealth Fund framework.
ir_summary: Pakistan government discusses 174 IMF-requested legal amendments for financial governance and state-owned enterprises with parliament.

title: PML-N’s Dr Najeeb Naqi sworn in as AJK president
text:
MUZAFFARABAD: Dr Najeeb Naqi of the ruling PML-N was sworn in as Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) president on Thurs­day, hours after being elected by a clear majority.

AJK Chief Justice Raja Saeed Akram administered the oath of office at a ceremony held at the President's House.

Dr Naqi is the 11th president since the introduction of the parliamentary form of government in 1975. Before that, AJK had a presidential system. Exclu­ding those who held the office in an interim capacity, he is the 23rd president of the region overall.

Earlier in the day, Dr Naqi secured 32 votes against 13 for PPP candidate Chaudhry Latif Akbar in the election held at the Legislative Assembly Secretariat.

As elections in seven constituencies of Poonch have yet to be held, the assembly's current strength is 46.

PPP lawmaker Chaudhry Qasim Majeed did not turn up for voting, reportedly because he was out of the country.

As presiding officer Ayaz Bashir announced the result inside the Assembly Hall, a large gathering outside erupted in celebration while watching the proceedings live on a large screen.

Dr Naqi, who was in the Speaker's Chamber, came out to thank the gathering and was showered with flower petals amid enthusiastic slogans.

In his brief address, he said Poonch was passing through a difficult period and expressed hope that the region would overcome its problems and return to the path of development.

"I will do my best to ensure that the new [AJK] government lives up to the expectations of its people," he said.

Back in the Assembly, PM Gillani, Leader of the Oppos­ition Chaudhry Muhammad Yasin and former premier Raja Farooq Haider took the floor to congratulate Dr Naqi.

Describing Dr Naqi as a "nob­le person", Mr Gillani said his election had brought a "breeze of fresh air" to the division. "…No one knows the Kashmir issue and matters concerning Azad Kashmir better than Dr Najeeb Naqi," he said.

Mr Gillani regretted that elections had not been held in seven constituencies of Poonch and Sudhnoti, saying the Assembly would remain incomplete until those seats were filled.

He said efforts were under way to complete the electoral process at the earliest.

Separately, PM Shehbaz Sharif also congratulated Dr Naqi on his election, which, he said, reflected the confidence of the people of AJK.

He expressed the hope that Dr Naqi would discharge his responsibilities effectively and contribute to the development, prosperity and welfare of the people of AJK. He also reaffirmed that Islamabad would extend its full cooperation to AJK.

For Dr Naqi, politics was never part of the plan. Born on Jan 19, 1964, he hails from a prominent political, social and educational family of Poonch whose public-service tradition stretches back several generations.

At the heart of that legacy stands his grandfather, Col Khan Muhammad Khan, popularly remembered as Khan Sahib and Baba-e-Poonch.

An old Aitchisonian and graduate of Lahore's prestigious King Edward Medical College, Dr Naqi had set his sights on medicine and was doing his house job at Mayo Hospital when fate intervened in the most unexpected way.

A day before the 1990 general elections in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), his father, retired Colonel Muhammad Naqi Khan, then minister for health, died in a tragic road accident while campaigning.

The family elders soon decided that his only son should carry forward the political legacy. At 26, and with little political experience, Dr Naqi was persuaded to take the plunge.

He contested the 1990 election on a Muslim Conference ticket but lost. The setback, however, proved only a temporary detour. The assembly was dissolved within a year, paving the way for fresh elections, in which the young doctor returned to the fray — and this time emerged victorious.

That was the beginning of a parliamentary career that would span more than three decades. He won again in 1996, but with the PPP forming the government, he spent the next five years on the opposition benches.

He lost the 2001 election but was subsequently elected by assembly members to the AJK Council, where he served until 2006.

Dr Naqi returned to the assembly in 2006 for a third term and served as minister for health and population welfare. He later held the portfolios of education and information technology. He was elected for a fourth term in 2011 on a PML-N ticket and remained on the opposition benches until 2016.

The 2016 election saw him come back for a fifth term. He subsequently served as minister for health and also held the finance and planning and development portfolios. Over the years, he thus occupied a range of responsibilities spanning health, education, information technology, finance and development.

After losing the 2021 election, Dr Naqi was set to stage a comeback in the 2026 polls. However, elections in seven constituencies of Poonch division, including his own, were put on hold because of the law and order situation. But luck had something else in store.

As the government formation process was completed on the basis of 46 seats — excluding the seven constituencies of Poonch and Sudhnoti — the top two constitutional offices also went to representatives from other divisions, with the speaker coming from Mirpur and the prime minister from Muzaffarabad.

This led to growing calls for the presidency to go to a representative of Poonch division. Dr Naqi, with his long parliamentary experience and roots in the region, soon emerged as the name around which those calls coalesced.
ir_summary: PML-N's Dr Najeeb Naqi sworn in as president of Azad Jammu and Kashmir after winning assembly election.

title: ‘Washington, Tehran exploring phased way out of war’
text:
WASHINGTON: US and Iranian negotiators in New York are exploring a phased path out of war that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran, sources close to the talks said.

The strait, through which a fifth of the world's oil passes, has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the war. Iran wants relief from a blockade that is strangling its economy; Washington wants free passage restored for ships on the vital oil route that Tehran has kept closed.

Talks are complicated by a familiar diplomatic problem: neither side wants to move first.

Two Iranian sources, two regional officials and two Western diplomats said the most workable option now on the table was a staged arrangement — Iran allowing ships through Hormuz in return for an end to the blockade and, potentially, access to frozen assets.

"One way forward would be to solve the crisis in stages. The first would be to end the blockade and reopen Hormuz," a senior Iranian official said on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

Such a deal would require Donald Trump to accept another interim arrangement, after a previous understanding collapsed in July. The US president has suggested a fuller agreement might only be reached after November's midterm elections. A senior European official said Iranian negotiators arrived in New York "with a very long list of demands".

The White House, for its part, has shown little urgency. "Iran is desperate for a deal, President Trump holds all the cards and will make whatever decision is best for the United States," a White House official said, adding that "crushing sanctions" and "one of the most successful blockades in history" had left Tehran "completely broke".

Trump, the official suggested, was content to let an "inevitable Iranian collapse" continue rather than be rushed into concessions.

Dennis Ross, a former US negotiator, put the chances of a deal before the midterms at roughly 30 per cent, though he noted both sides had reasons to want an agreement sooner rather than later.

"The blockade is what's really squeezing the Iranians. It's strangling them," he said. A pre-election deal could suit Trump too, easing Gulf tensions and helping bring down petrol prices at home. After the vote, Ross said, the president may feel freer to escalate pressure or consider military options.

Tehran, meanwhile, is hedging. Even as it explores a diplomatic exit, Iran is preparing for the possibility of renewed conflict, accusing Washington of using the blockade and the threat of force as instruments of coercion.

"Our fingers are on the trigger," the senior Iranian official said. "The Americans know what they need to do but, because of their excessive demands, the chances of diplomacy resolving this are extremely low."

Regional sources said Iran was prepared to drop, or at least set aside, its demand for transit fees on shipping through Hormuz in order to prioritise ending the blockade.

"Iran is not primarily focused on imposing tolls in Hormuz but on preserving its administrative control of the waterway," the senior official said. "Iran may be willing to defer the toll issue, but they are not going to give up administrative control of the strait."

At the heart of the diplomacy in New York is a fundamental tension. Washington wants pressure to produce concessions, Tehran wants pressure removed before making them, and the Gulf states want the conflict resolved without allowing the region's strategic waterways to become enduring bargaining chips.

In a separate meeting in New York, Gulf leaders pressed Trump for clarity on his strategy beyond the midterms, including whether Washington would resume military action if Iran refused to negotiate.

They made clear their rejection of any Iranian control over Hormuz, insisting freedom of navigation be restored and that the strait must not become a tool of coercion — while also urging de-escalation, reflecting Gulf states' desire to stay out of further confrontation.

"It's still not clear what Trump's endgame is, or what the alternative to the pressure campaign would be," said Ebtessam al-Ketbi, president of the Emirates Policy Center in Abu Dhabi.

"The Iranians, by contrast, know what they want. They're reshaping the regional landscape through Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb with a clear objective, while Washington has yet to define its roadmap."

Alan Eyre, another former US negotiator, warned that the blockade's pressure could backfire: rather than softening its position, he said, Tehran was more likely to escalate, believing that any sign of weakness would prove fatal to the regime.

Adding to the diplomatic pressure, a coalition of 80 countries called at the UN on Thursday for the full restoration of maritime navigation in the Gulf.

"We call for the full restoration of navigational rights and principles without delay," said Bahrain's Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid al-Zayani, reading a joint statement to journalists.

In a further sign of tightening pressure, the United Arab Emirates announced on Thursday that it would no longer accept flights operated by Iranian carriers, aligning itself with US sanctions targeting Iran's aviation sector.

Dubai has long been a key destination for Iranian airlines, serving multiple daily flights and a large Iranian community with close business ties to the emirate.

The UAE's General Civil Aviation Authority said the suspension was "based on the US sanctions imposed on Iranian airlines preventing them from using airports around the world".

The UAE, which was hit by thousands of Iranian missiles and drones early in the war, suspended trade and financial exchanges with Iran last month.

On Wednesday its central bank blocked transactions with Iran's Bank Melli, citing breaches of money-laundering, terrorism-financing and arms-proliferation rules.

One passenger told AFP an Iran Airtour flight from Tehran to Dubai was cancelled shortly before departure on Thursday, after tickets had already been issued.

Washington imposed sanctions on Iran's aviation sector in early September, giving airlines until Wednesday to comply — including by halting the refuelling of Iranian aircraft — or risk being cut off from the dollar-based financial system.

Iran's main carriers were forced to cancel international flights this week as neighbouring states adopted similar restrictions; Turkmenistan turned back a flight from Tehran to Dushanbe on Thursday, an Iranian aviation official said, because it had not authorised the airline to fly.

A handful of smaller Iranian carriers continue to operate abroad, notably to Armenia and to China, which has declined to follow Washington's sanctions.
ir_summary: US and Iran negotiate a phased deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz and lift economic blockade amid ongoing war tensions.

title: Pezeshkian reaffirms pledge to Islamabad MoU: PM
text:
NEW YORK: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has reaffirmed that the Islamabad Memo­randum of Understanding (MoU) remained "totally acceptable" to Iran, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said on Wednesday, adding that Tehran agreed that there was a need to move it forward.

Speaking to the media in New York after his meeting with President Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), the prime minister said the entire Pakistani leadership was united in its resolve to expedite the peace efforts outlined in the Islamabad MoU.

PM Shehbaz said the current situation in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, and the provocative activities taking place there, required brotherly and friendly countries to work together to reduce tensions.

"For this purpose, today I met the Iranian president, had a detailed meeting with him, and told him that restoring peace to the region is the need of the hour, a very important need," he said.

He said Pakistan, as it had done in the past, would continue working for peace with Iran, which he described as a "brotherly" and neighbouring country.

According to PM Shehbaz, President Pezeshkian appreciated Pakistan's efforts and reaffirmed Iran's acceptance of the Islamabad MoU.

"The Iranian president appreciated this and said the Islamabad MoU is still totally acceptable to us and there's a need to move it forward," he said.

The prime minister said Pakistan would continue working with friendly and brotherly countries to help reduce tensions and promote peace in the region.

He also highlighted what he described as close cooperation between Pakistan's political and military leadership, saying that this teamwork was contributing both to diplomatic efforts and economic stability.

"Similarly, the successful efforts we have made on the diplomatic front are the results of this teamwork," he added.

Asked about terrorism, the prime minister said the attacks Pakistan was witnessing were coming from Afghanistan.

He added that terrorists based in Afghanistan had killed Pakistani civilians as well as military and police personnel and that this was "extremely condemnable".

PM Shehbaz said Pakistan was giving a "befitting response" to terrorism and would continue its campaign until the threat was eliminated.

Asked whether he had taken the Iranian president into confidence about the Makkah defence accord, the prime minister said, "Yes, this was discussed, and we did apprise him."

Soon after the prime minister spoke, reporters asked Defence Minister Khawaja Asif whether Iran was on board with the Makkah accord.

He said Pakistan had discussed the agreement with Iran, but Tehran had not yet formally joined it. He added that Iran could join in the future, as several countries had expressed interest.

Member states, he said, were still in the process of setting up the accord's secretariat, after which further details would be discussed.

Earlier, PM Shehbaz met European Council President António Luís Santos da Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on the sidelines of the UNGA and reaffirmed Pakistan's commitment to continued engagement under the GSP+ scheme of the European Union.
