During the meeting, the leaders reviewed the full spectrum of Pakistan-EU relations and expressed satisfaction at the growing momentum in high-level exchanges and engagement between Pakistan and the EU, according to the PMO.

PM Shehbaz underscored the importance of "sustained leadership-level engagement" in providing greater direction and momentum to the relationship.

He reaffirmed Pakistan's commitment to further strengthening its "broad-based partnership" with the European Union and the full implementation of the Pakistan-EU Strategic Engagement Plan.

PM Shehbaz also met with his Bangladeshi counterpart Tarique Rahman, wherein they reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthen bilateral cooperation in multiple sectors including trade, investment, connectivity, education, tourism and people-to-people contacts.

Separately, PM Shehbaz invited Pakistani business personalities and professionals based in the US to invest in Pakistan, assuring them that the government was providing a conducive environment to promote investment and business activities.

The prime minister, while meeting delegations of Pakistani business personalities and professionals associated with information technology, artificial intelligence, automobiles, energy, construction and other sectors, said reforms in the Federal Board of Revenue had helped address the issues faced by the business community.

In a separate meeting with delegations of the US-based Pakistani community and youth, the premier invited them to propose improvements across various sectors and play their full role in the development of Pakistan.

He highlighted that his government was taking all-out measures to empower youth through information technology, artificial intelligence, and modern skills.
ir_summary: Iranian president reaffirms commitment to Islamabad MoU with Pakistan during UNGA meeting, discussing regional peace efforts.

title: Situationer: Déjà vu at D-Chowk?
text:
KHYBER Pakhtunkhwa is on edge again, and not just for the deteriorating security and volatility in the south, which has been bad for quite some time now.

It is the provincial government's avowed single-point agenda to secure its party's chairman's freedom from Adiala jail, or at the very least, get him some relief like shifting him to a private hospital in Islamabad.

But days before 'D-Day', i.e. Sept 27, one cannot help but be struck by an overwhelming sense of déjà vu: this is November 2024 all over again, albeit with some changes to the cast.

Ali Amin Gandapur, the chief minister at the time, who led the long march to D-Chowk, lost the job during his second year in office, allowing a young and relatively inexperienced Sohail Afr­idi to take up the mantle.

One year into his term, the 37-year-old CM Afridi is now playing his biggest political gambit since his foray into politics as a student activist of the PTI's student wing.

There is another change to the cast. Bushra Bibi, the former first lady who led the bloody Nov 24 D-Chowk March, is now serving a jail term in Adiala jail.

And so, the task of securing Imran Khan's release has passed on to another woman — his sister, Aleema Khan. She too, though, has now been taken into custody.

With the planned political onslaught on the federal capital just two days away, the clock is ticking, and worryingly, no one knows where and how this will end.

No one has a clue. Not even those who have planned for this day for months. And neither do the ones who have scrambled to throw in all possible measures to defend and protect Islamabad from yet another onslaught from KP. The stakes are high and everyone with an insight knows it.

The comparisons between the two guards are natural; Ali Amin was an old hack. He knew what he was getting into and would war-game it. But even he couldn't forestall a mob that crossed over into the so-called Red Zone, precipitating violence in a way that was not foreseen.

But Afridi is a relatively new campaigner, carrying the relentless pressure of the party's D-Chowk fiasco. It seems he doesn't know the full breadth of what he is getting into. These are uncharted waters for him and he doesn't have the comfort of many wise counsels.

Even the party's own decision-making system is so diffused that no one is willing to publicly take responsibility for any fallout of the impending march; everyone is looking towards each other.

Mehmood Khan Achakzai and Raja Nasir Abbas, the PTI's current political mentors, are there to lend their support. But any decision, they have made clear, has to come from the PTI itself.

Up until now, no one person knows what the whole plan is. With a crackdown on its leaders and lawmakers underway and authorities in Islamabad putting up several layers of security around the federal capital amid ominous warnings of nasty things to come, the PTI leadership can be under no illusions; this time around would be a different and dangerous gambit.

There are logistical and financial issues as well. A party which had no dearth of resources finds itself struggling to raise money to mobilise its workers and pay for logistics.

Adding to their woes is the unwillingness of private transporters to ferry party supporters, after having suffered huge losses to their vehicles in the Nov 2024 fiasco.

So, what could be the game plan once party workers and supporters are eventually mobilised despite all the difficulties and misgivings?

Stop at Swabi, just short of KP's boundary with the Punjab on the M1 Motorway, and block the many entry points into Punjab?

Stage a sit-in; but for how long? Will it be sustainable? Not just logistically but also politically, given the problems that the blockades would cause to the people, and the food and fuel shortages that these would give rise to?

Or, will the PTI surge ahead, removing all the hurdles and battling police and Rangers to find an opening to enter Islamabad and bring the federal government to its knees, forcing it to accept their demands?

If that is the case, then who will lead the charge? Who will take responsibility in the event of something going terribly wrong? It doesn't take long for a seemingly well-organised ral­ly to turn into a mob; after all, even Ali Amin had not foreseen what would happen when his party workers entered the Red Zone. The risks are too high and everyone knows it — most of all the minders in Islamabad. PTI leaders now say, they are showing signs of panic by barricading their territory, placing containers and digging up roads to make them impassable.

For the federal authorities, the risk of mob violence is too real to ignore. The events of Nov 2024 are still fresh in their memory and they can't afford ano­ther violent confrontation so close to the Red Zone.

Allowing the PTI to stage a sit-in anywhere near Islamabad is a big no-no for them; it was tried and tested, and it failed.

The choices are limited. The PTI cannot afford a repeat of what happened in November 2024. Such an eventuality, they know, will hurt them gravely and might even cost them their government in KP.

It is a suspense thriller, that's for sure. No one kno­ws, neither in Peshawar, nor in Islamabad, how eve­nts will unfold in the days to come.

Most worryingly, though, no one is talking to anyone, and no one knows who will initiate negotiations to end this deadlock. For some strange reason, in the words of a senior PTI lawmaker, they are looking to divine intervention to toss up some middle ground, or face-saving.
ir_summary: PTI-led KP government plans a protest march to Islamabad to demand Imran Khan's release from jail, raising political tensions.

title: PTI ‘still in two minds’ over march plans to Islamabad
text:
ISLAMABAD: A PTI leader on Thursday hinted at the possibility of postponing its protest march if the federal government agreed to hold elections within six to eight months, release party chief Imran Khan and other political prisoners, and investigate May 9 and November 26 crackdowns on the opposition party.

Advocate Naeem Haider Panjutha told Dawn that the protest could be postponed if these three assurances were given by the government.

There was no clarity on where such a proposal originated from, which added to confusion about the PTI's plans for its Sept 27 protest. Party spokesperson Sheikh Waqas Akram, however, denied any such proposal was being discussed at any party forum, saying only Imran Khan could take a decision even if such a proposal was on the table.

"The first and primary condition is that the public mandate be respected and for that free, fair and tran­s­parent elections must be held within six to eight months," Mr Panj­utha said, while demanding a clear guarantee that elections would be held before the end of this financial year.

All political prisoners, including Imran Khan, must be released — not through any deal or political settlement, but through the courts and due process of law, he said, adding that all cases against Imran Khan were "weak".

The third demand was for a judicial inquiry into the events of May 9 and November 26. "If these three demands are fulfilled, the march can be postponed," he said, adding that in case these demands were ignored, the PTI would be "coming with no compromise, no retreat, and no turning back".

On the other hand, Sheikh Waqas Akram told Dawn the above mentioned conditions were shared with the government after the D-Chowk incident, but the government had not responded positively, so the conditions were then withdrawn on the order of Imran Khan. "We have not received any concrete offer from the government side, so the long march will be held come what may. Even if we get an offer, we will demand to arrange a meeting with Imran Khan, as only he can postpone it," he added. Sheikh Waqas said the PTI cannot afford to announce postponement of march, especially when its ministers were being abducted.

In a meeting held at the opposition chamber in the Senate, PTI interim chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan and former senator Mustafa Nawaz Khokhar met Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas and discussed preparations for the planned long march. According to a statement issued by the Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayeen-i-Paki­stan (TTAP), the participants held a detailed discussion on the prevailing situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and growing challenges to provincial autonomy. The meeting also focused on the Sept 27 march, preparations for the event and the strategy to be adopted in the coming days.

Separately, the federal government approved the deployment of Rangers in Islamabad and several districts of Punjab from Sept 20 to Oct 5. "Pursuant to the request made by the chief commissioner, Islamabad Capital Territory … and Home Department, government of Punjab …, the federal government is pleased to authorise deployment of sufficient strength of troops of Pakistan Rangers (Punjab) in ICT and different districts of Punjab province," an interior ministry notification read.

The deployment has been aut­h­orised under Sections 7(b) and 10 of the Pakistan Rangers Ordin­ance, 1959, and Sections 4 and 5 of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997, to perform functions specified under the laws, as authorised by the Islamabad chief commissioner or the provincial government.

"The deployed troops may respond appropriately in self-defence to any threats or violent activities encountered in the course of their duties as per rules/regulations in vogue," the notification stated. The Punjab government also sent a letter to the interior ministry requesting mobile and internet services at specific locations in Rawalpindi and Attock to be downgraded or jam­med on Sept 27.
ir_summary: PTI considers postponing protest march if government meets demands for elections, prisoner releases, and investigations.
